items.title: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
items.summary: Wreaths are laid as 10,000 armed forces veterans, including 12 from World War Two, pay tribute in central London.

scraped.title: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
scraped.description: Wreaths are laid as 10,000 armed forces veterans, including 12 from World War Two, pay tribute in central London.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

The King led the Royal Family and political leaders in the Remembrance Service in London

King Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.

On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.

That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".

Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.

And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath at the Cenotaph

Queen Camilla and Catherine, Princess of Wales, watched the event from the balcony of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office

The Prince of Wales and the Princess Royal were among royals in attendance, along with military chiefs, senior politicians, diplomats and faith leaders, watched by big crowds squeezed behind railings along Whitehall.

Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales watched from a balcony above the Cenotaph in the Foreign Office.

Among the flags on the roof of that Whitehall building was the Ukrainian blue and yellow. It went up when Russia invaded and four years later it is now visibly frayed - a reminder of the length of that war and of current threats.

At 11:00 GMT, as the first strike of Big Ben echoed from the nearby Houses of Parliament, the big two-minute silence filled the usually frenetic streets, before the playing of the Last Post.

The King had his eyes closed, the crowds in Whitehall stopped for their own thoughts, in a rare moment of calm in the capital.

Veterans arrived at Whitehall ahead of the service

The poignant parade past the Cenotaph included representatives of about 340 different military and civilian groups, from the Royal Naval Association and the Royal Marines Association to Transport for London and the Royal National Lifeboat Institute.

Alongside those marching were flotillas of disability scooters and families helping veterans in wheelchairs.

Those who took part in WW2 are now increasingly frail - and there were 12 participants in the march-past compared to 20 last year. The oldest participant this year was aged 105.

"In everlasting remembrance" the King wrote on the wreath he laid at the Cenotaph

Annie Duplock had joined the Land Army at the age of 16

Taking part for the first time was 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who had been part of the Land Army that had helped to feed the country at war.

She had joined the Land Army in 1940 as a 16-year-old, having lied about her age, and worked on a farm in Leicestershire.

"I feel very honoured to be taking part in the parade and to represent the Land Girls. I'm very excited, although a little apprehensive as I don't quite know what to expect," she said.

"I think it will be a very emotional day, bringing back memories of all those who didn't return home. It will be lovely to be there and remember them."

(Top left to bottom right) former Prime Ministers Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson, Theresa May, Lord Cameron, Gordon Brown, Sir Tony Blair and Sir John Major

Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally led those gathered at the Cenotaph in prayer

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the annual event was a time to "reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others".

He earlier announced that he wanted to tackle the problem of homelessness among ex-service personnel to "ensure that any veteran sleeping rough is offered appropriate accommodation before Christmas".

Mark Atkinson, the director general of the Royal British Legion, said: "As we come together on Remembrance Sunday, we pay tribute to all those who have served and sacrificed, from generations past to those still serving today."

Remembrance events took place across the country as thousands gathered to pay their respects to those who died in past conflicts.

First Minister of Scotland John Swinney placed a wreath at the Stone of Remembrance outside the City Chambers during an event in Edinburgh.

Veterans, military personnel and cadets also marched through the centres of British cities such as Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds.

A silent poppy drop was held as part of the Festival of Remembrance at Durham Cathedral while wreaths were laid at Canterbury Cathedral.

For more than a century, this national Remembrance event has been held around the Cenotaph.

The monument was built as a focal point for honouring those who had fought and died in World War One, including those who had no grave, and as a place to mourn for those families who might not be able to visit war cemeteries overseas.

The word "cenotaph" means "empty tomb" in Greek and it was designed by the architect Sir Edwin Lutyens in a simple, austere style, with no sense of triumphalism and with almost no decoration.

The monument had been originally built in 1919 as a temporary, plaster and wood structure. But it proved so popular with the public that it was replaced in 1920 with a permanent version, in the same design but in stone.

It was opened at 11:00 on 11 November 1920 by King George V. His great-grandson, Charles, was there again, on an overcast morning 106 years later, to continue paying respect.

items.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
items.summary: Several carriages derailed after two trains travelling in the same direction crashed outside the city of Giza.

scraped.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
scraped.description: Several carriages derailed after two trains travelling in the same direction crashed outside the city of Giza.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in Egypt

At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.

The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.

Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.

Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".

The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.

Uninjured passengers and passersby searched derailed carriages for injured people

The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.

Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.

The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.

The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.

Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.

Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains.

The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.

The train continued for around nine kilometres (5.6 miles) before coming to a halt.

In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.

Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.

There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt.

Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them.

One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south.

It is yet unclear what caused the accident but Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said an investigation was underway and would "hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence".

scraped.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
scraped.description: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 30 miles from Cairo
scraped.author: Associated Press
scraped.h1: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
scraped.body_text:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 30 miles from Cairo

Seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles south of Cairo, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. He said some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

scraped.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
scraped.description: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives
scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/chris-osuh
scraped.h1: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
scraped.body_text:
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester .

See My World , a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations .

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

scraped.title: No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks
scraped.description: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who will lead a caretaker government while negotiations take place, said: "I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks".
scraped.h1: No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks
scraped.body_text:
By

The Associated Press

New Zealand Prime Minister and National Party leader, Christopher Luxon addresses party faithful in Auckland, New Zealand, Saturday, Nov.7, 2026. Alex Robertson/AP hide caption

WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday's election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.

The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon's center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday's numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour.

The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand's economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins, chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government.

Wong's pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on Saturday's results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago.

Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, "who won the election 2026" was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won't begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they've won.

With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon's National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn't claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power.

Speaking to reporters Sunday, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand's trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters' rancor over living costs.

Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn't appear to benefit on Saturday. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect.

Electoral officials were due on Sunday to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks.

Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can't be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote.

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins addresses party faithful in Upper Hutt, New Zealand, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Mark Tantrum/AP hide caption

"I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached.

Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, Saturday night was bleak for his party.

Several of National's most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party's traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing.

Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience.

The Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong poses for a portrait outside Parliament in Wellington, New Zealand, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP hide caption

New Zealanders don't vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative.

The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand's direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years.

National won just 29.21% of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separateconfidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.

However, Labour also won just 29.36% of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races.

Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.

The total number of seats in New Zealand's Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority.

Luxon's conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.

Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc's seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern.

Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

items.title: After a successful trip to Uruguay, Pope Leo heads to Argentina

scraped.title: After a successful trip to Uruguay, Pope Leo heads to Argentina
scraped.description: On Sunday, tens of thousands packed the main square in Florida, Uruguay, to watch Pope Leo speak.
scraped.h1: After a successful trip to Uruguay, Pope Leo heads to Argentina
scraped.body_text:
By

The Associated Press

Pope Leo XIV plays with a child as he arrived at the square outside the Cathedral Basilica of Florida, Uruguay, the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Thirty-Three, to preside over Mass on the third day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Andrew Medichini/AP hide caption

FLORIDA, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV wrapped up his visit to Uruguay on Sunday by praising the women who have passed the Catholic faith onto younger generations, as he highlighted the role the church has played since the founding of Latin America's most secular country.

Leo traveled to the city of Florida, north of Montevideo, to mark an important Catholic feast day before heading to Argentina for the second leg of his South American tour. It's expected to be the most politically delicate stop, given the Catholic Church's sharp criticisms of the austerity program of libertarian President Javier Milei.

For his final event in Uruguay, Leo celebrated the feast of the Virgin of the Thirty-three. According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in Florida on Aug. 25, 1825.

Leo became the first pope in nearly four decades to visit Uruguay, in hopes of reminding its people that the Catholic Church is part of their very identity as a nation — even if, in subsequent decades, the country went on a deeply secular, and at times anticlerical, route.

In his homily, delivered in front of Florida's cathedral, Leo recalled the presence of the statue at the time of independence in reminding Uruguayans that "the history of peoples, too, cannot be fully understood without reference to God," and especially a mother.

He thanked all the mothers and grandmothers who have passed the faith onto younger generations, and acknowledged their pain when their efforts didn't stick.

"You taught your children to pray, and today they no longer do so. You used to attend Mass together, and it has been years since they entered a church," he said. But he urged them to not despair.

"Mothers and grandmothers: never tire of passing on the faith!"

Tens of thousands of people packed Florida's main square for the Mass under brilliant blue skies, some walking for several kilometers (miles) to reach the site. The city has a population of about 40,000 but the Vatican estimated 50,000 were on hand.

Fiama Pirez, an English professor, traveled from Montevideo for the Mass even though she could have seen Leo in the capital. She said she preferred a family outing to Florida so her mother could fulfill a dream to see a pope.

"I'm religious in my own way, and although I never strayed far from the Catholic faith, I'm rediscovering it today," she said.

Pope Leo XIV is cheered by faithful as he arrives for a prayer vigil at Centenario Stadium in Montevideo, on the second day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Andrew Medichini/AP hide caption

In Buenos Aires, Milei is due to greet Leo at the airport before the two appear together for the traditional welcome ceremony and exchange of speeches. The Catholic Church has criticized Milei's austerity measures that have slashed social spending, and his embrace of artificial intelligence.

Milei has staked his presidency on cutting social spending to overhaul Argentina's troubled economy and deliver a long-elusive budget surplus. He has called social justice "an aberration" that amounts to stealing, and mocked as "huge stupidity" the increasingly common complaint in Argentina that families squeezed by his austerity program can't make it to the end of the month.

Leo, who took his name from the 19th-century pope whose encyclical on labor laid the foundation of Catholic social teaching, has made the poor and vulnerable a focus of his papacy, carrying on the legacy of his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis.

Posters reading "At last, a Lion who unites" appeared across Buenos Aires this weekend, a jab playing on the pope's name in Spanish — León, or lion — and the lion imagery Milei often uses to portray himself on social media.

"Argentina is a society currently experiencing significant upheaval, deep polarization, and an economic crisis, along with a president who defies conventional protocol — a leader who, at one point, even challenged Pope Francis," said Luis Bahamondes, a professor at the Center for Judaic Studies at the University of Chile.

Since taking office in December 2023, Milei has slashed Argentina's healthcare budget by 48% in real terms. Planned cuts to the public university system, which represents a near-universal point of pride in the crisis-prone country, sent students into the streets.

According to official data, poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of the population during the first half of 2026, representing about 15 million people.

Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts as part of a necessary reform process to remake Argentina's troubled economy and eliminate fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy.

Like Trump, Milei has also courted AI investment and data centers with promises of limited regulation. Leo has warned that the AI race poses threats to humanity and the environment and called for strict, internationally policed safeguards on its development.

Milei's government insists the papal trip is purely religious. "The pope belongs to all Argentines. He doesn't belong to a political party or a political camp," Karina Milei, the president's sister and secretary-general of the presidency, told reporters after a recent planning meeting for Leo's visit with church leaders.

In Argentina, Leo is completing unfinished business left by Francis. The Argentine Jesuit, the former archbishop of Buenos Aires, never returned home during his 12-year pontificate, confounding friends and foes alike.

"There's a lot of disagreement over Francis and his legacy in Argentina," said David Lantigua, a theology professor and faculty fellow at the University of Notre Dame's Kellogg Institute, which focuses especially on Latin American affairs.

Much of the polemics stems from his tenure in Buenos Aires, when the former Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio was a slum priest who advocated for the poorest and most marginalized — the sector of Argentines feeling Milei's social spending cuts the most.

"I think we'll see that kind of tension with Leo — that's the ministry Francis left behind," Lantigua said.

Leo, who spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru ministering to poor people, is very much a pastor in Francis' image and owes his pontificate to the late pope. But unlike Francis, he is returning home to Peru on the last leg of this trip, visiting a country where he spent two decades as a missionary.

Argentina's state intelligence agency said Saturday that a person had been arrested over death threats against Leo ahead of his arrival. A federal court in Campana, some 70 kilometers (45 miles) northwest of Buenos Aires, ordered the arrest less than 24 hours after the agency was tipped off, it said, without elaborating.

items.title: Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault
items.summary: Comedian Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday. Comedian Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.(Image credit: Alastair Grant)

scraped.title: Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault
scraped.description: Comedian Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.
scraped.h1: Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault
scraped.body_text:
By

Kate Bartlett

Comedian and actor Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court in London, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Alastair Grant/AP hide caption

Comedian Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.

On Thursday the one-time MTV host turned Christian and spiritual influencer was found guilty on three counts of sexual assault and one of rape, after a four-week trial that garnered massive media attention.

Brand had denied all charges and said he never had sex without consent.

After the jury handed down the verdict, Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand, 51, that he faced a "significant custodial term."

Danny Shaw, a crime commentator and former BBC correspondent, posted on X that while the maximum sentence for rape in the UK is life, 10 years is the average sentence, and Brand was likely to receive between four to 13 years of prison time.

The trial examined seven historic charges against Brand, brought forward by six different women. He was found guilty on four of the charges: for raping a woman who'd been to one of his comedy shows in 2009, and sexually assaulting three others between 2004 and 2009. The locations of the sexual assaults were a bar, radio station and TV studio. Brand was also found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand's lawyer asked the judge on Thursday to grant his client bail so that he could spend the weekend with his three children, which the judge denied. Instead the one-time celebrity darling spent his first weekend in a prison cell in London.

He showed little emotion when the verdict was handed down, though his wife Laura — who has supported him throughout — quickly left the courtroom.

Many have called the verdict a significant milestone in the #MeToo movement, which has seen influential men held to account for using their power to abuse women.

Brand has also faced allegations of crimes in the United States. In 2023, a woman, named only as "Jane Doe," accused Brand of sexually assaulting her while she was working as a film extra during the making of the 2010 comedy movie "Arthur." That year, Brand married pop star Katy Perry, though the union lasted for just over a year before they divorced.

Addressing the media last week, London police detective Andy Furphy said that Brand had "used his influence, status and fame to prey on women — as his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."

Camilla Long, a journalist for The Sunday Times — one of the first newspapers that investigated allegations of abuse against Brand — wrote in a column this weekend that "To sit in court 3 at Southwark crown court, hearing how Brand grabbed, pushed, groped and degraded his victims, was one of the most disgusting experiences of my life."

Long questioned how Brand got away with his behavior for so long, saying: "Never has a predator so loudly declared himself, yet been so roundly ignored."

scraped.title: Detroit Lions wear Jack Campbell jerseys ahead of Miami Dolphins game to honor injured teammate
scraped.description: Detroit Lions players wore Jack Campbell jerseys arriving for the Miami Dolphins game, rallying around their injured linebacker one week after his neck injury.
scraped.author: Armando Salguero
scraped.h1: Detroit Lions wear Jack Campbell jerseys ahead of Miami Dolphins game to honor injured teammate
scraped.body_text:
Dr. Stephanie Widmer joins ‘America’s Newsroom’ to examine Jack Campbell’s neck injury and recovery, the risks of CTE among NFL players and the tragic death of 24-year-old New York City Marathon runner Rachel Apa.

The Detroit Lions have gone from crying about Jack Campbell to using the unfortunate injury to their linebacker and defensive team captain as part of their culture for the remainder of the 2026 season.

One week after Campbell was removed on an immobilization stretcher and cart from the field during the game against the Minnesota Vikings , the Lions are reporting for work in South Florida for the game against the Miami Dolphins wearing Campbell jerseys.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

About half-a-dozen players wore Campbell's No. 46 jersey to the game.

AWFUL SCENE AS LEO CHANEL SUFFERS NECK INJURY, MARKING SECOND STRAIGHT WEEK WASHINGTON COMMANDERS SUFFER SCARE

Even some players who did not wear the Campbell jersey paid tribute to their teammate somehow.

Aidan Hutchinson carried the gallon jug marked "Jack" into the stadium as a tribute to his fallen teammate.

Hutchinson was in some ways the face of how the Lions reacted when Campbell suffered a serious neck injury during Detroit’s victory over Minnesota last Sunday.

Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell is injured against the Minnesota Vikings during the second half of an NFL game Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Rey Del Rio)

The edge rusher was seen crying as trainers and doctors attended to Campbell as he lay motionless on the turf.

TEARS FROM TEAMMATES AS IMMOBILIZED DETROIT LIONS LINEBACKER JACK CAMPBELL CARTED OFF FIELD AND HOSPITALIZED

This week has been about "playing like 46," for the Lions.

"This is for him, man," fellow linebacker Derrick Barnes told reporters. "One of our keys to victory is preparing to play like No. 46.

"Jack's a fighter, we all know Jack. Knowing Jack, he wants us to keep going throughout our day. That's why we all love Jack. To hear that from coach (Wednesday) morning was awesome."

Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell is taken off the field due to injury against the Minnesota Vikings during the second half of an NFL game Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

One of the people wearing No. 46 jerseys on Sunday was defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard, who explained what it means to prepare and play like Campbell .

"Every meeting I told the unit, every walkthrough, every play, you all know how Jack prepares. You all know how he plays," Sheppard said. "The way you honor him is to wipe those tears from your eyes and make sure we prepare and play like him."

Trainers tend to Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell after an injury during the fourth quarter against the Minnesota Vikings at Ford Field in Detroit, Mich., on Nov. 1, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Campbell has full movement in his lower body and is making progress on trying to regain full mobility to his upper body, according to the statement he issued Wednesday.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

scraped.title: Philip Rivers finalizing agreement to return to NC State as Wolfpack’s new head coach in remarkable move
scraped.description: Philip Rivers appears poised to take the NC State football head coaching job at his alma mater. NIL fundraising and transfer portal resources were key parts of negotiations.
scraped.author: Trey Wallace
scraped.h1: Philip Rivers finalizing agreement to return to NC State as Wolfpack’s new head coach in remarkable move
scraped.body_text:
"There are no dominant teams in college football. There's no juggernaut out there. Like this time a year ago, you really could tell Indiana was legitimate, that they were a powerhouse."

After N.C. State officials made the trek to Fairhope, Alabama earlier this week to formally meet with Philip Rivers , the former Wolfpack and NFL quarterback appears to be set to take the head coaching position at his alma mater.

The two sides are finalizing an agreement that is expected to be hammered out over the next 24 hours, sources told OutKick. The board of trustees at N.C. State have a meeting this coming week to approve the contract.

Conversations about Rivers taking the job in Raleigh had picked up after the school announced that Dave Doeren had been fired nearly two weeks ago.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Following a series of informal discussions with major donors about what it would take to make N.C. State competitive in the current era of college athletics, several Wolfpack boosters put a plan in motion to provide Rivers with the resources needed to hit the ground running.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

By the end of the week, all that was needed was pen to paper for the NC State alum.

But first, Rivers was going to finish his job as head coach of St. Michael Catholic in the Alabama high school football playoffs. His season came to an end on Friday night in Fairhope, as they lost in the opening round.

Phillip Rivers of the North Carolina State Wolfpack throws a pass against the Maryland Terrapins at Byrd Stadium in College Park, Md., on Nov. 9, 2002. (Getty Images)

According to multiple sources, Rivers had already begun putting together a coaching and front office staff for when he formally accepted the job offer and signed a contract.

On Friday night, Rivers was coaching St. Michael Catholic in their Alabama high school playoff game, where his son Gunner also plays. In addition to the intrigue of coaching for the first time in college, Gunner is also committed to NC State and will enroll in January to start his own collegiate career.

One of the biggest points of emphasis for Rivers taking the job in Raleigh was that he would be given enough money to work with for a veteran coaching staff, given that this will be his first college job.

Sources tell OutKick that one of his contract asks was that he be given a big enough pool of money to attract assistant coaches with college experience that would be open to making a move to Raleigh.

Former NC State quarterback Philip Rivers attends the game between the North Carolina Tar Heels and the NC State Wolfpack at Carter-Finley Stadium in Raleigh, N.C., on Nov. 29, 2025. (Getty Images)

Also, having the NIL resources outside of the revenue-sharing that schools participate in was a key part of negotiations for NC State athletic director Boo Corrigan landing the former NFL quarterback.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S JERRY JONES? TEXAS TECH BOOSTER CODY CAMPBELL DEMANDS RETURN ON INVESTMENT

From a fan perspective, it's obvious that the Wolfpack would be making a hire that would excite the base, and more importantly help sell tickets and also lead to an influx of donations needed to help fund rosters in the future.

This is seen as a win-win for both sides, given that this would obviously be an interesting splash around college football, especially in recruiting players who are familiar with the new head coach.

But there is also the obvious fact that players are going to go where the money leads them, though that's clearly not the case for every player.

Still, putting together a formidable roster that can compete in the ACC and subsequently for a spot in the upcoming expanded College Football Playoff is key to making sure this hire doesn’t turn into a dud over the next few years.

NICK SABAN SPEAKS TRUTH ON CFP EXPANSION: ‘THERE’S NOT 24 TEAMS’ THAT CAN WIN A NATIONAL TITLE, BUT MONEY WINS

We have seen countless coordinators in the college ranks receive their first shot at a head coaching job and watch it turn into chaos; just look at what is taking place with Tosh Lupoi at Cal this season, where general manager Ron Rivera is already sounding the alarms.

But, for a high school coach to be given an opportunity to start their collegiate career at the top, and especially at a school like NC State, goes to show you how much Wolfpack officials think about Rivers.

Philip Rivers No. 17 of the Indianapolis Colts walks off the field at halftime against the San Francisco 49ers at Lucas Oil Stadium on Dec. 22, 2025, in Indianapolis, Ind. (Getty Images)

Now, the donors who have promised Rivers with the funds needed to compete will be tasked with making sure he can attack the transfer portal to add players to this NC State roster so that he can hit the ground running for the 2027 season.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

This will be an interesting situation to watch unfold over the next few months, with NC State fans expecting this team to once again start competing for ACC titles on a yearly basis.

Welcome to college football, Philip Rivers.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

items.title: The week of the backup QB in the NFL kicks off as Sanders, Milton, Minshew, Lock, and Wentz start
items.summary: Five NFL backup quarterbacks start in Week 9, with Shedeur Sanders, Carson Wentz, and Drew Lock all stepping in for playoff-contending teams. It is the week of the backup quarterback around the NFL and by the time we're done, we could come to understand why the quarterback-driven league is, for some teams, a backup-quarterback-driven week.Five backup quarterbacks are starting for their teams in Week 9, with three of those players thrust into the starting job on teams with playoff expectations...

scraped.title: The week of the backup QB in the NFL kicks off as Sanders, Milton, Minshew, Lock, and Wentz start
scraped.description: Five NFL backup quarterbacks start in Week 9, including Shedeur Sanders, Drew Lock, Carson Wentz, Gardner Minshew and Joe Milton on teams navigating injuries and playoff races.
scraped.author: Armando Salguero
scraped.h1: The week of the backup QB in the NFL kicks off as Sanders, Milton, Minshew, Lock, and Wentz start
scraped.body_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-7, and Nick Wright has called them the "biggest disappointment in NFL history." Chris Broussard and Kevin Wildes discuss this take and ask if it’s valid, and they discuss Shedeur Sanders being in line to start for the Cleveland Browns as Deshaun Watson is in concussion protocol.

It is the week of the backup quarterback around the NFL and by the time we're done, we could come to understand why the quarterback-driven league is, for some teams, a backup-quarterback-driven week.

Five backup quarterbacks are starting for their teams in Week 9, with three of those players thrust into the starting job on teams with playoff expectations.

MINNESOTA VIKINGS' SOFT BENCHING OF KYLER MURRAY LEADS TO CARSON WENTZ TAKING OVER AS NEW STARTING QB

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Arizona Cardinals quarterback Gardner Minshew II is sacked by Dallas Cowboys linebacker Tyrus Wheat and defensive tackle Lt. Overton in the first half at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Aug. 22, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

This is the week Shedeur Sanders starts for Deshaun Watson with the Cleveland Browns, Drew Lock starts instead of Sam Darnold for the Seattle Seahawks, Carson Wentz starts for Kyler Murray with the Minnesota Vikings – all playing on teams in thick of a playoff hunt.

The situation is probably different for the Arizona Cardinals, who are starting Gardner Minshew, and the Philadelphia Eagles, who are turning to Joe Milton because both those teams are currently outside the playoff picture and indeed under .500.

So here's the breakdown of five new starters and what is at stake:

Minshew's last start before this week was Oct. 6, 2024, with the Raiders, and unlike most of the others in this group, he has already been given a chance to extend his tenure beyond this game.

Tanner McKee and Joe Milton of the Philadelphia Eagles look on before the game against the Carolina Panthers at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pa., on Oct. 18, 2026. (Getty Images)

EAGLES' JALEN HURTS PLACED ON INJURED RESERVE AFTER SUPERFICIAL BLOOD CLOT FOUND IN HIS CALF AREA

This will be Milton’s first NFL start, and while the Eagles have not committed beyond this game, Hurts’ season-ending injury gives Milton a legitimate opportunity to keep the job if he plays well.

Minnesota Vikings quarterback Carson Wentz (11) drops back to pass against the Los Angeles Chargers during the first half at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, on Oct. 23, 2025. (Gary A. Vasquez/Imagn Images)

Lock’s most recent start was Sept. 20 against Arizona, when he threw for 235 yards and three touchdowns. Darnold is expected to reclaim the job when healthy.

Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders throws a pass to tight end Carsen Ryan during the first half against the Buffalo Bills at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, Ohio, on Aug. 22, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Sanders last started an NFL regular season game on Jan. 4, 2026, in the Browns’ 20-18 victory over Cincinnati, the seventh of his 2025 rookie season.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Sanders is not expected to take the starting job from Watson although playing well opens the door for him to be considered more of an option if Watson suddenly reverts to the type of play that made him something of an enigma in Cleveland before the 2026 season.

The biggest opportunity of the week is sitting there for Wentz. He has thrown 5 TD passes in 101 snaps for the Vikings this year.

Murray, meanwhile, has been inconsistent and thrown 6 TDs in over 300 snaps.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

scraped.body_text:
For You

Settings

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I hope one of the first things that the Congress does is to stop these Medicaid cuts, stop the SNAP cuts, roll back the cuts, the effective cuts in the Affordable Care Act,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday.

Shapiro noted that in Pennsylvania alone, 510,000 people are losing healthcare and 143,000 more are losing SNAP or food assistance due to cuts approved during President Donald Trump’s second term.

“In general, though, I think Democrats need to have an aggressive agenda that cuts costs, that ends the war, that gets put on the president’s desk,” he said. “Hopefully, he will sign it because it’ll be common-sense stuff that makes people’s lives better.”

Trump has said that he intends to work with Democrats when Congress begins its new term, though he has also touted a new “VETO”-branded hat since Republicans lost the majority in the midterm elections.

Shapiro said that if Trump chooses to veto Democrats’ legislation, “it’s yet another signal to the American people the president actually doesn’t care about their well-being.”

While the governor stressed the importance of revitalizing Medicaid and SNAP programs, he also said Democrats shouldn’t forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I think the Congress needs to be responsive to where voters are on corruption, and there has to be real accountability for this administration,” Shapiro said, adding that Democrats need to “walk and chew gum at the same time” to pass effective legislation and also “have real accountability for the corruption that exists in Washington.”

“It can’t be either/or,” he said. “It has to be both/and.”

Shapiro added that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker of the House, “has made very clear that both are going to be on the agenda for the first 100 days and for these next two years.”

The governor said that he doesn’t think Democrats should be thinking about the 2028 elections yet. Instead, “we should be thinking about how to make people’s lives better in 2027,” he said.

“It’s incumbent upon the Congress to now do that, and it’s incumbent upon governors now to continue to lead the way in our states,” Shapiro said.

Shapiro, who has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, did not commit to running.

Asked whether he is more likely to run than not, Shapiro answered that his focus was on “figuring how we advance policies like raising the minimum wage and many other things that have been blocked by Republicans,” as Pennsylvania Democrats won a majority in the state legislature Tuesday.

He also did not directly answer whether he was committed to serving his full four-year term.

“Well, I committed to run for governor, and that’s the work I’m focused on doing,” Shapiro said. “And if I’ve got something to say about my future, I’d love to come back on your show and talk about it.”

Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

items.title: Transcript: Sen. Elizabeth Warren on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
items.summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.

scraped.title: Transcript: Sen. Elizabeth Warren on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
scraped.description: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.
scraped.h1: Transcript: Sen. Elizabeth Warren on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 8, 2026 / 1:12 PM EST / CBS News

The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We go now to Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren, the expected incoming Senate Banking Committee Chair, and she joins us from Cambridge. Good morning to you, Senator.

SEN. ELIZABETH WARREN: Good morning.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you have written an outline here, an op-ed about what it's going to look like with Democrats in the majority. You said Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who are unafraid to call out corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the expense of everyone else. That has echoes of President Trump's populist economic message. Not what he said there, of course, but certainly what he has said to voters again and again. What specific policies do you think you can work with him on?

SEN. WARREN: Look, President Trump himself said that he wants to reduce interest rates on credit cards to 10%. I got the bill, I'm ready to go. President Trump says he wants to do more on housing. We're ready. We have the bills ready to go. And besides that, we got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure that people have access to health care. We have a lot of work lined out that we can do. In fact, one of the best parts of this election was how many Democrats stood up and didn't just say, "I'm for the middle class." They said, "Here, I understand what is broken. Here are my specific plans to fix it, and I am committed to doing that." So you end up with this situation where, in Michigan and Texas, you've got the candidates saying the same thing, break up big medicine. You end up with a situation where in Kansas and in South Carolina, you've got the Democratic candidates saying, "We love that road to housing bill, but we want to go bolder, bigger, more housing." Situation where in North Carolina and Alaska, we've got candidates saying, "Hey, we need to break up the grocery monopolies--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN:--and stop price gouging." Iowa and Maine, where- where the Senate candidates there said "We're going to shore up Social Security and make billionaires pay their fair share," and you know, Margaret, those may sound like lots of different pieces.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SEN. WARREN: They're not. They're all about economic power--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--

SEN. WARREN: --and people have told us that's what they want, and we've got the team to deliver now.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I mean, I don't have to tell you it's different to campaign than it is to actually legislate. But President Trump has said he does want to work with Democrats on a few things here: immigration, tax cuts- or cuts, or quote "maybe certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient, a lot of economic development initiatives." Does that track with your expectations of how this White House will be able to work with you, run by Stephen Miller and of course President Trump?

SEN. WARREN: Look, let's- let's be clear. The American people are the ones who've really set the agenda here. They're the ones who have told us what they wanted. They didn't just tell Democrats. They delivered a message to the Republicans--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN:--pretty loud and clear. And I just follow through on what happened in the- just this last summer. We put together a bipartisan housing bill that is going to expand the supply of housing and help bring down the cost of housing, and for the first time ever in American history--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN: --going to ban private equity. Donald Trump didn't even sign the damn thing, and yet it is now law. We got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be part of it or not.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you got a veto-proof majority on that particular bill, that's going to be perhaps more challenging. You have said you want to bring big tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations who may have broken the law to face consequences. To be clear, is your focus going to be legislation or is it going to be investigation?

SEN. WARREN: Look, we- we have to do both. But I do want to be clear: if you've been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you better get ready for some investigations, serious ones.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Who do you have in mind there when you say that?

SEN. WARREN: Anyone who's been cheating. That's what investigations are all about.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so you don't have a list of people you plan to subpoena yet. You- even though you're going to be in this chair?

SEN. WARREN: We- I- it is important that we go through the steps--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

SEN. WARREN: --for investigation because look, the American people are just damn sick of this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--

SEN. WARREN: They are sick of a White House that wouldn't enforce the laws even when they got cheated. They are sick of a White House that dropped investigations that said, "Oh, if you make a nice contribution to Donald Trump's ballroom--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN: --then there won't be any enforcement of the law when you've cheated millions of American customers."

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--

SEN. WARREN: That has to end.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Under- and we saw that in the polling, a concern about corruption. Senator Chris Coons, who is slated to take over Senate Foreign Relations in the new Congress, has said he wants questions answered about- it appears to be Nvidia, the chip maker, and its CEO Jensen Huang--

SEN. WARREN: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The New York Times says he may have had a close relationship with a spy from China. Is there anything you can tell us about that? Is AI going to be a focus for you, and specifically this tech- this chip maker?

SEN. WARREN: Well, on the chip maker specifically, you know, this is an issue where we have actually substantial bipartisan support in the Banking Committee. We've got- we've got Republicans and Democrats. I'm on bipartisan bills in order to- to put more restraints on the ability to export our chips to China.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN: In fact, we have worked on a bipartisan basis to try to stop Donald Trump from encouraging Nvidia, permitting Nvidia to send these chips to China, and now we're seeing some of the consequences of that. So, we've got a lot of places where work needs to be done and a lot of different avenues to do it, but the central part is going to be lowering costs for families and rooting out the corruption. It's- it's not a long agenda.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, one of the things Democrats promised was to end the war with Iran. There are a few more weeks left in this Republican--

SEN. WARREN: Yeah.

MARGARET BRENNAN: --majority. You sit on the Armed Services Committee. There are senators like Senators Bennet and Senator Mark Kelly who have said something to the effect of Democrats should cut off funding for White House operations in order to pressure President Trump to end the war. There are people in the House making noise like that. I mean, what does this look like? Are we looking at cutting off all government funding? Are we looking at a government shutdown in the next few weeks?

SEN. WARREN: Look, the pressure is building to end this war. People have told us they want us to stop the war, a war that is illegal, that is halfway around the world, that to this day, the Trump administration can't explain what their goals are, and what their exit ramp looks like. They want us to stop it. They want us not to spend money over there. They want to be able to buy gasoline and heating oil fuel because they want this economy to work again. The way I think of this is the wind is at our backs to end this war, we got a lot of different tools on the table to get this done--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Leverage, you mean?

SEN. WARREN: This is a democracy, and- yes, and the American people have spoken, and it is time to listen to the American people. Democrats are ready to fight for that, and we invite the Republicans to join us.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will watch for what that looks like. Senator Elizabeth Warren, thank you for joining us today. Face the Nation will be back in one minute. Stay with us.
