scraped.title: Live Updates: Iran downplays new U.S. task force aimed at disrupting ground transport routes
scraped.description: The U.S. did not say whether any military action would be involved in preventing weapons technology or sanctioned items from entering Iran.
scraped.h1: Live Updates: Iran downplays new U.S. task force aimed at disrupting ground transport routes
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 8, 2026 / 1:01 PM EST / CBS News

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that it's "time for the White House to make its own [choice]" about how to proceed as negotiations to end the war stretch on into a fifth week.

"American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own," Araghchi said in a social media post.

"Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results," the post continued. "Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell."

Araghchi previously said that, during mediated, indirect talks with the U.S., Iran had presented a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. agreed to certain conditions.

Yemen's Houthis on Sunday claimed responsibility for an attack on the financial district of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, which witnesses said caused damage to a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Aramco. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis had said earlier Sunday that its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions.

In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Iran-backed group carried out four military operations using ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones. Saree said the Riyadh airport was targeted in addition to the financial center, Aramco oil storage tanks, and the eastern Saudi city of Abqaiq.

He said the Houthis were responding to attacks in recent days on a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and at a market in southwestern Yemen, which he said left dozens dead or wounded and blamed on Saudi Arabia.

Aramco facilities and infrastructure have been repeatedly struck by the Houthis in recent months, with tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company headquarters all targeted by the group.

"Aramco tower in KAFD has been targeted, that's the sure thing," one witness told AFP, referring to the King Abdullah Financial District. Two other witnesses confirmed seeing damage to the building.

One witness in the area of the Aramco skyscraper told AFP they saw a projectile strike the building but they were unsure what type of projectile it was.

The Saudi Energy Ministry said there were no casualties at the Aramco facility.

AP/AFP

Israel's defense minister hinted at a resuming attacks on Iran on Sunday, saying the "mission is not complete."

"With regard to Iran, the mission is still not complete. Iran is trying to renew its efforts to obtain nuclear weapons -- alongside other grave efforts that place the State of Israel in real danger," Israel Katz said.

He also warned the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon to not join Tehran in retaliating against Israel.

"We will not withdraw from the security zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and if the terrorist organisation Hezbollah chooses to join Iran in an attack on Israel, it will suffer extremely severe blows," Katz said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose political bloc failed to reach a majority in the country's elections, has previously suggested he wants to resume attacks on Iran.

However, on the eve of the midterm elections President Trump told the Financial Times newspaper he had no plans to strike Iran.

CBS/AFP

Witnesses in the Saudi capital of Riyadh said they heard a loud explosion Sunday morning and described damage across multiple floors of an Aramco building in the King Abdullah Financial District Some floors appeared to be heavily damaged.

The witnesses spoke on condition of anonymity because of security concerns.

The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions early Sunday, accusing the Houthis of launching the weapons.

The Saudi Energy Ministry said the attempted attack resulted in "falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building." It added that there were no casualties.

CBS/AP

Iran's military has dismissed the U.S.'s new task force which aims to disrupt Iranian ground shipping routes as "wordplay."

In a statement to Iran's semi-official Fars news agency, a Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman said Tehran had made preparations and communicates closely with neighbours.

"The Iron Gate plan is merely a wordplay, the Americans cannot achieve their objectives of imposing ‌severe economic pressure ‌to cause economic ⁠collapse in Iran ‌through ⁠this approach," Mohebbi told the semi-official Fars news agency.

CBS/AFP

Houthi authorities said Sunday that Saudi strikes killed 33 people, many of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country's revived civil war.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country.

The death toll from the Saudi-led coalition's strikes on Al-Shariya village located east of Yemen's capital Sanaa has risen to 33, with 39 people wounded, Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi said in a post on X.

The Houthis' Saba news agency said on Saturday that operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes."

"According to the near-final figures, the dead include 12 men, 8 women and 13 children, while the injured include 16 men, 10 women and 13 children," Alasbahi said.

Saudi Arabia, fighting in Yemen in support of the internationally-recognized government, has not commented on the report. The Saudi-led coalition in a statement on Saturday said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh province.

The Iran-backed Houthis, meanwhile, said they had launched multiple missile and drone attacks against Saudi troops and infrastructure both in the Gulf kingdom and Yemen.

Yemen slipped back into war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government in July after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the conflict in the Middle East.

Since then, Saudi Arabia has regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has expanded its attacks against the oil-rich kingdom.

U.S. forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times, U.S. Central Command said.

A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St.Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, which disabled the ship after the crew was directed to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port, CENTCOM said.

"All mariners transiting near Iranian coastal areas or surrounding waters are advised to heed blockade warnings from U.S. forces," CENTCOM said.

Earlier Saturday, CENTCOM said "strict enforcement" of the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz continues.

Iran established a chokehold on the strait, a vital strategic waterway in global trade, at the beginning of the war, and has claimed attacks on tankers. The U.S. says its blockade had redirected 144 commercial vessels through the end of October.

-CBS/AP

In what the U.S. military is calling an expansion of the naval blockade, U.S. Central Command announced a new task force Saturday aimed at disrupting the illegal shipment of prohibited items like military technology or illegal revenue streams over ground transportation routes.

"The establishment of Task Force Iron Gate reinforces the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea," U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement. "Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with U.S. interagency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military."

The U.S. said the task force will be made up of about 20 civilian and military personnel, based in Florida, and will be tasked with the goal of "preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea."

The announcement made no mention of how the task force would be carrying out its goal, including whether any military operations will be involved.

China, Iran's largest trade partner, has taken to conducting commerce over land, especially by train across central Asia due to the blockade on Iranian ports. The U.S. said the blockade has prevented some $25 billion in Iranian crude oil from being sold, much of it in Asia.

In addition to China, Iran has conducted large amounts of trade over land and via the Caspian Sea with Russia. The landlocked Caspian Sea has proven especially advantageous with a direct route between southwest Russia and northern Iran. Tehran is located just 80 miles south of the Caspian Sea.

Whether any U.S. ships could take to the Caspian Sea was again unclear. CBS News has reached out to the White House for more details.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it has lifted a self-proclaimed limit of 1,200 miles on the range of its ballistic missiles, suggesting the country may seek to develop missiles capable of reaching more distant targets amid fears of renewed all-out war.

The comments by the spokesman of Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard came days after the country's supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khomeini, warned "any kind and level of threat" from the U.S. or Israel would face a response without geographic limits.

Asked at a Tehran press conference about the limit on missile ranges, Gen. Hossein Mohebbi said, "That restriction has been lifted for us."

He did not say whether Iran had missiles capable of exceeding the limit, saying only Iran would "demonstrate these capabilities in practice" rather than make statements.

Iran is not known to have missiles that can go beyond the 1,200-mile limit — a range that puts parts of Greece and the Balkans, the entire Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and most of Egypt within reach. However, U.S. officials have said technology from Iran's space program can be repurposed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles.

The Iranian military, meanwhile, said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz had hit a naval mine and caught fire. It did not identify the nationality or destination of the tanker, which it said had turned off its navigational beacon and was sailing in a "prohibited area."

Saudi strikes killed 22 people, most of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country's civil war, Houthi media said on Saturday.

More than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country, according to the U.N.

"The number of victims of the Saudi enemy warplane massacre in the Al-Shariyah area ... has risen to 22 citizens, most of them children and women, while the number of wounded has risen to 30," the Houthis' Saba news agency said.

The Iran-backed group's Al-Masirah TV provided the same toll.

Saba said earlier Saturday that operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes."

The Saudi-led coalition in a statement on Saturday said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched toward Riyadh province.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province killed 30 people. The Houthis said Saudi airstrikes were to blame, while Yemen's government forces accused the Iran-backed group of having fired a ballistic missile at the site.

AFP/CBS

Iran's military is "stronger" and more motivated than it was when the United States and Israel started the war in February, Iranian state media reported on Saturday, citing an army spokesman.

"Today, the Islamic Republic's armed forces... having gained experience from direct confrontation with the United States and the Israeli regime, are on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war," spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said, according to the state news agency IRNA.

"They now possess greater motivation, commitment, and self-confidence."

CBS/AFP

President Trump confirmed on Friday the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" in Iran, after local state media reported missiles striking Qeshm Island on the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Mr. Trump was asked whether the U.S. carried out more strikes on the island.

"I don't want to talk about it," the president said. "We do minor strikes. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe 5."

On Saturday, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm island, added that there was no official information on the damage. Iranian state television also reported two explosions on the island.

The Trump administration is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear program, the U.S. military's Central Command announced Friday.

The reward , which is being administered through the State Department's Rewards for Justice national security program, also comes with "possible relocation" for the tipster.

The State Department said it is calling for "information about Iran's nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above."

Since the U.S. launched its war with Iran in February, President Trump has repeatedly reiterated that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.

In its reward form, the State Department noted that according to the United Nations' International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran's uranium stockpile is believed to include uranium that has been enriched to 60% purity – "a level that is a short technical step from" the 90% level required to produce nuclear weapons.

"Iran is the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce uranium at such a high enrichment level," the State Department said in its Rewards for Justice post. "Experts estimate this quantity, if enriched further, could be enough for several nuclear weapons."

Iran suspended IAEA inspections following the June 2025 strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities by the U.S. and Israel.

"The regime's lack of compliance with the IAEA on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like centrifuges," the State Department said Friday.

The Treasury Department on Friday targeted several firms exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for allegedly helping Tehran evade sanctions and fund its proxies.

Some of the providers dealt with Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges already sanctioned by Washington.

The latest targets were coordinated with the Canadian government as several of the individuals and entities named are based in Vancouver and Toronto.

"Anyone, anywhere in the world, who helps Tehran evade sanctions risks being held accountable," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement .

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to embark on his first post-midterm foreign trip to attend a Group of Seven foreign ministers meeting in France next week.

He'll likely face questions about the Trump administration's policies, namely in Iran, after huge Republican losses in elections that gave Democrats control of Congress.

The State Department said Friday that Rubio would travel to Paris to meet his counterparts from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan on Monday and Tuesday.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Friday that a Saudi strike on a market in southwestern Yemen had killed or wounded 30 people.

The Houthis' Saba news agency said the "horrific massacre" had "resulted in the martyrdom and injury of more than 30 citizens."

The Houthis' political bureau said in a statement carried by Saba: "It is regrettable that these documented Saudi crimes have become like a forgotten file in the drawers of the United Nations and the so-called international community."

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said Friday that the Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognized government had targeted a market in the southwest of the country, killing and wounding "dozens of civilians."

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X that Saudi aircraft struck the Al-Hadara market in the Taiz governorate on Friday "with three airstrikes, leaving dozens of civilians dead and wounded."

"These brutal crimes will not go unanswered and unpunished," he added.

The Saudi-led coalition said Friday , meanwhile, that air defense systems had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis at Najran, a major city in southwest Saudi Arabia.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed Friday to have destroyed another U.S. drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

In a statement carried by the state TV network IRIB, the IRGC said a U.S. MQ-1 drone was "intercepted and destroyed over Qeshm Island by the IRGC's new advanced air defense system."

The IRGC claimed this was the 16th American MQ-1 drone it had intercepted during the war, and the second in two days . Iranian forces have also claimed to have shot down other U.S. drones, including more than two dozen of the more advanced, and more expensive MQ-9 Reapers .

A seafarer was killed in an explosion caused by a suspected missile attack on an oil tanker Thursday in the Persian Gulf, a Greek company that manages the vessel said Friday.

The MT Velos Sapphire, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker, which was not carrying cargo, was hit Thursday as it sailed toward Bahrain, management firm Velos Tankers said in a statement, according to Reuters.

"The company is greatly saddened to report the death of one of its seafarers, who was found fatally injured on board after having initially been reported missing in the aftermath of the explosion," the statement said.

Velos said, according to Reuters, that no crew members were injured and they managed to extinguish a fire on the ship caused by the blast.

The vessel was brought to Khalifa Bin Salman Port in Bahrain, and the damage to its hull was still being assessed, Reuters said.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis said Friday that it had intercepted a drone in the region of Mecca, Islam's holiest city, following repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Yemeni rebels.

"Interception and destruction of a drone in the Mecca region," Turki al-Malki, the coalition's spokesman, wrote on X , without elaborating.

Since the breakdown of a truce in July, Saudi Arabia has traded blows with the Houthis, who have retaliated with strikes on Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military sites that killed at least 20 people in October.

The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting the holy cities of Mecca or Medina in Saudi Arabia and said they would not do so.

On Thursday, the Saudi coalition said it intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis at the Medina region, a claim rejected by the Iranian proxy group as a "blatant and grave falsehood."

CBS/AFP

The Iranian supreme leader's adviser on international affairs, Aliakbar Velayati, said Friday that Iran was now "one of the main architects" of security in the Middle East.

Referring to how the U.S.-Iran war has changed the region in a series of posts on X , Velayati said that a "tsunami of geopolitical changes in West Asia swept up the Israeli and U.S. elections," and that "Iran is now one of the main architects of the regional order, a reality that cannot be erased or replaced."

Iran is a "bridge between the Persian Gulf, Central Asia, the Caucasus, and the Sea of Oman," he added, saying that "any energy or transit corridor seeking to bypass us will either be costly or unstable."

"The domino effect of crises, from Gaza to the Red Sea and from Lebanon to Iraq, has shown that regional security is indivisible," Velayati said. "Either collective security is achieved, or everyone will experience collective insecurity."

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since being wounded in the strikes that killed his father on Feb. 28.

A tanker was hit by an explosion Thursday in the Strait of Hormuz, a British navy agency said Friday.

The master of a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz near Oman's coast reported "an explosion at the waterline" of the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said, adding that the crew were all safe and the ship was "still under its own power and is continuing on its voyage."

Iran's state media reported Thursday that five oil tankers and a tugboat had caught on fire in or near the strait after hitting sea mines. It was unclear if the UKMTO report was in relation to one of those incidents claimed by Iran.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Friday, in a statement carried by state media, that two more oil tankers had hit mines and caught on fire in or near the strait.

President Trump has accused Iran of lying about such incidents in an effort to drive up energy prices.

President Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war, a U.S. official confirmed to CBS News Friday, amid a diplomatic push to avoid a new round of major hostilities.

Their discussion, which the White House had not provided any information about by Friday morning, came as Iran's top diplomat made his own calls Thursday to counterparts across the Persian Gulf aimed at maintaining "stability in the region" amid concerns in many Gulf capitals that Mr. Trump will order major new U.S. strikes.

Al Thani received a call from Mr. Trump, according to a statement from the emir's office , during which the pair discussed "the latest regional developments, particularly diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region."

The emir "emphasized the importance of continuing dialogue and relying on diplomatic means to settle disputes and prevent further escalation," the statement said.

Motorists could soon see U.S. gas prices drop below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.

Patrick De Haan, a petroleum analyst at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News he expected the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday and early Friday morning, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving.

Gas and diesel prices have both dropped over the last week, thanks largely to market expectations that the U.S. midterm election results would underscore public dissatisfaction with the Iran war and pile pressure on the Trump administration to make a deal to end the conflict, De Haan said.

"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."

Read more here.

The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government said Friday that air defense systems had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels at Najran, a major city in southwest Saudi Arabia.

"Debris fell as a result of the interception, and damage assessment is underway," the statement said.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement carried by state media Friday that two oil tankers hit mines and caught fire in or near the Strait of Hormuz, a day after Tehran claimed five other tankers had met similar fates.

"Two violating oil tankers — one east of the Strait of Hormuz and the other within the Strait itself — that attempted to transit via an unauthorized route struck mines," the IRGC said in a statement, according to state news outlets.

"These two tankers had deactivated all their navigation and identification systems. Supported by the aggressive and terrorist U.S. military, they attempted to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an unauthorized path; however, upon striking mines, they caught fire and were immobilized," the statement said.

On Thursday, Iranian media reported that five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz in similar incidents.

There has been no confirmation of any of the incidents from maritime officials, and President Trump has accused Iran of making up such attacks to drive up global energy prices.

A U.K. naval agency said earlier this week , however, that despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe, there were at least 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region during October alone, a record high.

Since the war began with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran has sought to control traffic through the strait, a key passage through which, before the war, about a fifth of global crude oil supplies would typically pass. In response, the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian ports.

The U.S. military has escorted tankers through the strait, which, along with other routes has helped bring shipments from the Gulf back up to or at least near to pre-war levels, but ships continue coming under attack.

CBS/AFP

Russian President Vladimir Putin met Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between the two countries, including with the potential construction of a pipeline for Iran to import Russian gas.

Speaking with journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to the Iranian embassy in Moscow.

"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," Rezaei was quoted as saying by Iranian state TV.

He noted the aim was to enable Iran "to address its own gas shortages while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighboring countries."

Despite being a major producer, Iran has long suffered natural gas shortages, which have been exacerbated by the war with the United States and Israel.

During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.

CBS/AFP

President Trump said Thursday that people will soon know his decision on whether to order a new round of U.S. strikes on Iran.

Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that he believed it would take Iran 25 years to rebuild the country from the damage already inflicted during the war.

The president said he didn't want to bring further destruction to the country, but he may not have a choice.

Mr. Trump kept the possibility of a major new U.S. assault on Iran on the table in the run-up to the midterm elections this week, but hadn't renewed the threat since his Republican Party's dismal performance in the vote, which he acknowledged was, at least in part, a repudiation of the war.

Mr. Trump told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday evening, as U.S. ballots were counted, that he had no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran.

items.title: El-Sayed: Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
items.summary: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed joins "This Week" after his historic victory against Republican Mike Rogers in the midterm election.

scraped.title: Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
scraped.description: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed joins "This Week" after his historic victory against Republican Mike Rogers in the midterm election.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
scraped.body_text:
The Michigan senator-elect called the president "an unserious fool."

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said Sunday that Democrats will work with President Donald Trump to help the American people if "he wants to act serious," but if the president instead chooses "foolishness," the incoming senator said he will not find a willing partner in Congress.

"Let's talk about how he is an unserious fool. Think about this war in Iran that every single president had resisted fighting because, of course, it was a dumb idea," El-Sayed told ABC "This Week" in an exclusive interview. "Let's talk about the foolishness of a tariff war with Canada. ... Let's talk about the foolishness of gutting Medicaid to pass tax cuts for the richest people in America."

"So look, if he wants to act serious, we are happy to work alongside him to actually address these issues," El-Sayed continued. "He is the president of the United States. But if he wants to continue to fool, he will hire people like Stephen Miller to run the White House, and he gets to choose where he goes next."

President Trump on Friday said White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller would assume the role of chief of staff effective Monday, replacing Susie Wiles.

With his victory in Michigan's Senate race last Tuesday, El-Sayed is set to make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. During his campaign, El-Sayed said he focused his message on three issues: "to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for all."

But the issue that most defined both the contentious and close primary campaign against fellow Democrat Haley Stevens and the general election campaign against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers was U.S. support for Israel. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of the Israeli government and U.S. military aid to Israel.

Asked on "This Week" if he's heard from his Republican opponent, El-Sayed said, "Not that I know of. I think he had a flight to catch to Florida."

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Iran live updates: Saudis say Houthi missiles targeted Riyadh, Aramco tower damaged
scraped.body_text:
The Houthis have been launching attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.

See the most recent developments below.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday night.

The unnamed tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz," the alert read. "All crew are safe and accounted for and there is no reported environmental impact at this time."

In another incident on Saturday night, the UKMTO said "military authorities" reported a tanker on fire in the Strait of Hormuz which resulted in the evacuation of the ship's crew. The incident occurred 8 nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, the UKMTO said.

Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry on Sunday confirmed that a building in Riyadh owned by the country's state-owned energy giant Aramco was damaged during a Houthi attack on the city.

"The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported," the ministry said in a statement posted to X.

Saudi Arabian military spokesperson Col. Turki al-Maliki said in a series of posts to X on Sunday that Saudi air defenses intercepted three Houthi ballistic missiles, two cruise missiles and one drone launched toward Saudi regions.

Two of the ballistic missiles and both cruise missiles targeted the capital Riyadh, Maliki said.

The General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defense on Sunday morning issues safety warnings for the capital city of Riyadh and for the southwestern city of Najran.

Shortly after the warnings were issued, the directorate said the danger had passed in both areas.

The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have been firing missiles and drones toward Saudi cities and critical infrastructure sites in recent months.

items.title: Hundreds of thousands join Amsterdam’s ‘Red Line’ protest against Israel
items.summary: Protesters seek stricter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.

scraped.title: Hundreds of thousands join Amsterdam’s ‘Red Line’ protest against Israel
scraped.description: Protesters seek stricter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.
scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: Hundreds of thousands join Amsterdam’s ‘Red Line’ protest against Israel
scraped.body_text:
Protesters seek tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.

Save

Share

More than 200,000 people have taken to the streets of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, demanding government action against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers.

Sunday’s ‘Red Line’ protesters, many wearing red items of clothing, called for tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.

“What is happening there is inhumane,” Mike van Dongen said as he walked in the huge throng of people.

“As far as I’m concerned, [the Dutch authorities] are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”

As the protesters marched along a normally busy Amsterdam street that was closed to traffic on Sunday, a man stood at a bus stop with a loudspeaker shouting, “Free, free Palestine!” Many of the marchers echoed his cry as they passed.

Israel’s genocidal war has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, since October 2023.

Sunday’s protest was similar to one in early October last year. That followed ‘Red Line’ demonstrations last June when protesters marched through the streets of The Hague.

A “ ceasefire ” took effect in Gaza on October 10 last year, but Israeli attacks and killings have continued on an almost-daily basis since.

The war in Gaza has strained relations between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel.

Since then, a new minority coalition government took power in February and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal – the ban provoked a diplomatic spat with Israel.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took part in a march last year but was not present on Sunday, defended his government’s actions at his weekly news conference on Friday.

“Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said.

He added that his administration is “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza.

scraped.h1: Photos: Diwali celebrations light up India and its global diaspora
scraped.body_text:
In Pictures

Celebrations feature fireworks, prayers, reunions, rangoli designs, feasting, and the sharing of sweets and gifts.

Save

Share

Diwali, the festival of lights, is being celebrated across India and among its vast diaspora, marking one of the most important days of the year for Hindus.

More than one billion people of different faiths take part in the celebrations in the world’s most populous nation, gathering for prayers, family reunions and the lighting of fireworks.

The name Diwali comes from “Deepavali”, meaning “a row of lights”, and many families place clay oil lamps outside their homes to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance.

The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar and usually falls in late October or early November. This year, Diwali is marked on November 8.

While Diwali is rooted in Hindu tradition, it is also observed by Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists, with regional origin stories that share a common theme – the victory of good over evil.

Celebrations often include feasting, new clothes, rangoli floor designs, and the exchange of sweets and gifts with friends and neighbours.

items.title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance
items.summary: The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.

scraped.title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance
scraped.description: The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.
scraped.h1: South Africa's ANC hit by worst-ever performance in local elections
scraped.body_text:
The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.

South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) turned in a historically poor election performance , with the the final tally published on Sunday giving them less than 31% of the vote in Wednesday's municipal polls .

Their closes rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), won just under 25% of the vote.

The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa 's Electoral Commission said on Saturday. With no outright winner declared in several major cities, politicians are expected enter tough coalition talks to form municipal governments.

While the ANC remains the most popular party in the country, they have been struggling with growing backlash from voters. In 2026, many South Africans are frustrated by water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities. High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are high on the public agenda.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa , has not yet addressed his party's poor performance. In his weekly presidential letter, however, he admitted that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.

"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.

The ANC had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.

Once led by Nelson Mandela , the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.

The pro-business, center-right DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.
scraped.lead_paragraph: The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.

scraped.h1: Egypt train crash leaves several dead, many injured
scraped.body_text:
A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying scores of passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.

At least seven people were killed in the train collision in Egypt on Sunday, with authorities also confirming over 100 people were injured.

The collision involved one train hitting the rear end of another while traveling through the Giza province on the line between Cairo and the southern Nile city of Aswan. One of the trains then derailed and several cars flipped, according to the Egyptian authorities.

Officials said 52 ambulances were deployed to the scene some 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo. Emergency crews and cranes were also working to clear the line and restore railway traffic through Giza's al-Ayyat district.

The cause of the accident was not immediately clear.

In a social media post, Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said he ordered an investigation. He also urged the state agencies to "hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent."

The crash tool place in the same area as the worst train disaster in Egypt's history, which saw over 370 people were killed in a train fire in 2002. Several crashes also claimed dozens of lives in the same region in 2009.

In recent years, Egypt has invested billions of dollars into new highways and high-speed rail lines , but is still facing safety issues and repeated crashes while attempting to revamp its aging rail network .

items.title: Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government
items.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.

scraped.title: Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government
scraped.description: Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.
scraped.h1: Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government
scraped.body_text:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.

Israel President Isaac Herzog has officially tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government.

Eisenkot, the head of the centrist Yashar party, will have 28 days to secure a coalition to replace current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's religious-nationalist government, with Herzog having the authority to prolong Eisenkot's mandate by 14 days.

"The conversations with the different parties were open and transparent, while also resurfacing the many voices in Israeli society. They reminded us the fact that all Israeli citizens have an equal voice, from all parts of society," Herzog said.

He stressed that Eisenkot received the clearest support from the majority of Knesset members when it comes to the question of forming the next government.

"The challenges we face are giant. Iran is not waiting a second in its threats. We have to start building a future in the region and proceed with Trump's 20-point plan in Gaza, as well as negotiating the future with Lebanon and other neighbors," the Israeli president said, adding that "Israel needs a stable government that faces these challenges."

Herzog said that he expected Eisenkot to do his best to form a government that would serve all parts of the Israeli people.

In turn, Eisenkot stressed that he is committed to establishing a national emergency government.

"We do not have the privilege of endless rounds of elections. I will send an official approach to all of the Knesset's members, as parties and individuals, for talks," he added.

Eisenkot also addressed Knesset members. "The public looks up to us... We are in the most complicated political situation since Israel's establishment," he said.

Yashar was Israel's second biggest party in Israel's October elections with 21 parliament seats, behind Netanyahu's Likud with 27. However, more members of the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, recommended Eisenkot as the man who should be given the first right to try and secure a government.

In comparison to Eisenkot's 67 recommendations, Netanyahu received the backing of 46 members, with the ultraorthodox Ashkenazi party United Torah Judaism (UTJ) deciding not to make any recommendations despite having joined Netanyahu's governments of the past 17 years.

Should Eisenkot fail to form a coalition, President Isaac Herzog will have the authority to pass the task on to a different Knesset member, with the second person in line expected to be Netanyahu.

If the Likud leader, too, will not manage to form a government, and if no other parliament member will claim to have enough support to head a government, Israel will likely head to another round of elections.

Dividing Israel's Zionist parties into blocs results in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist allies receiving 53 seats, with the Eisenkot-led anti-Netanyahu bloc having 48 seats.

Israel's two Arab parties, which with 19 seats received historic support due to the high turnout in Arab and Palestinian communities, already voiced their willingness to support the Zionist opposition in ousting Netanyahu and his government. Mostly the religious Muslim party Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, said it is willing to join a coalition once again in a bid to improve Israel's Arab and Palestinian communities' lives.

In 2021, Ra'am made history in becoming the first-ever Arab party to join an Israeli coalition, signing an agreement with right-wing candidate Naftali Bennet and liberal politician Yair Lapid.

The other Arab party, the Joint List, is a union of several smaller parties. While its members have never joined an Israeli coalition, its politicians did provide political support for an Israeli government from the opposition during Yitzhak Rabin's second term as prime minister as his government pushed through the Oslo Accords with the Palestinians, a term which was cut short by Rabin's murder in November 1995.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Both sides of Israel's Zionist political divide promised not to rely on votes by Arab parties to form a coalition, meaning Eisenkot's bloc will have to track back on one of its election promises to form a government with them.

However, a poll by the Accord Center of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem carried out two days after the elections found that 59 percent of Israel's Zionist opposition voters would rather have a government with Ra'am, and with the Joint List's abstention, than any other alternative.

Another option touted by Israeli media in the past week was the country's two ultraorthodox parties potentially joining an Eisenkot-led coalition. UTJ and Sepharadi party Shas have seven seats each, but a coalition with any of them would require Eisenkot to backtrack on another campaign promise: to pass through a legislation to secure the army conscription of young ultraorthodox men, which the two parties strictly object, citing fears over the future of religious studies in Israel.

Moreover, Shas supporters are known to hold right-wing views favorable to Netanyahu, with party head Arye Deri being considered as one of the politicians closest to Israel's longest-serving prime minister.

The government formed is bound to have wide-ranging implications on the lives of Palestinians in the Occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

The Netanyahu-led current coalition also includes far-right parties Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, which received 13 seats in the October election. The two parties support annexing the West Bank — a territory illegally occupied by Israel — as well as re-establishing Israeli settlements in the Gaza Strip and carrying out the so-called "wilful migration," the plan to move Gaza's 2.1 million Palestinians to other countries. Large parts of Netanyahu's Likud, too, support the plan.

The two parties often provide political backing to the violent settlers carrying out attacks against Palestinians in the Occupied West Bank.

Eisenkot himself promised to secure a Gaza Strip without Hamas rule within 18 months of becoming prime minister. This stands in contrast to the Netanyahu government's current policy of allowing Hamas to control certain parts of the enclave, despite the US-brokered ceasefire agreement saying a board of technocrats should take over Gaza from Hamas.

While Gadi Eisenkot's bloc includes several right-wing parties, their positions differ from those of Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition. Naftali Bennet , the head of the opposition's second biggest party Beyachad, labels himself as a right-winger and a supporter of settlements.

However, he has repeatedly used strong terms to condemn settler attacks on Palestinians. Eisenkot himself, too, condemned settler violence towards Palestinians, saying they are the result of the Netanyahu government's policies.

items.title: As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
items.summary: With fears of cyberattacks, conflict and major disruption to daily life grow in Europe, governments are urging citizens to prepare for emergencies. But in Britain, the culture of stockpiling supplies and being ready to face a crisis needs gentle and convincing persuasion.

scraped.title: As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness | CBC News
scraped.description: With fears of cyberattacks, conflict and major disruption to daily life grow in Europe, governments are urging citizens to prepare for emergencies. But in Britain, the culture of stockpiling supplies and being ready to face a crisis needs gentle and convincing persuasion.
scraped.h1: As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
scraped.body_text:
The last time any British government launched a national public preparedness campaign was at the peak of the Cold War in 1980.

The “Protect and Survive” message was delivered in short, eerie-looking public information broadcasts and booklets, meant to advise people on how to prepare for a nuclear attack. The campaign — whose guidance included hiding under a heavy table or tips about how to store a dead body in the house for five days — backfired and was ridiculed. Brits realized little would protect them from a thermonuclear strike, leaving them feeling that preparation was pointless as survival would be futile.

Nearly 50 years on, the head of the British Army, Gen. Sir Roland Walker, addressed some 700 soldiers last month at Britain's biggest garrison in northern England. The "business of soldiering" had returned to the national psyche, he told members of the light, high-readiness global response force, adding that anyone following world affairs will realize there is “extreme jeopardy."

“The political leaders of this country,” he said, “will start to have a frank conversation with the citizens of this country about just what is going on, and where the risk lies, and what the nation ... must need to be prepared to do.”

Exactly one week later, Britain’s “Be Ready” campaign was unveiled, a guide on preparing for 72 hours of self-sufficiency in the event of an emergency, be it a climate crisis, cyber disruptions or threats by hostile states.

“It’s something that emergency planners have been wanting for a very long time,” said Lucy Easthope, a global disaster recovery specialist. Easthope has advised in emergencies from the Novichok poisonings in Salisbury, England, to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami and 9/11.

Easthope says what the public wants is reassurance — not negative and depressing messaging.

“Ancient DNA, by that I mean 30 years ago, is being reawoken,” she told CBC News. “This is reawakening the idea that it's perfectly survivable.

“I’m really pleased in the U.K. we haven’t resorted to fear messaging.”

Other European nations have also recently introduced or updated their emergency guidance, including France, Ireland, Sweden, Norway, Germany and Poland.

Ottawa, too, has reiterated its longstanding advice . But unlike Canada with its emergency preparedness week — an annual event since 1996 — Britain faces a cultural hurdle, with the word "preparedness" not even being in most Brits' vocabulary. The U.K. has largely relied on community resilience to short-term disruptions, rather than self sufficiency. Now, it faces the challenge of convincing people that they must be prepared for the worst — without sending them into a panic.

In Hertfordshire, north of London, family physician Nyari Matebwe says her first reaction was to roll her eyes and ignore it.

“I feel like it’s scaremonger-y, or the skeptic in me thinks maybe they’re hiding something from us … another distraction from the real issues,” she said.

The recent suspected hacking attacks on supermarket freezers in multiple European countries and attempts to raise temperatures in French medical fridges containing critical blood donation stocks have made her question her own skepticism.

“After the recent airplane bomb hoaxes, I did start to think about it a bit more,” said Matebwe, whose teenage daughter is pushing her to take the prepping message seriously.

Sweden is advising seven days , Germany up to 10 , but the U.K., like Canada, has settled on three days' survival off-grid.

Europe's wave of bomb threats spreads from airports to newsrooms

School parents’ WhatsApp groups are lighting up with conversations

“I want to stockpile but I’m in a state of inertia,” one parent wrote. “My husband is totally unbothered.”

Another asked, “How will we cook if there’s no gas or electricity?” while one raised concern about rising crime rates and the risk of keeping cash at home.

Warnings have been widespread recently.

Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which is part of the government’s signals agency GCHQ and the Five Eyes intelligence sharing group that includes Canada, told CBC News: “This is a moment of urgency.”

Russia continues its attacks on power facilities in Kyiv as temperatures drop ahead of winter

The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready?

The NCSC says AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the power stations, airports and hospitals in the U.K. within two years.

In Horne’s annual state of the cyber nation address, he said “military networks are subjected to sustained and persistent, widespread attempts to penetrate our systems."

That included Russian hybrid warfare campaigns, he said.

“All countries need to be taking this moment seriously," he told CBC News. “There are loads of vulnerabilities that do not need to be there,” which he said the country's adversaries are exploiting.

Outside the need for companies to keep their technology safe, Horne said at home it is a case of keeping devices up to date and using passkeys.

“You do need to be thinking about, 'do I need to be having the levels of connectivity of devices across my house, apartment' … not unnecessarily introducing potential vulnerabilities.”

There are some who see the “Be Ready” messaging as another example of the "nanny state," or the government telling them how to live.

Others think cultural attitudes play a part.

Getting prepped to deal with emergencies

Luis Martinez Arnal, an IT professional from Spain now based in London, says his Mexican wife automatically prepares for emergencies, having grown up in a country prone to earthquakes.

“But in the U.K.,” Arnal said, “hard times have been forgotten.”

The accessibility of everything, he added, “psychologically is making us feel more comfortable.”

The recent cyberattacks have created a heightened sense of anxiety across Europe, and as people grow more reliant on the internet, questions are being asked how anyone can prepare to stay connected if it went down. Those haven't been easily answered — especially as Britain has long planned to switch all copper-wire landline phones to internet use-only from the end of January 2027.

“Call me crazy, but following the new guidelines, I do feel a bit nervous,” said one London mother, Amee Doshi, pointing to talk about the potential for a world war.

A Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is seen stopped at a police roadblock on Sept. 27, in Fairford, U.K. Police declared a major incident after evacuating residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about 1.6 kilometres from RAF Fairford, a military base that hosts U.S. Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict. (David Bown/Getty Images)

Others appear to be taking to it like true preppers.

“We bulk-buy,” said Preyal Shah, a working mother from Harrow in northwest London.

“I even now have 10 kilograms of rice, five kilograms of pasta … multiple cases of tinned food, each type being 12 tins.”

Preyal said she is also stockpiling newspapers to light a coal-burning stove: “Back to basics.”

In October, British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned that the country needs to be “ready for war in 1,000 days," flagging the potential of Russian aggression.

“To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it,” he said.

“We’ve just got so many competing crises at the moment … and war in Europe,” said Reena Patel, a lawyer from north London, referring to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“It’s not necessarily that I’m thinking war is coming but…” she said, listing off all she wants to buy, from a wind-up radio to water purification filters.

“The only thing I have in my control is to try to be a little bit prepared.”

Anna Cunningham is a freelance correspondent in London, England. She has reported for the CBC since 2009, and was previously based in Mumbai, Paris and Lagos, Nigeria.

scraped.description: At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, authorities said.
scraped.h1: Train collision in Egypt kills 4 and injures 88 south of Cairo
scraped.body_text:
At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, authorities said.

The crash occurred in the al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 52 kilometers south of Cairo. A train travelling to the southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the Transportation Ministry. One of the trains derailed, it said, but did not specify which.

The Health Ministry said at least four people were killed and 88 others were wounded. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.

People gather at the site of the derailed passenger train south of Cairo. (The Associated Press)

President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post that he ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

items.title: Poland in mourning after deadly mass shooting in Krakow
items.summary: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, after authorities say a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.

scraped.title: Poland in mourning after deadly mass shooting in Krakow | CBC News
scraped.description: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, after authorities say a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.
scraped.h1: Poland in mourning after deadly mass shooting in Krakow
scraped.body_text:
Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, after authorities say a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.

The attack, which Poland’s defence minister described as an "act of terror," happened on Saturday in Main Square in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town. The area is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.

By evening, mourners had left candles in memory of the victims. The square remained partially closed on Sunday morning as authorities continued their investigation.

Krakow shooting leaves 6 dead, more than a dozen injured

Marie-Ange Collaer wrote on Facebook that she and her family survived the shooting during a trip to Krakow from Brussels.

"We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around," she wrote. "Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere."

Collaer said her family was "quite in shock" after returning to their hotel but everyone was grateful to be alive.

"We saw a few that did not make it, true horror," she wrote.

Polish police say gunman kills 6 in 'act of terror'; 3 more dead found at suspect's home

St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight in tribute to the victims. It is the first time the call has been missed since the Second World War.

Four women and two men were killed in the Main Square shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from an unidentified foreign country were also among the dead.

The two police officers who stopped the attacker remain in hospital. One of them is still in a coma while the other woke up from a coma, Klęczar said. Officials launched an appeal for blood donations for the benefit of the most seriously wounded policeman.

Cordoned-off areas at Krakow's Main Market Square following Saturday's mass shooting. (Jakub Porzycki/Reuters)

"If it weren’t for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher," Klęczar said.

Five non-Poles are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

The suspect is also in a critical state, having been operated on multiple times.

There was confusion on Saturday about the shooter’s age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24.

The prosecutors said on Sunday they started an investigation for murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act "constituting a terrorist offence."

Authorities say they also found three dead bodies at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers northeast of Krakow. The police said on Sunday they were the bodies of the attacker’s sister, mother and father.

The family members likely died from gunshot wounds, the police said.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the attacker holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Videos posted on social media by witnesses show people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims. In one video, a police officer is seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who is lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse to the ground himself.

People stand near candles and flowers left near the Main Market Square in tribute for victims after Saturday's mass shooting. (Jakub Porzycki/Reuters)

Klęczar said the attacker’s father owned over 10 guns legally and that the attacker also owned guns. Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found in the possession of the attacker in Krakow or in his car.

Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising, particularly because of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and fear of instability in the region.

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects.

The Krakow attacker’s military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other "extreme-right lone actors" committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague.

" We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland."

CBC’s Darren McCaffrey speaks with Christian Leuprecht regarding shooting in Poland

items.title: Calls for next Victorian government to invest in prisons
items.summary: Victoria's prisons are already at 92 per cent capacity, but experts say the crime policies of both major parties would see more people locked up. Victoria's prisons are at 92 per cent capacity and more people are likely to end up behind bars under both major parties' crime election pledges.

scraped.title: Calls for next Victorian government to invest in prisons
scraped.description: Victoria's prisons are already at 92 per cent capacity, but experts say the crime policies of both major parties would see more people locked up.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/richard-willingham/8654628
scraped.h1: Calls for next Victorian government to invest in prisons
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic: Prisons

Victoria's prisons are at 92 per cent capacity and more people are likely to end up behind bars under both major parties' crime election pledges. ( AFP )

Victoria's prisons are already at 92 per cent capacity and experts say the crime policies of both major parties would see more people locked up.

Neither party has responded to the ABC's question about whether they have planned for more prison beds and corrections officers.

Voters go to the polls on November 28.

The next Victorian government, regardless of who wins office, could be forced to expand or build new jails as the major parties promise to crack down on law and order, adding to an already tight budget.

At the start of the month, the state's prisons were 92 per cent full, with 4,624 people serving a sentence in Victorian jails and another 3,268 on remand.

Reserve capacity is needed to maintain flexibility that ensures certain inmates are not housed together, and to meet increased demand.

But with Premier Ben Carroll introducing tougher laws and the Jess Wilson's Coalition promising to be even tougher on justice, more people are likely to end up in prison.

Building a new prison could cost more than $1 billion — the new 1,292-bed maximum-security Western Plains prison near Lara cost $1.19 billion to build. Its current operational capacity is 1,094.

The dilapidated Port Phillip Prison closed in 2025.

Port Phillip Prison in Truganina closed last year. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

There is also the additional cost of hiring and training new corrections officers, as well as money to increase the capacity of the already overworked courts.

Both sides are also recruiting more police. Jess Wilson is promising an extra 1,500 recruits on top of the 1,500 being sought by the Labor government.

The ABC asked both Labor and the Coalition if it had factored in extra corrections officers and prison space in their crackdown on crime policies.

Neither responded directly to questions about extra costs.

Shadow Police and Corrections Minister Brad Battin said a Liberal and Nationals government would work with Corrections Victoria to manage prisoner numbers within the existing network of facilities.

"Make no mistake, under a Liberal and Nationals government, if you do the wrong thing, there'll be a prison cell and bed ready for you,'' Mr Battin said.

A Labor spokesperson said it had already invested in more than 1,200 additional prison beds, and an extra 1,200 prison officers have been recruited, with $727 million allocated in the 2025-26 state budget.

Topic: State and Territory Elections

Topic: State and Territory Elections

Analysis by Richard Willingham

Topic: State and Territory Elections

Topic: Elections

On Sunday, Mr Carroll promised to spend $204 million to set up a new therapeutic rehabilitation detention program at Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre .

The former chair of the Sentencing Advisory Council, Arie Freiberg, said more police and tougher rules would result in pressure on the prison system, warning it would result in more people being held in police cells.

Dr Freiberg, chair for 18 years from 2004, said the public needed to be aware that there was a high flow-on cost from tougher law and order policies

"It has extensive and expensive consequences down to all other parts of the criminal justice system. And we have to be prepared for that, and we have to pay for that. Justice is not cheap,'' he said.

Arie Freiberg says tough-on-crime policies will put more pressure on Victoria's prison system. ( Supplied )

Dr Freiberg also said law enforcement needed to be based on intelligence, not flooding the streets with more police. He was concerned that a more punitive approach to lower-level offending could place a further burden on the already busy courts.

"We're finding more and more people who are suffering from mental illness, mental disorders, drug-related, alcohol-related crime,'' he said.

"We need to deal with those in a social manner and not through the criminal justice system."

He said investing in those services rather than prisons was far more cost-effective.

Swinburne University law professor Mirko Bagaric said Victoria's crime wave was a direct result of lenient and soft sentencing under the Labor government.

"Crime is solvable,'' he said. "If we need more prisons, then that is a good investment."

Between 2019 and 2025, Victoria's prison population dropped from 8,102 to 5,915, while the crime rate soared.

"We need to lock up those that scare us; not those that annoy us [like property offenders],'' he said,

He said the state needed to make sure the right types of people were being sent to prison; namely violent offenders and sexual offenders.

Dr Bagaric said Melbourne had more firebombings than any other city in the world because there was no serious punishment for the dangerous crime.

Mirko Bagaric says investing in Victoria's prison system could solve the state's crime crisis. ( ABC News: Melanie Vujkovic )

Labor is also promising to recruit 200 more police reservists to work at police counters in stations as part of its bid to re-open police stations.

As part of the $370 million pledge, Labor is also promising to build or upgrade police stations at Watergardens, Doncaster, Keilor Downs, Greensborough, Moonee Ponds and Clayton.

Ms Wilson is also set to focus on law and order on Monday with a pledge to introduce an "Aidan's Law" in memory of 22-year-old Aidan Becker, who was killed when trying to protect a 14-year-old boy at Mernda state station in March.

The law is designed to ensure courts specifically consider whether an offender has attacked someone acting as a good Samaritan.

The Coalition says the change would explicitly recognise attacks on Samaritans as an aggravating circumstance when determining a criminal sentence.
