scraped.title: Top US, China officials raise trade 'concerns' as APEC approaches
scraped.description: Top officials from Washington and Beijing held "frank" talks on their countries' testy trade relationship on Friday, ahead of an Asia-Pacific summit in China this month where their leaders are due to meet.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: Top US, China officials raise trade ‘concerns’ as APEC approaches
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Top officials from Washington and Beijing held “frank” talks on their countries’ testy trade relationship on Friday, ahead of an Asia-Pacific summit in China this month where their leaders are due to meet.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer held a call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and discussed economic and trade commitments over the last year, both sides said.

The Americans stressed “the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments” and highlighted “concerns about recent Chinese actions”, according to a statement released by the US Treasury Department.

China’s He, meanwhile, expressed “serious concerns over recent economic and trade restrictive measures imposed by the United States”, according to a state media report shared online by Beijing’s commerce ministry on Saturday.

The report did not specify which measures He was referring to, but added that the talks were “frank, in-depth and constructive”.

Bessent “underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement”, said the Treasury.

The statement referenced China’s commitments from an October 2025 meeting between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Busan, South Korea, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit .

China is hosting this year’s APEC gathering from November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, which could also see a trilateral meeting with Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Beijing’s foreign ministry said this week it was in contact with Washington and Moscow about the possibility.

The Busan agreement, which reflected calming tensions between the superpowers after they had exchanged tariff escalations earlier in 2025, required China to purchase US soybeans this year and through 2028.

China also agreed to suspend new export controls on rare earths and to issue general licences for exports of the materials.

The accord initially covered one year, but the two sides extended the ceasefire through to January 10, 2027, during Xi’s September visit to the White House.

Both sides agreed during Friday’s call to “properly manage differences” and promote a “stable” US-China trade relationship, according to the Chinese commerce ministry’s readout on Saturday.

In a separate statement, the ministry reiterated China’s “firm” opposition to new US sanctions targeting Cuba, which affected two Chinese companies.

The statement from an unnamed spokesperson added that Washington’s recent sanctions “escalation” against China ran counter to the consensus reached by Trump and Xi.

Trade experts have said one of the main sources of friction is over the level of Chinese rare-earth exports, which are crucial for the production of smartphones, automobiles and military equipment.

Published - November 08, 2026 11:19 pm IST - Amsterdam

Demonstrators march during the fourth "Red Line" protest, with the focus on the Dutch economic and military ties with Israel, in Amsterdam, Netherlands, on November 8, 2026. File | Photo Credit: AP

Tens of thousands of people, many of them dressed in red, marched through Amsterdam on Sunday (November 8, 2026) in a mass demonstration aimed at pressing the Dutch government to take more decisive action against Israel over Gaza.

The organisers of the “Red Line” demonstrations in the Netherlands called for measures including stricter trade sanctions on Israel, officially declaring that Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide, and halting all arms sales to Israel. The Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers, said in an online post that more than 200,000 people joined the march.

“What is happening there is inhumane,” said Mike van Dongen, as he walked in the huge throng. He was critical of the Dutch government’s actions. “As far as I’m concerned, they are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”

As the protesters marched along a normally busy Amsterdam street that was closed to traffic on Sunday, a man stood on a bus stop with a loudspeaker shouting “Free, free Palestine!” Many of the marchers echoed his cry as they passed.

Israel strongly rejects suggestions it is committing genocide in Gaza in its military campaign, which followed the attacks by Hamas-led militants in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. Militants killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages.

Israel’s retaliatory offensive has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and destroyed much of Gaza. More than 1,550 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed by the Israeli military since a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas began in October 2025, according to the territory’s Health Ministry.

The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, does not distinguish between civilians and militants, though it says women and children make up roughly half of the dead.

The campaign in Gaza has strained relations between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch Foreign Minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel. Since then, a new minority coalition government has taken power and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal, a move that provoked a diplomatic spat with Israel.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took part in a march last year but was not present on Sunday, defended his government’s actions at his weekly press conference on Friday (November 6, 2026). “Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said.

He added that his administration was “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza. At the same time, he said, the government was applying more pressure on Hamas and other organisations that continue to carry out “various operations that endanger the safety of ordinary Israelis.”

U.S. President Donald Trump and Elon Musk. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Tech megabillionaire Elon Musk and President ‌Donald Trump's newly appointed White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, ​will likely be targets of congressional probes when Democrats take control ⁠of Congress in January, a senior lawmaker said on Sunday (November 8, 2026).

California Representative Robert Garcia, who is in line to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee next year after Democrats' sweeping midterm election victory, ‌said investigations will focus on Mr. Musk's involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency's firing of federal workers last year, and Mr. Miller's role in Mr. Trump's ‌hardline immigration crackdown.

"I think there's a lot of interest, not just from ‌our committee, ⁠but from committees across the Congress to speak to Mr. Musk," Mr. Garcia ⁠told CNN's "State of the Union."

Mr. Miller — whom Mr. Garcia called the architect of a "horrific, unjust" immigration policy — has been promoted to White House chief of staff, Mr. Trump said on Friday (November 6, 2026).

"Stephen Miller is at the centre ​of the major policy decisions that ‌are happening in the administration, and so it does deserve oversight and investigation," Mr. Garcia said.

The crackdown on immigration, which included operations in which two people were fatally shot in Minnesota by federal agents, has proven widely unpopular. A Reuters/Ipsos ‌poll in October found that only 37% approved of Mr. Trump's handling of immigration, ​down from 50% when he took office.

Voters delivered a historic rebuke to Republicans in Tuesday's (November 3, 2026) midterm election, but with Mr. Miller as White ⁠House chief of staff, the Trump administration is expected to continue its aggressive approach to immigration enforcement, amplify cultural conflicts and give no ground to a Democratic-controlled Congress, say officials ‌and experts who spoke to Reuters .

Hakeem Jeffries, who will become speaker of the U.S. House in January, said on Sunday (November 8, 2026) that Democrats would support a measure to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a congressional process that could remove him from office.

Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, has said he will reintroduce articles of impeachment against Mr. Hegseth soon. Mr. Jeffries said he is a "hard yes" on ‌backing that measure.

"Pete Hegseth has got to go... I believe there will be incredibly strong support for ​that resolution," Mr. Jeffries told ABC 's "This Week," citing the defense secretary's oversight of the unpopular Iran war launched by Mr. Trump in February, which has led ⁠to a spike in gas prices.

Attorney General Todd Blanche signalled on Sunday (November 8, 2026) that the Trump ⁠administration was prepared to battle the Democrats in Congress, calling threats by some Democrats to target administration officials and allies "not something we can tolerate in ‌this country."

"If that's what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready," Mr. Blanche said. "If you work in this administration, you have a lawyer. ​It's me."

scraped.description: Police across Japan are struggling to contain a rapidly spreading social media trend known as "Shorinji Racing," in which children and teenagers shout "Shorinji" outside police stations and police boxes before running away, with Osaka police recording approximately 280 related incidents and taking around 50 minors aged between 7 and 16 into protective custody or questioning them.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Seven-Year-Old Taken Into Custody Over Shorinji Racing
scraped.body_text:
OSAKA - Police across Japan are struggling to contain a rapidly spreading social media trend known as "Shorinji Racing," in which children and teenagers shout "Shorinji" outside police stations and police boxes before running away, with Osaka police recording approximately 280 related incidents and taking around 50 minors aged between 7 and 16 into protective custody or questioning them.

The bizarre activity, which has spread through videos posted on social media, involves young people deliberately provoking police officers, sometimes by approaching police facilities under false pretenses or making nuisance calls before fleeing. The youngest child taken into protective custody in Osaka was a 7-year-old first-grade elementary school student. The trend has gained momentum in recent weeks, with videos showing participants approaching police boxes, shouting the phrase and running away while companions record their actions. items.title: Kyoto Shopping Arcade Preserves 150 Years of Culinary Traditions

scraped.title: Kyoto Shopping Arcade Preserves 150 Years of Culinary Traditions
scraped.description: Kyoto
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Kyoto Shopping Arcade Preserves 150 Years of Culinary Traditions
scraped.body_text:
KYOTO - Kyoto's Shin-Kyogoku Shopping Street, a bustling 500-meter arcade with more than 150 years of history, is home to some of the city's oldest restaurants, seven Buddhist temples and a Shinto shrine, while a recently rediscovered 90-year-old restaurant manual has revealed unusual dishes and the philosophy of a pioneering Western-style restaurant.

Stretching north from Shijo Street to Sanjo Street in central Kyoto, Shin-Kyogoku is one of the city's best-known shopping destinations, attracting both local residents and tourists. Yet behind its modern storefronts lies a history closely connected to Kyoto's transformation during the early Meiji period. One of the street's most unusual features is the presence of seven temples and one shrine nestled among the shops. Their entrances stand alongside retail businesses, creating a distinctive streetscape where religious institutions and commercial establishments share the same narrow thoroughfare. The arrangement reflects the area's origins as temple grounds. Before the Meiji era, much of what is now Shin-Kyogoku formed part of the precincts of Buddhist temples, some with histories stretching back more than 1,000 years. The shopping street emerged following major political and social changes in the early Meiji period. After the emperor relocated to Tokyo in 1869, Kyoto experienced a significant decline in population and economic activity, leaving parts of the former capital struggling to recover. A government ordinance issued in 1871 reorganizing land held by temples and shrines provided an opportunity to redevelop the area. A new commercial street was established through former temple grounds as part of efforts to restore economic vitality to central Kyoto. The name Shin-Kyogoku, meaning "New Kyogoku," was derived from the neighboring Teramachi Street, historically associated with the eastern edge of the old capital. The new thoroughfare was intended to create a lively commercial district that would help revive the city's economy. Among its longest-established businesses is Sarashina Honten, a restaurant founded 152 years ago that specializes in kishimen, the flat wheat noodles more commonly associated with Nagoya. Now operated by the sixth generation of the founding family, Sarashina traces its distinctive menu to its first proprietor, who came from Aichi Prefecture and introduced kishimen to Kyoto at a time when the dish was relatively unfamiliar to local diners. Although the restaurant is one of Shin-Kyogoku's oldest surviving businesses, its operators say that 150 years is still considered relatively young in Kyoto, where some merchants have operated for 300 or 400 years and temples can trace their histories back 600 to 800 years or longer. Sarashina's signature kishimen has evolved considerably from its Nagoya origins. The restaurant developed an exceptionally thin version of the noodles, measuring less than one millimeter in thickness, to complement Kyoto's delicate broth. Achieving that texture required changes to the flour mixture because noodles rolled so thinly are particularly prone to breaking. The restaurant also refined its individual dishes to suit local tastes, gradually establishing a distinctive Kyoto-style kishimen. The noodles are served with ingredients including bonito flakes and fried tofu, which absorbs the broth. The thinner noodles have a greater surface area relative to their thickness, allowing the soup to coat them particularly well. The restaurant's continued success followed years of experimentation. When kishimen was first introduced, Kyoto residents showed little interest in a noodle dish associated with another region, making it difficult to attract customers. Rather than abandon the specialty, successive generations adapted the recipe until it became an established part of the local dining scene. Another landmark of Shin-Kyogoku is Star Shokudo, a Western-style restaurant that celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2025 and has grown into a business operating 17 locations, mainly in Kyoto. Founded by Kotaro, who had traveled to the United States before returning to Japan, the restaurant was established with the ambition of making Western cuisine accessible to ordinary Japanese diners. At the time, Western-style meals were still unfamiliar to many people in Kyoto. Even knives and forks were a novelty for some customers, and the restaurant's early mission was to introduce new dining customs as well as new dishes. Its founder displayed a message promoting the popularization of Western cuisine, reflecting his belief that access to such food was part of Japan's broader modernization and rising prosperity. Over the following century, Star Shokudo became a familiar destination for Kyoto residents seeking Western-style dishes for family outings and special occasions. Its most popular dish today is an omurice gratin with cheese and demi-glace sauce, combining the Japanese interpretation of a Western omelet with baked gratin. The dish is designed to remain relatively light despite its rich appearance, with the seasoning of the rice, cheese and sauce carefully balanced to avoid overwhelming flavors. However, one of the restaurant's most remarkable discoveries came during preparations for its centennial celebrations, when staff researching the company's history uncovered a service manual dating to 1935, just 10 years after the business was founded. The document, preserved for approximately 90 years, provides an unusually detailed account of how restaurant employees were expected to conduct themselves during the early Showa period. Because the original is fragile, the restaurant has scanned its pages and produced printed copies for examination. The manual contains practical instructions covering customer service, personal appearance, language and professional conduct. Employees were told to speak standard Japanese rather than regional dialects and to greet customers properly when they entered the restaurant. It also contains a system of abbreviated names for menu items, providing a glimpse into dishes served at the restaurant during its early years. Among the more surprising entries is rabbit cutlet, abbreviated as "Usa-Ka," indicating that rabbit meat once appeared on the restaurant's menu. Other entries include seasonal ingredients such as matsutake mushrooms, suggesting that the restaurant incorporated both Western culinary influences and traditional Japanese seasonal foods. Perhaps the most puzzling discovery was a menu item described as "newspaper breakfast," alongside references to newspaper-related meals. The exact meaning remains uncertain, but restaurant staff suggested that customers may once have been able to order breakfast accompanied by access to a newspaper. At a time when newspapers were relatively expensive and not necessarily available in every household, the opportunity to read one while eating could have been an attraction in itself. The theory remains speculative, however, and the original purpose of the unusual menu item has not been established. Beyond its descriptions of food and service, the manual contains a series of philosophical statements expressing the founder's views on work, personal development and the meaning of life. One passage declares, "To live is not merely to breathe, but to accomplish something." Another states, "Those who have never eaten bread with tears cannot understand the taste of life." The sayings suggest that the founder viewed restaurant employment as more than simply a means of earning a living. Staff were encouraged to develop their character, take responsibility for their futures and pursue ambitions beyond their immediate duties. The manual also promoted the idea that employees should think of themselves as future leaders rather than permanent subordinates, encouraging them to acquire the knowledge and confidence necessary to become independent. The rediscovered document has impressed current restaurant executives, who say its advice remains relevant despite the enormous changes in Japan's restaurant industry over the past nine decades. What began as a collection of workplace instructions has come to be regarded as a broader guide to personal and professional life, emphasizing courtesy, determination, responsibility and individual achievement. The discovery illustrates how Shin-Kyogoku's long-established businesses have preserved not only recipes and commercial traditions but also the ideals of the entrepreneurs who helped shape modern Kyoto. Join Shizuka as she strolls the iconic street food and rolls up her sleeves to make Nagano soba from scratch! ( Japan by Food )

scraped.h1: Typhoon No. 32 Set to Intensify Before Approaching Japan Islands
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - As of 9 p.m. on November 8, Typhoon No. 32, known internationally as Champaka, was moving west-northwest over waters south of Japan with a central atmospheric pressure of 970 hectopascals and maximum sustained winds of 35 meters per second, with forecasts indicating that it could intensify into a very strong typhoon before approaching the Ogasawara Islands around Wednesday, November 11.

Satellite imagery showed a well-developed spiral of clouds surrounding the storm's center over waters south of the Ogasawara Islands, with particularly active cloud formations near its core. Additional rain clouds were developing north of the storm along a frontal system, raising concerns that unsettled weather could reach the islands even before the typhoon itself approaches. The typhoon was traveling west-northwest at approximately 20 kilometers per hour on November 8 and was expected to maintain that general direction through the morning of November 9. Its movement was then forecast to slow considerably, with the storm potentially becoming almost stationary by the evening. During this period of slower movement, Typhoon No. 32 was expected to strengthen further, with maximum sustained winds near its center reaching 45 meters per second, equivalent to approximately 162 kilometers per hour, bringing it into the very strong typhoon category. An approaching upper-level trough was expected to alter the prevailing winds and steer the typhoon eastward from November 10. By the evening, the storm was forecast to move across waters southwest of the Ogasawara Islands while maintaining very strong intensity. Current projections suggest the typhoon is most likely to pass south of Chichijima and Hahajima during the morning of November 11, although changes in its track could affect the severity of conditions across the islands. The storm is expected to weaken rapidly after November 11 as it continues eastward, moving away from the Japanese archipelago. By November 12 and November 13, it is forecast to approach waters near the International Date Line while continuing to lose strength. Heavy rain could begin affecting the Ogasawara Islands on November 10 as the frontal system extending north of the typhoon brings rain clouds into the area. Forecasters warned that significant rainfall could develop even while the storm's center remains some distance from the islands. Rain is expected to continue intermittently from the night of November 10 through the morning of November 11, with periods of locally intense rainfall possible. Although the latest projected track suggests that the most developed rain clouds surrounding the typhoon's center are unlikely to pass directly over the islands, residents have been advised to remain alert to sudden increases in rainfall. Strong winds are also expected, particularly from the latter half of November 10 through November 11. While the typhoon is currently forecast to pass far enough south to avoid bringing its most destructive winds directly across the islands, atmospheric conditions could still produce hazardous gusts. As the typhoon moves eastward, a high-pressure system is expected to extend southward from the north, increasing the pressure difference across the region. This could strengthen winds around the Ogasawara Islands independently of the typhoon's immediate circulation. Forecasters said strong winds could develop during this period, with instantaneous gusts potentially exceeding 20 meters per second, or 72 kilometers per hour, in some locations. Marine conditions are also expected to deteriorate as the typhoon approaches. Waves around parts of the Ogasawara Islands could reach heights of 3 to 4 meters around November 11, with elevated seas expected to persist throughout at least that day. The combination of intermittent heavy rain, strong winds and high waves could create hazardous conditions around Chichijima, Hahajima and surrounding coastal waters, particularly between November 10 and November 11. Residents and visitors have been urged to prepare for deteriorating weather, exercise caution near coastlines and monitor updated forecasts, as the typhoon's precise track and intensity will determine the extent of its impact on the islands.

A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck central Japan early on November 8th, registering an upper 5 on Japan's seismic intensity scale in Aichi Prefecture and injuring at least 21 people, while damaging buildings and disrupting Shinkansen and conventional railway services across the region.

The Tokaido Shinkansen resumed normal-speed operations across its entire route at 8:57 a.m. on November 8th after a magnitude 5.7 earthquake disrupted rail services across central Japan, with JR Central reporting delays to 29 bullet trains affecting approximately 17,000 passengers, while Meitetsu restored services across its entire network by 9:15 a.m. following widespread morning suspensions.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree placing the Russian operations of Japan Tobacco (JT) under the temporary management of a local company, effectively stripping the Japanese tobacco giant of control over its business in the country and prompting a formal protest from Tokyo demanding that the measure be immediately withdrawn.

Bears preparing for winter hibernation may be able to determine when astringent persimmons have lost their bitterness and become suitable to eat, according to research by the University of Hyogo, which suggests that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees could help prevent bears from entering residential areas.

Osaka's iconic Midosuji boulevard hosted its first-ever bread-eating race on November 6 as part of a three-day event exploring new ways to use public space, with 1,200 servings of sweet bean buns and dorayaki pancakes prepared for participants over two days as the city moves ahead with plans to transform the major thoroughfare into a more pedestrian-friendly destination by 2037.

Sapporo deployed its distinctive Sasara snow-clearing tram for the first time this season early on November 7th, the second-earliest deployment in 10 years, after snowfall reached 8 centimeters at 4 a.m., prompting a vehicle to leave its depot to clear snow from the city's streetcar tracks.

East Japan Railway (JR East) opened its Haneda Airport Access Line construction site to the media on November 6, offering a glimpse of a major underground railway project that will connect Haneda Airport directly with central Tokyo, with services scheduled to begin in fiscal 2031.

Residents of Awaji Island, one of the Kansai region's most popular resort destinations, are facing growing disruption from vacation rentals, with complaints involving late-night drinking, outdoor barbecues, fireworks, illegal parking and garbage disposal violations, while one property operator has been accused of destroying a warning sign installed by neighbors.

A bear cub charged toward a family standing outside their home in Ome, western Tokyo, on November 3rd, rushing straight toward the front door moments after a high-pitched cry was heard from nearby bushes, in an encounter that left the resident shaken.

As of 3 a.m. on November 6, Typhoon No. 31 (In-fa) was moving northeast across the Pacific Ocean east of Japan at 75 kilometers per hour and was expected to become an extratropical cyclone by Friday afternoon, although dangerous swells and high waves could continue along Japan's Pacific coast throughout the day.

Six Pakistani nationals have been arrested on suspicion of repeatedly operating unauthorized taxi services for foreign tourists in Kyoto and other sightseeing destinations, with police investigating what they believe may be an organized operation involving additional suspects.

A smartphone caught fire at Narita Airport's Terminal 1 shortly after 7:30 a.m. on November 4th, prompting the dispatch of 10 fire trucks and other emergency vehicles before the blaze was extinguished about 30 minutes later, with no injuries reported.

scraped.title: An 11-Day-Old Baby Couldn’t Stop Bleeding. For Hours, the ER Didn’t Provide a Critical Vitamin Shot.
scraped.description: As more parents reject a long-standard shot for babies, hospitals are seeing cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding — once considered virtually eliminated. Doctors don’t always recognize or know how to treat the life-threatening condition.
scraped.author: Duaa Eldeib
scraped.h1: An 11-Day-Old Baby Couldn’t Stop Bleeding. For Hours, the ER Didn’t Provide a Critical Vitamin Shot.
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

A Simple Shot

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches , a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

The emergency room was a mile from their Texas home. Stephanie and Eric Biesenbach took comfort in that when their newborn daughter, Gwen, wouldn’t stop bleeding from her belly button. They buckled Gwen into her car seat and made the drive over.

Medical records from that warm August evening in 2023 described her condition as a “generic problem” of a bleeding umbilical cord stump. The doctor on duty, Nicole Malouf, had treated plenty of those as an emergency room specialist. She covered Gwen’s oozing belly button with a special gauze to stanch the flow, and when it appeared to stop, she sent Stephanie, Eric and Gwen on their way.

They made it as far as the parking lot before they noticed Gwen had bled through her footed pajamas. Eric slid his arm under the car seat handle and lifted his 11-day-old daughter out of the car. They walked back toward the glaring lights of the Lonestar 24HR ER, a freestanding emergency department in New Braunfels next to a car wash, a McDonald’s and a deli.

Stephanie told Malouf that Gwen had been bleeding a bit after the scab that replaced her umbilical cord stump fell off. The amount of blood they saw that night worried them. She ticked through Gwen’s history. No fever. No vomiting. Exclusively breastfed. She mentioned that she and Eric had declined a vitamin K shot when Gwen was born and instead had been giving Gwen oral vitamin K drops, which they trusted would protect her.

Malouf tried another type of pretreated gauze. When that didn’t work, medical records show, she turned to silver nitrate, a chemical applied to the tip of a long matchlike stick that cauterizes blood vessels. Malouf rotated one stick after another inside Gwen’s belly button.

Since the 1960s, the vast majority of newborns in the United States have received a vitamin K shot. The injection virtually eliminated vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare condition that can cause catastrophic bleeding and even death.

But a shift in recent years has threatened to upend the unwavering protection that many doctors and hospitals had taken for granted. Families — mistrustful of medical interventions, misled by social media and devoted to a birth experience they deem natural — have begun to shun the vitamin K shot.

A pair of studies published last week, both of which involved millions of births, found that babies who didn’t get the vitamin K shot had an increased risk of bleeding. One of the studies found that between 2017 and 2025, the rate of vitamin K deficiency bleeding increased a staggering 347%.

Without the single, inexpensive shot — which is not a vaccine — babies are dying . Autopsies reveal how babies’ systems shut down without warning and well-meaning parents who declined the vitamin K shot were left mourning the loss of their children.

Malouf kept trying to stop the bleeding. Over the course of nearly three hours, she used seven methods. At one point, she applied so much pressure to a bandage that, Stephanie said, Gwen threw up. The remedies essentially treated the symptoms and not the cause, like putting a cover on a leaking faucet.

Malouf said she called her husband, who’s also a doctor, as well as a nurse at a local hospital, to see if she was missing something. They, too, were at a loss. The nurse’s only suggestions were the ones that Malouf had already tried.

Malouf decided to transfer Gwen to a small, local hospital, which at least had pediatric specialists and a neonatal intensive care unit. But while she waited for a call back to confirm the hospital would accept Gwen, Stephanie walked out of the room to tell her that Gwen had bled through the latest dressing. Malouf, according to the records, quickly checked to see how long it was taking her blood vessels to refill. It was slower than when she arrived.

Gwen’s condition was growing more dire, and Malouf had reached the limits of what she could do. What followed also wouldn’t be enough.

Stephanie had given birth to Gwen without complications in an inflatable tub in their living room. She was perfect, with doelike eyes and a full head of brown hair that, when the light hit it, hinted at the red of her father’s beard.

Her older brothers and sisters fussed over her like a birthday present. Her aunts from California and Louisiana came in to meet her. When the house quieted, Gwen fell asleep to the calming rhythm of Stephanie’s chest rising and falling.

Stephanie marveled at the way Gwen seemed to study the faces of everyone who carried her. She wasn’t two weeks yet, but the corners of her mouth constantly turned up to form what her parents insisted were smiles. Even when her siblings passed her around, she rarely cried in protest.

Stephanie and Eric met in 2010, when they both worked at Chili’s. Texas natives, they had just returned home after spending time in Florida, where Stephanie spent a semester interning at Walt Disney World Resort.

“I was doing lawn care work and maintenance on restaurants,” Eric said before Stephanie interjected. “He moved there for a girl,” she said as the two erupted in laughter.

He proposed to Stephanie on Christmas Eve. They married at a vineyard on Halloween. The venue capped off the night with fireworks.

Life moved quickly after that. They had a daughter and two sons, then adopted the daughter of a relative who was too young to care for the child herself. Just when they thought their family was complete, Stephanie got pregnant with Gwen.

Overjoyed, they decided to name her after Stephanie’s grandmother, Gwendolyn, who passed down her flowered baby blanket with “Gwen” embroidered in the corner.

There were no signs something could be wrong with Gwen until the day her parents took her to the ER. Stephanie had texted her midwife first.

“So sorry to bother you,” she typed into her phone, writing that Gwen’s belly button had been bleeding most of the day and they couldn’t get it to stop.

“How much blood is too much blood,” she asked.

The midwife told her to send a photo. Stephanie sent two, one of dried blood on Gwen’s stomach and the other of a pile of bloodied tissues. The midwife instructed Stephanie to tape some gauze over Gwen’s belly button. About 90 minutes later, just before going to bed, she checked on Gwen again. She snapped another picture, this one with bright red blood soaking through the gauze and diaper, and texted it to the midwife. “Are you sure this is fine?”

The midwife told her to go to the emergency room.

In many states, all emergency rooms are in hospitals, where patients can be transferred to other units for more care. Not so in Texas, where more than 200 ERs are freestanding, separate and distinct from a hospital. At the ER, Gwen grew increasingly pale. Her heart raced at 177 beats a minute. Around 1:40 a.m., Stephanie and Eric received their first piece of good news: Malouf was transferring Gwen. She had scrapped her plan to send Gwen to the local hospital and would instead transfer her to North Central Baptist, a larger hospital in nearby San Antonio with more specialists. North Central was only about half an hour away, and it was sending a NICU transport team to get Gwen.

Eric’s eyes fixated on the large clock hanging in the room. Ten minutes passed, then 20, then 30, then an hour. He couldn’t understand what was taking so long. He stepped into the hallway and asked if he could just drive Gwen to the hospital.

But, he said, Malouf told him he couldn’t because it would be too dangerous. Malouf, however, said she told him that if he did leave, he would have to sign paperwork acknowledging he was doing so against medical advice. The transport team, she told him, would have blood and IVs. Besides, she said, Gwen was stable. Malouf called to check on the status of the ambulance; she was told they were on their way.

Stephanie and Eric said that was the last time they spoke to Malouf that night.

By the time the ambulance arrived, it had been nearly two hours since Malouf had requested it. One of the team’s first questions was whether Gwen had received a vitamin K shot.

The ER nurse told them they didn’t have the shot on hand.

It was the first time since walking into the ER, Stephanie said, that anyone suggested that vitamin K may be the culprit — and the cure.

At 3:45 a.m., within minutes of the ambulance team’s arrival, they gave Gwen a vitamin K shot in her left thigh. They spent the next two hours at her bedside, hooking her up to an IV, drawing blood for lab tests and giving her antibiotics — all things that, the records show, hadn’t been done yet. Malouf didn’t respond to questions about why not.

Stephanie and Eric observed the ambulance team as they worked, bantering, discussing another call that had come in and, just as they were about to leave, waiting for one of them to go to the bathroom. Between what they viewed as the team’s laidback pace and Malouf’s reassurances that Gwen was stable, Stephanie and Eric were encouraged enough to split up. Eric went home to the kids, who had been with his mom all night, to get them ready for their first day of school. Stephanie stayed and planned to ride with Gwen in the ambulance.

“Grab me a change of clothes and coffee,” Stephanie called to him as he was leaving.

The team transferred Gwen to a temperature-controlled enclosed incubator. As they packed up to leave, Gwen began to whimper. With each breath, Stephanie said, she let out a weak, high-pitched sound. It was unnatural. Stephanie reached through the incubator’s opening and ran her hands back and forth across her daughter’s chest.

The team loaded Gwen onto the ambulance and flipped on the sirens and lights. At 5:55 a.m., they headed down Interstate 35. It had been seven hours since Gwen was first admitted to the ER.

Stephanie appreciated the importance of vitamin K. All of her other children got the vitamin K shot shortly after they were born. But over the years, she and her husband had grown wary of medical intervention. When their youngest son was nearly 2, they fell behind on his vaccines. After getting several vaccines at one appointment, they said, he developed a high fever and suddenly stopped talking for about a year. He was later diagnosed with autism.

“I think that they just gave him too much at once,” Eric said.

Research studies from numerous sources have found that multiple vaccines taken at once do not overwhelm or weaken a child’s immune system. They also do not increase the risk of serious or long-term adverse effects.

Still, seeing their son struggle to speak, Stephanie and Eric were convinced there was a connection. They stopped vaccinating their children after that.

Before Gwen’s birth, Stephanie’s midwife gave her a five-page handout on newborn vitamin K. It covered why babies need vitamin K to help their blood clot and cautioned that babies who don’t have enough of it can start to bleed without warning.

The handout compared the pros and cons of the vitamin K shot with oral vitamin K drops, noting that the drawbacks of the drops are that some babies may not be able to absorb them or may spit them up. They also don’t eliminate the risk of bleeding entirely. Stephanie initially signed the document agreeing to the shot, but as her due date neared, she and Eric changed their minds. If both are effective, they reasoned, why not go for the option that didn’t involve sticking their baby with a needle?

“We did our own research. I don’t remember feeling like there were red flags,” Stephanie said. “I felt like the information we had was sufficient.”

She doesn’t recall exactly what sources she consulted, but she read articles online and spoke to some people who worked in the medical field. No one, she said, warned her against the drops. But she didn’t ask her mother, Lauren Hoel, a longtime family nurse practitioner. Stephanie knew exactly what her mom would say.

Many medical experts consider the drops inferior for several reasons, including those mentioned in the handout. There are also concerns about harried parents of a newborn forgetting a dose and the fact that cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding have been reported even when drops are used.

Only limited data exists about vitamin K drops, and much of it is from Europe, where the drops are more common. In the U.S., the Food and Drug Administration does not provide oversight of the drops. Instead, parents can simply add them to their Amazon carts without any verification of what’s in them, or whether they’re safe or effective.

A single vitamin K shot acts quickly, and then the liver stores the rest of the vitamin K to slowly release into the baby’s system over months.

For decades, the recommendation from doctors, hospitals and medical organizations has been the shot. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the World Health Organization call for giving the shot to all newborns.

“While some countries outside of the U.S. sometimes administer vitamin K orally, it has not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration,” the American Academy of Pediatrics wrote in May , reiterating its longstanding position, “and it is less effective than an intramuscular injection.”

Stephanie and Eric’s choice to opt for the drops reflects a broader trend. Vaccine skepticism grew after the COVID-19 pandemic, and under the direction of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a fierce vaccine critic and champion of the Make America Healthy Again movement, the federal government has fed those doubts. Stephanie and Eric, who voted for President Donald Trump and are ardent supporters of both Kennedy and MAHA, welcomed the change.

In December, the CDC stopped recommending that all newborns get the hepatitis B vaccine. In January, the agency revised its childhood vaccination schedule, reducing the number of routinely recommended shots by six. A federal judge temporarily blocked that move in March, but the CDC’s decisions appear to have caused a ripple effect beyond vaccines.

After the January change to the vaccine schedule, an analysis of more than a million newborns found a rise in the rate of babies not receiving the vitamin K shot so sharp that it resembled a hockey stick. Between January and June of this year, the analysis found, the rate jumped from 5.2% to 8.1%. Despite being asked multiple times at a congressional hearing to assure parents that the vitamin K shot is safe, Kennedy responded by declaring that he has not said anything publicly about the shot. An HHS spokesperson did not answer ProPublica’s questions but said that the CDC recommends that parents give newborns the vitamin K shot within six hours of their birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

In the ambulance, Gwen’s blood pressure dropped.

“Infant looks much more lethargic,” the team wrote in their notes.

They placed a mask on Gwen to increase her oxygen and gave her an infusion of saline in hopes of improving her blood volume.

Gwen’s condition continued to deteriorate. Almost immediately after they arrived at the hospital, her heart stopped. Doctors inserted a breathing tube then began pressing down on her chest with two fingers to manually pump blood through her body. They pushed epinephrine into her IV to stimulate her heart. That appeared to work.

Stephanie couldn’t comprehend what was happening. All night, she said, no one had acted like Gwen’s life was in danger. Suddenly, her daughter was covered in tubes and doctors were performing CPR.

Stephanie said she heard someone yelling into a phone, “Where is the blood?”

She texted her family. “I need you to pray for Gwen like her life depends on it,” she wrote.

She called Eric. “You need to get here now,” she told him.

Eric pressed on the gas pedal of Stephanie’s Honda and sped to the hospital. There, he pushed through a clutch of doctors to find Stephanie crying in the corner of the room. The same wave of shock that had washed over his wife minutes earlier crashed over him. For the first time, he worried he might lose his daughter.

They prayed together, and the chaplain stopped by the room to check on them. He noted, according to records, that they were anxious but hopeful.

Less than two hours after she was admitted, Gwen crashed again. The medical team called a code blue. Doctors performed CPR for the next 34 minutes. They gave her epinephrine four more times. She had lost so much blood. Her heart was barely pumping. Doctors told Stephanie and Eric that they could keep trying to resuscitate Gwen or they could take her off the machines for her parents to hold her.

Stephanie sobbed. Eric collapsed at her knees. She told him she couldn’t make the call. Eric said they wanted to spend the final moments with their daughter. The doctors unhooked Gwen from the beeping machines and handed her to him. Stephanie and Eric told Gwen how much they loved her and how much they were going to miss her.

Shortly after 9 a.m., nearly 11 hours after they’d first brought her to the ER, Gwen took her last breath. The team ushered them to another room where families can mourn in private. They spent hours there. They gave Gwen a bath. Family stopped by. Stephanie’s sister picked up their kids from school so they could say goodbye to their baby sister. Two nurses came in to create molds of Gwen’s hands and feet.

When Eric and Stephanie finally left the hospital, Gwen’s car seat was empty. Their two youngest children slept in their bed that night. At one point, Stephanie jolted awake. She turned to Eric. The look in his eyes told her that it hadn’t been a dream. Without making a sound that could wake their kids, they cried themselves back to sleep.

Eric’s grief soon morphed into anger. His brother-in-law drove him to the Lonestar ER to ask for Gwen’s medical records. He didn’t trust himself to go in, so he asked his brother-in-law to retrieve them.

The file was just 15 pages with the payment and registration forms. They searched for any clue that could explain what happened to their daughter.

“I was constantly assured that it wasn’t that bad,” Eric said. “I can’t tell you how many times they said, ‘Don’t worry, babies are very resilient.’”

They planned Gwen’s funeral. When they couldn’t find a coffin small enough to fit her tiny 8-pound body, Eric’s brother, who makes custom cabinets, built one. They wrapped Gwen in the flowered baby blanket from Stephanie’s grandmother for the viewing.

Stephanie and Eric operated on parallel tracks those next several months: mourning their daughter and trying to understand what led to her death. The family attended a grief camp put on by a local hospice group. They painted a garden pole with things that reminded them of Gwen. When Thanksgiving approached, they escaped to Stephanie’s sister’s house in Colorado to avoid questions about how they were doing.

Eric got Gwen’s handprints tattooed on his chest, the last place he felt them before she died. Stephanie picked Gwen’s footprints, but the tattoo artist had to size them down to fit.

“She had such big feet,” Eric said. “She was gonna be a tall girl.”

“Or clown,” Stephanie said, half laughing, half crying. “One of the two.”

They also reached out to Byron Miller, a medical malpractice attorney, who sought records from Malouf, the ER, the ambulance company and the hospital. Miller investigated whether negligence in Gwen’s care resulted in her death. But the medical expert hired to review the case homed in on Stephanie and Eric’s decision to give Gwen the vitamin K drops instead of the shot. Without an expert’s supporting opinion, which Miller said was a state requirement, his office was unable to continue pursuing a case. Miller recommended that Stephanie and Eric follow up with the Texas Medical Board.

The ER, the ambulance company and the hospital did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The nurse on duty at Lonestar that night also did not respond to requests for comment.

Stephanie had several conversations with her mother, who remembers learning in the 1980s, while in nursing school, that all babies need a vitamin K shot at birth. Hoel didn’t know that Stephanie and Eric didn’t get the vitamin K shot for Gwen.

“It never occurred to me that people would refuse the vitamin K shot,” she said.

Even with that, Hoel couldn’t look past Malouf’s actions that night.

“She should have said, ‘That’s a newborn. Take it to a NICU,’” Hoel said. “And by not doing that, the fate was sealed.”

That next December, Stephanie sat down at the kitchen table and pulled out her laptop. Someone, she said, had to hold Malouf accountable. She found the website for the Texas Medical Board and followed the instructions to file a complaint.

“When Dr Malouf decided to provide medical care to our daughter, despite her lack of training in neonatal emergency care, and lack of appropriate monitoring equipment,” Stephanie wrote to the board, “Gwen was deprived of any potential life saving intervention.”

The seven hours they spent at the ER that night, she continued, could have been used to save Gwen’s life. And she stressed that the ER nurse said the facility didn’t carry the vitamin K injection.

“If Vitamin K was a vital part of the evening,” she wrote, “then we should have been pointed to another location that was fully equipped sooner.”

Malouf became the target of her anger and her anguish. She described how painful it was to drive by the Lonestar billboard with Malouf’s giant photo near her house every day. She wrote that Malouf failed to recognize that her daughter’s life was in danger. “I just don’t understand how it can go from a calm relaxed environment to all of a sudden your child is dead,” she wrote to the board. She recounted feeling intimidated when Eric asked if they could leave when Gwen’s color began to change and Malouf advised against it.

“To this date,” she wrote, “Dr Nicole Malouf does not even know that my daughter died under her care.”

After Gwen died, Malouf said, a doctor from the hospital called. The news, she said, came as a surprise.

Sitting in her home office, her framed degrees hanging on the wall behind her, Malouf spoke to ProPublica for nearly three hours about what happened. Malouf and her husband have three daughters, for whom she is team mom for cheerleading and president of the Fine Arts Boosters. Racks of uniforms filled her home’s entryway in preparation for an upcoming sale.

She said she repeatedly relived the details of that night with her therapist. The first few sessions, she said, were just the two of them crying. She said they discussed what was in her control and what wasn’t. Every life is precious, she said, but it’s one thing to lose a 95-year-old grandmother with a long list of medical problems. It’s another to lose a baby.

“I still have my three daughters,” Malouf said, pushing back her long, dark hair, “and now she has lost hers.”

Malouf said the doctor who called said the hospital would conduct its own review. Malouf said the doctor mentioned that they had already identified some issues, including questions about the transport team.

The hospital wasn’t the only one probing the night’s events. The state Medical Board also launched an investigation. The board subpoenaed records and reviewed the medical documents.

In September 2025, the board held a virtual hearing, which was closed to the public. Stephanie and Eric appeared, as did Malouf and her attorney. The board staff attorney charged that Malouf did not meet the standard of care in her treatment of Gwen and that she failed to halt or limit Gwen’s bleeding. Her lack of timely care, the board’s attorney alleged, ultimately resulted in Gwen’s death. Citing confidentiality, the board would not release a recording or transcript of the hearing.

The next month, the board issued its decision. It found that Malouf failed to recognize that Gwen had a life-threatening vitamin K-dependent bleeding disorder. The ER did not have vitamin K shots on site, and Malouf failed to immediately transfer Gwen to a regional pediatric referral hospital better equipped to handle Gwen’s condition. Finally, the board found that Malouf had failed to quantify the amount of blood lost by Gwen.

The board required her to take 24 hours of continuing medical education; she said she completed her hours in courses on pediatric advanced life support, communicating with patients and vitamin K deficiency bleeding. She also had to inform her employers that she had been disciplined. Malouf neither admitted nor denied the allegations but agreed to abide by the board’s final order.

A board spokesperson would not answer specific questions about Gwen’s case but said the board expects all licensees “to provide appropriate treatment and, if the necessary supplies are not available, to make arrangements for transport to a higher level of care.”

“I felt that I had done everything that I could with the resources I had,” Malouf told ProPublica.

She said she did know that Gwen had vitamin K deficiency bleeding, even though she did not immediately give Gwen a vitamin K shot. Malouf said she thinks the board didn’t believe that she knew because she didn’t act “in a panicked manner.” It remains unclear, even to her, whether the ER carried the vitamin K shot at the time or if it was just in a spot where the nurse couldn’t find it. But she said she asked the nurse for it.

Either way, she believed that giving Gwen vitamin K at that point would just be to make her chart look good.

“It’s really not even going to take effect at that stage,” Malouf said. “As soon as you give vitamin K, the earliest it’s even going to start working is 10 to 12 hours.”

But several doctors told ProPublica that vitamin K should be given immediately if there’s even a suspicion that a baby has vitamin K deficiency bleeding. It’s so vital to stopping the bleeding that they don’t even need to wait for a confirmation. There is no downside, they said, to giving it. Vitamin K, they said, may need to be followed up by blood or blood products, such as fresh frozen plasma, which is rich in the proteins that help the blood clot.

While vitamin K can quickly help to halt the bleeding, it can’t reverse the bleeding that’s already occurred. It also has to be given in time, and some babies need more than one dose of vitamin K to recover. Gwen, as one doctor who reviewed her medical records put it, needed vitamin K, blood and blood products much sooner than she got them.

Malouf said she had learned about vitamin K deficiency bleeding in medical school and during her residency, but she doesn’t recall ever seeing it in practice. Nearly every medical student learns about the coagulation cascade, but not all doctors know or remember how to diagnose and treat an infant who shows up in an ER bleeding, often in the brain and invisible to the eye. Some completed their training at a time when vitamin K deficiency bleeding was still considered a historic condition, much like measles.

The ER staff, Malouf said, has been subsequently trained on the importance of vitamin K, and the ER keeps it in stock. All ERs, she said, should carry vitamin K.

“I still gravely regret that the outcome was still the same,” she said, “even after again assuming that, ‘Hey, I’m putting this baby in y’all’s hands. You guys are the experts. Fix her.’”

Malouf doesn’t understand how the board found that her care that night fell short. She didn’t intentionally harm her patient.

“I can state my whole case and literally one of the board members goes, ‘Well, I just don’t believe you,’” Malouf recalled. “I said, ‘Well, then I don’t know what more to tell you.’”

In addition to working at the ER, she had a part-time job doing telehealth. The telehealth company that employed her, she said, fired her once she disclosed the board’s action. As of August, she was still working some shifts at Lonestar ER; the board’s decision didn’t affect her ability to practice. Following the interview with ProPublica, she declined further comment.

“I feel like the only way to change the outcome is to go back to the beginning, that fork in the road,” Malouf said. “And go, ‘OK, well let’s give vitamin K after birth.”

Stephanie and Eric also have asked themselves what they would have done differently. They wished they had left the ER that night and driven Gwen to a hospital.

“We were just trusting that the person who went to school their whole life for this would know more than us,” Eric said.

In their minds, the role of vitamin K has overshadowed the medical mistakes they believe are most responsible for their daughter’s death. By the time Gwen had arrived at the hospital, her organs were already starting to shut down. The autopsy found that she had tiny spots of bleeding in her kidneys and small intestine and a small scrape on her chest where doctors pushed down for CPR. The medical examiner noted Gwen’s precipitous decline and listed her cause of death as vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

If they could go back, both agreed they would get the vitamin K shot for Gwen.

“I don’t trust a lot of things,” Stephanie said, “but get peace of mind and get the vitamin K shot.”

A few months after Gwen’s death, Stephanie found out she was pregnant with a little girl. They were so ready to love a baby again. She gave birth to her in 2024. This summer, they welcomed another baby girl.

Both got vitamin K shots.

scraped.h1: The Unrelenting Ordeal of Wildfire Recovery
scraped.body_text:
Second of two stories about the effort to support Lahaina fire survivors’ health in the long, hard aftermath. Read the first story, about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, here .

LAHAINA, Hawaiʻi—As Mikey Burke walked into her acupuncture appointment on a Wednesday morning in May, she felt the energy shift, just as she always does.

Noelani Ahia, 51, an acupuncturist and Hawaiian healer, greeted Burke, 42, with a smile and a hug, and led her away from the sunlit, open-air courtyard of the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center and into a dark room, walled in with dividers and empty except for a single bed, a chair and a few small tables. As they settled in, they spoke about Lahaina.

Burke, a mother of four, has been going to the local health center since her home burned down three years ago in the deadliest U.S. wildfires in more than a century. Sometimes, it feels like these appointments are the only time she can truly breathe.

“I don’t think people realize how hard a time people are still having,” said Ahia, who directs Maui Medic Healers Hui, a community organization that operates out of the state-run center. “Pretty much no one is fine.”

“And we’re almost worse off now than we were right after the fires,” Burke replied.

“Can you say a little bit more about that,” Ahia asked, softly.

Burke’s appointment was one day before a construction crew would pour the cement foundation of her family’s future home, and the same week that the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study might be shutting down for good.

As she started to speak, Burke fought back tears.

“The fire was a point in time,” she began, her voice breaking as she laid out a chronology that disaster survivors know all too well.

In the immediate aftermath, the first, most acute trauma was that everything was gone, she explained. But now there’s a slower, unrelenting ordeal of all that has fallen apart since.

It’s not just about the destruction of her family’s house, which she’d fought for years to find and secure. It’s her family’s mental health, the loss of friends and neighbors who were priced out and moved away, the fights to address water access, regain local control of land rights, advocate for her children’s Hawaiian immersion school and protect her people’s ability to be Hawaiian in this place that has been taken over by colonizers and corporate interests again and again. She and her neighbors have to be strong for every battle. Everything feels too important; nothing can fall through the cracks.

It was in this building that Burke found out about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, a University of Hawai‘i research project both quantifying the health impacts of the wildfires and helping survivors navigate them. Burke participated in MauiWES with her husband and four boys, and it was through the study that she learned that her twins, then just 10, were showing signs of post-traumatic stress disorder. It was also how she’d enrolled them in therapy.

Noelani Ahia inserts acupuncture needles in Mikey Burke’s leg, part of her practice with Maui Medic Healers Hui.

But keeping the study funded had been an ongoing struggle, and a few days before Burke’s acupuncture appointment, organizers held a weekend-long event to collect survivors’ health information for what they feared could be the last time.

It made Burke angry. She’d seen what the study had done for her boys. She felt how deeply her community was still struggling. If no one tracked her community’s health, then how would they know, years from now, how the fires changed them? How would they know how to heal?

“There’s always something that we have to fight,” she continued, her tears now falling fast. “We can’t even just be in our own grief.”

The Maui wildfires on Aug. 8, 2023, destroyed more than 2,200 buildings and killed more than 100 people. The Burkes were among the nearly 13,000 displaced.

For months after the fires, Mikey, her husband, Rob, their four sons and four dogs were shuttled between family and friends’ homes, hotel rooms and finally to the two-bedroom, one-bathroom rental where they’re now living, another waystation in the long wait for a new home.

Three years out, she was still meeting people who hadn’t heard about the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center or MauiWES, who had been so swept up in surviving, day-to-day, they hadn’t had time to seek support. It was clear to her there was a pressing need for these health resources.

In the dimly lit room at the health center, the magnitude of it all rose and took over. She fell into Ahia’s arms, shaking, and the older woman stroked her back with strong, fluid movements.

“I’ve got you,” Ahia said. “You’re carrying so much.”

Burke took a deep breath through her tears.

“Just for today, just for this little bit of time, we’re gonna set it down,” Ahia continued, her voice low and calm. “We’re going to take the pōhaku out, even though the pōhaku is your kuleana.”

Her worldly responsibilities, her kuleana, are like pōhaku, stones, weighing her down every day, Ahia explained. But for now, she could set them aside.

Burke’s shoulders softened, the tension of the morning dissipating.

This is a central part of Ahia’s work. Her clients come in with a lifetime of wounds, small and large, their nervous systems shot by unending, compounding traumas. She refers to it as colonial inflammation, how years of layered injustices pile on and manifest in a physiological response to stress. A Native Hawaiian diaspora kid who grew up on the continent and returned to Hawai‘i as a young adult, Ahia blends teachings from Hawaiian healing and traditional Chinese medicine into her practice.

She co-founded what grew into Maui Medic Healers Hui in 2019 to care for protesters opposing an observatory on Mauna Kea, a volcano on Hawai‘i island considered sacred by many Native Hawaiians. After the 2023 fires, the organization mobilized to support survivors. Now, many of Ahia’s patients are still feeling the disaster’s aftershocks.

“Can I share a thought?” Ahia asked cautiously, and Burke nodded, her breathing slowing down.

“Before the fires, we all knew about the colonial bullshit that we all go through and how difficult it is, but we had our regular daily lives to keep us busy so we didn’t always have to see it and acknowledge it,” Ahia said.

Burke nodded again as Ahia continued.

“But one patient said to me that now that everything is literally, physically gone, there’s nowhere to hide. So all the pieces of the historical trauma and the current colonial structure that we’re still being oppressed by are screaming at us,” she said.

Lahaina was once the royal seat of the Hawaiian Kingdom and had a lush, green landscape with abundant waterways. But centuries of colonial extraction—first through sugar and pineapple plantations run by American and European companies and then through tourism—diverted water away from Lahaina and helped create today’s arid conditions.

The 2023 fires added fuel to West Maui’s longstanding water conflict. They also highlighted challenges to land ownership for Native Hawaiians and other long-time local families dealing with insurance shortfalls, foreclosure threats, complicated rebuilding requirements and long waitlists for housing.

“The wound is wide open and it’s constantly having dirt put in it,” Ahia continued. “We have to help each other take the dirt out of the wounds.”

Burke and many of her neighbors saw in the aftermath of the fires an opportunity to change course and rebuild with local priorities at the forefront. She helped found the Lahaina Community Land Trust , a nonprofit that works to help families rebuild and keep land in local hands.

For Burke, standing up for Lahaina doesn’t feel like a choice. It’s her kuleana, her responsibility. She can’t imagine another way of being than to be in the fight.

But even as she advocates for resources to help her neighbors, Burke hesitates to accept help for her own family, which faces the same challenges. The aid could go to someone else who needs it more, she tells herself.

“We shouldn’t have to be this strong and resilient,” Ahia said, and Burke laughed in agreement. “So for right now you don’t have to be strong or resilient, you can just be unmasked.”

Burke climbed onto the table, lay on her back and closed her eyes. Ahia swabbed each of her ears and began placing acupuncture needles in her hands and feet.

Her hands over Burke’s chest, Ahia began a pule ho‘ōla, a healing prayer. Her voice reverberated as she chanted, asking for the heavens to open, the rain to fall, the earth and its people to be nourished.

Burke was distracted when she arrived that morning, thinking about the lei she had to make for her twin boys’ fifth-grade graduation later that day. Flowering trees used to be abundant, found in every neighbor’s backyard. In recent years they’d dwindled as gentrification pushed local families away. Then the fires came, burning most homes and trees down. Now, she knows of just a handful of flowering trees remaining in Lahaina, their blossoms in high demand. Just one more thing the flames took.

Burke comes to the center for talk therapy as well as her sessions with Ahia. Her twin boys attend therapy and a weekly video gaming group. Her husband, a transplant from California, doesn’t like talking about his feelings and isn’t drawn to talk therapy. But his body is showing the toll of the stress from the fires and a lifetime of manual labor.

Rob had an appointment scheduled for September, just before his 45th birthday, to remove a lesion on his nose, his latest bout with skin cancer. And when MauiWES ran tests on him, he learned that he—like many wildfire survivors here, including his wife—had elevated levels of heavy metals in his body and breathing problems. He listened to Mikey talk about her experience at the center and agreed to sign up for acupuncture and lomilomi massage there, too.

A few hours after Mikey Burke’s appointment, in the room next door, 11-year-old Makoa Burke was laser-focused on smashing Mario to a pulp.

He’d taken a couple of hits so far, but it was still early in the game. He was facing straight ahead, camo baseball hat turned to one side, eyes narrowed with concentration, feet fidgeting in and out of his Crocs.

Then, Makoa’s avatar ballooned on screen and his hammer came down hard on his opponent. A few feet away, Kaleohano Burke spun his chair around, eyes wide, watching his twin brother’s victory with glee. His lei were lying on the table, but he still wore the gray kīhei, knotted at his left shoulder, from their fifth-grade graduation ceremony that day. Raising a hand covered in bright orange powder, he scarfed down a Cheeto.

Makoa’s eyes remained trained on the screen.

“I’m surviving,” he said to the room, or maybe to himself. “No more dying.”

Christopher Knightsbridge, a therapist who works on the MauiWES study, sat quietly to the side of the room and watched the boys, leaning back in his chair with his hands behind his head.

As the hour went by, the table piled up with empty bags of Doritos, SunChips and the clear crowd favorite, Cheetos. About half an hour in, the Capri-Suns had run out, so Kaleohano cracked open a pack of organic apple juice boxes.

Since the fires, Mikey and Rob Burke had seen changes in their sons. Kaleohano began having nightmares and Makoa, who had always been a fiercely independent child, hovered around his parents, distraught at a hint of separation. They’d get triggered by smoke from a neighbor’s barbecue, unsettled until their parents took them to the source and proved, beyond a shred of doubt, that it was something distinct from the fire they’d fled as it burned their home, their street and nearly their entire town clear to the ground.

For months, the Burkes knew their kids were struggling. They were too. But the family was in survival mode, and addressing their mental health was one item on a long and impossible to-do list that included insurance paperwork, emergency housing, school, the logistics of rebuilding and continuing to support their community, where they counted their family lucky—sheltered and at least visibly uninjured. On top of everything, both parents had busy jobs: Rob as a construction worker and Mikey as the new West Maui community liaison for the state’s largest utility, Hawaiian Electric, which dealt with legal fallout after the fires.

Mikey remembers being in a state of shock when MauiWES staff said both boys were showing signs of PTSD. But Knightsbridge walked her over to the front desk of the center and helped her sign them up to see one of the mental health counselors there for free. In their second year of testing with MauiWES, after regular therapy and Knightsbridge’s gaming group sessions, their mental health scores had returned to a normal range.

The gaming group is separate from formal therapy, but Knightsbridge sees it as a part of the center’s holistic approach to healing. Many of the children he sees are navigating instability at home and trauma from the fires. The gaming group gives them a reason to leave their homes and socialize. Sometimes, it’s a safe, low-stakes space to open up.

But everything feels precarious. That week, it looked like MauiWES would be shutting down. And after leaving the Department of Health in the spring, Knightsbridge was working at the center on a federal emergency response grant that was nearing an end. He lives on O‘ahu but was spending half of most weeks on Maui, and he couldn’t imagine leaving his patients.

The next morning, Rob Burke stood surveying a construction crew at the site of the family’s former and future home. The sun beat down hard from a cloudless sky, and the empty lot offered no shade for the workers.

This was therapy for Rob. Watching as their build began at last was the first time since the fires that he felt he could really breathe.

Rob was dressed to shield his skin from the sun: dark sunglasses and a black, long-sleeve zip-up with the hood pulled over his head. From under each sleeve and on one leg beneath knee-length shorts, thick, bold tattoos emerged. The only other skin left uncovered was his nose, already bright pink and sunburnt.

Rob does finishing work for Crescent Homes, a local company, and plans to take that on at his family’s home too. For now, the house was just a grid on the ground under the blazing sun. Pipes stuck out where the bathrooms and laundry room will take shape.

Rob jokes that his body, his pale skin and Irish blood, wasn’t made for Hawaiʻi. But his soul was. Even with his home burned to ash and skyrocketing prices for seemingly everything, he couldn’t imagine leaving Lahaina. The place is special. It’s the land, its spirit, its mana. As soon as he moved here, he could feel it. It’s the only place Mikey had ever wanted to bring up their kids. Now, he feels the same way.

Mikey had just parked her car and was walking up the road to their house. In contrast to Rob’s head-to-toe sun protection, she was dressed for summer in denim shorts, a short-sleeved button down and a baseball hat that read, “You Are On Native Land.”

As he spotted his wife, Rob brightened, then quickly sobered. As excited as he was, he knew this would be a difficult day for her.

She approached Rob and they hugged, the weight of the morning left unsaid. Before long, a cement truck backed in from the street, and by a quarter to 10, the crew started pouring the foundation. Cement churned in the truck and was pushed through a crane before it gushed out of a vertical pipe and filled the grid on the ground.

Behind her sunglasses, Mikey began to cry. Rob pulled her into another hug as she shook with the sobs.

It was May, nearly three years since the fires, and they were only just starting to rebuild. She and Rob are taking on the job as owner-builders, without a general contractor. She doesn’t know when they’ll be able to get the materials to start building its frame. The length of the road ahead, full of unending unknowns, scares her. Her oldest son will be 18 by the time they’re ready to move back in, if they’re lucky. He might not even want to live here anymore.

The sun stayed high as the hours ticked by and the crew—most of whom Rob knew from work—labored steadily, pouring and smoothing the concrete. Rob passed around cool drinks and pizza.

As the day progressed, Mikey’s mood gradually lifted. The slab pouring felt like a metaphor. The foundation of the house, the start of their homecoming, the beginning of a new chapter in their family’s life. As the ground hardened, she and Rob could see it all beginning to take shape.

Around 1 p.m., Mikey left to pick up her kids a little early from school—she wanted them to be there to see this.

On the brief drive, she passed a neighbor’s home on the corner that was in the midst of construction. She remembered the beautiful house that had burned down, built in Lahaina’s plantation-era style and renovated by the current owner’s father, who has since passed away. That house was his legacy.

Throughout the burn zone, Lahaina was reemerging. The streets were bustling daily with construction crews in pickup trucks. A single block could house every stage of the construction process: a fully built home next to a wooden frame, beside two stories of scaffolding plastered with Tyvec paper flapping in the wind. Scattered throughout were empty lots, where homeowners moved away, sold their land or just haven’t been able to start building yet. Of the more than 2,200 structures destroyed by the fires, just over 300 have been rebuilt three years later.

Mikey picked up her son Maleko, then 16, at Lahainaluna High School and drove to Princess Nāhiʻenaʻena Elementary School just below it.
