scraped.title: Xi Jinping’s Chinese Dream Has Replaced the Maoist Credo
scraped.description: China’s leaders now appeal to the vision of a rejuvenated future rather than a revolutionary past. The new social contract between the people and the party state is a pragmatic one: social stability in return for continued economic growth.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

China’s leaders now appeal to the vision of a rejuvenated future rather than a revolutionary past. The new social contract between the people and the party state is a pragmatic one: social stability in return for continued economic growth.

Xi Jinping has promoted the idea of the “Chinese dream,” which is not merely a Chinese version of its American counterpart. While the American dream focuses on the individual, the Chinese dream is one of national rejuvenation. (Greg Baker / AFP via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

S ince 1978, China has undergone a series of seismic changes in its economic order that have radically altered its citizens’ relationship to both labor and land. They have unmade the socialist working class and are in the process of expropriating the peasantry, transforming both into a propertyless proletariat.

At the same time, China’s political structure has not undergone a similar revolution. Accordingly, the contradiction between its systems of economic and political organization is increasingly acute.

T he disjunctive fates of rural and urban China have been part of a single story ever since the establishment of the People’s Republic. It is the impoverished hinterland that subsidized the rise of the urban industry under state socialism.

Unlike in England during its industrial revolution, this development did not require the expropriation of rural land and a concomitant displacement of the peasantry. There, the enclosure movement provided both the capital and the labor for industrial development. In China, in contrast, there was no shortage of labor, and the state preferred to keep the peasants precisely where they were rather than allowing them to flow into cities and coalesce into a potentially explosive proletariat of the kind that had become common in much of the developing world.

To obtain industrial capital, the state simply extracted the economic surplus produced by the peasants while keeping the peasants themselves in place. This was the essence of primitive socialist accumulation. After China’s transition to state capitalism, the countryside has continued to subsidize urban development, supporting not only state capital but also private Chinese capital and global capital.

Urban industry no longer extracts just the product of rural labor but the peasants themselves, albeit on a rotational and provisional basis. This has taken the form of a “floating population” made up of hundreds of millions of semi-proletarianized migrant workers who continue to rely in part on collectively owned, nontransferable rural land cultivated by villagers left behind.

With the enclosure of rural land, China is in the process of converting its migrant labor force into permanent city dwellers, transforming an existing reserve army of workers into a reserve army of consumers as well — making them fully proletarianized. Moreover, it is not only the former migrant workers who are proletarianized as their displacement becomes permanent: the arrival of agrarian capitalism proletarianizes even those who remain in the countryside.

T he exploitation of the countryside for industrial development is emphatically not unique to China. Indeed, when viewed from a longer historical perspective, the birth of the new Chinese working class seems rather unexceptional: we have come to take it for granted that people work for wages. However, the sociologist Charles Tilly observes that as recently as 1700, only about 10 percent of the global workforce made their living by selling their labor power — “by selling themselves,” in Karl Marx’s phrase — whereas today, most of us do so.

What is distinctive about the fate of the Chinese working class is the specific way in which state socialism and state capitalism have become conjoined in China, with the former providing the foundation for the latter, as well as the temporal and spatial dimensions of this evolution. Processes of commodification of land and labor that took place over centuries in England have been compressed into just a few decades.

What is more, the People’s Republic of China claims an imperial footprint more encompassing than any other twentieth-century revolutionary state. Because of both the staggering speed of its transformation and its equally staggering size, China plays an oversize role in the development of global capitalism. Accordingly, the incorporation of rural and urban land, as well as rural and urban labor, into a single regime of state capitalism has both local and global implications.

The massive post-1978 reorganization of land, labor, and capital has left China with a series of internal contradictions. Perhaps the most outstanding one is the disjunction between its economic and political orders. The philosopher Jiwei Ci describes it as a contradiction between a radically new organization of desire and a largely unchanged political and ideological structure.

As the state has disavowed its material responsibilities to workers, economic relations have been reconfigured as those of freedom — essentially the freedom of being left alone to fend for oneself. Ci call this “de facto freedom,” a kind of freedom by default. While it is negative in origin, signifying the retreat of the state rather than a result of a social struggle, it has opened the way for seeking the satisfaction of private desires.

To the extent that the state wants China to become a nation of consumers, cultivating this desiring subject has become an economic imperative: while needs are limited, desires are boundless, and only desire can fuel consumption without limits. Ci contrasts this de facto economic freedom with freedom as a positive moral or political value.

I n the absence of a liberal ideology valorizing it, freedom by default is not capable of giving meaning to material prosperity, even if one is fortunate (or well connected) enough to have prospered in the new regime of economic inequality. It is notable, however, that the dominant language of public critique today is overwhelmingly concerned with “social justice” — associated with labor and land protests as well anti-corruption agitation more generally — rather than “democracy” or political freedom more generally.

This reflects at least in part the fact that the discourse of social justice allows people to appeal to the state in terms of its own professed commitment to socialism. In some ways, this makes it potentially an even more damaging critique than a direct challenge to the political order: the gaping, and growing, economic inequality is a threat not only to social stability but to the very legitimacy of the regime.

At the same time, the turn to the idiom of social justice rather than Maoism is a sign of the diminished nature of Chinese socialism. As a result of four decades of “reform,” there exists today, for the first time in China’s history, a vast industrial proletariat of both urban and rural origin. But despite its unquestionable existence in a socioeconomic sense, it has not yet emerged as a political subject with a collective identity. In addition to material obstacles to labor organization, workers do not have access to an adequate public language in which to articulate their grievances.

Responding to these political and economic contradictions, Xi Jinping’s ascendancy has coincided with the rise of neo-Maoist rhetoric. One of the most notable forms worker protest has taken is dagong shige , a form of subaltern writing by migrant workers, often translated as “battler poetry.” However, its political efficacy remains circumscribed: it is subject to state sanction when too critical, and to state co-optation when less so.

After Deng Xiaoping’s singular emphasis on economic development and the need to allow some people “to get rich first,” Xi Jinping is mindful of the need to balance growth with escalating demands for social justice and environmental protection, stressing the need for “common prosperity” ( gongtong fuyu ) and the construction of “an ecological civilization” ( shengtai wenming ).

The invocations of ecological civilization began under Hu Jintao but are now associated with Xi, who wrote the term into China’s constitution in 2018, in symbolic recognition of the damage wrought by rural industry in particular: land and water contamination, soil erosion, environmental disease, declining food safety, the depletion of fisheries, and so on. In the same vein, Xi has made the eradication of rural poverty one of his signature initiatives. In 2021, he declared that China had achieved a “total elimination of absolute poverty,” with every village in China above the official poverty line.

Yet even this victory — partly semantic, given the arbitrariness of any official definition of poverty — relied on neoliberal means, such as teaching electronic marketing to peasants and making entire villages switch to cash crops in order to raise their incomes by the announced deadline. As Ryan Martinez Mitchell observes, what might have been a radical redistributive project turned instead into a campaign “to embed entrepreneurialism as a character trait into society at large,” including rural China.

H owever, the state’s reliance on neoliberal solutions is far from unqualified. Chinese neoliberalism is similar to the North Atlantic variant to the extent that it makes individuals responsible for themselves in economic circumstances that are beyond their control. However, it does not represent a full subsumption of the state by the logic of capital. It is a selective, strategic, and ultimately political deployment of market institutions in the service of the party state.

China’s future is therefore not determined by the dictates of capital alone, nor is the outcome of the rural enclosure preordained. If it so desires, the Chinese leadership can recalibrate its strategies of industrial development and rethink its current trajectory. In fact, because of its centralized structures of political authority, it is able to act more decisively than a liberal capitalist regime. Nonetheless, and despite the push and pull of policy, the long-term trend has been to continue enclosing rural land and commercializing the Chinese lifeworld.

At the same time, it is important to recognize that this trend has improved peasants’ lives in significant ways. Most villages now have running water, electricity, paved roads, and internet, for example. The arrival of capital has helped diversify the rural economy. While there is great regional variation, there are villages that bear a resemblance to middle-class suburbs.

On the other hand, even the households that manage to hold on to their land in defiance of “dragonhead enterprises” and other new commercial actors become fully reliant on buying inputs from the market and cultivating crops for the market. The less fortunate landless peasants who are unable to find rural employment are in turn compelled to join the urban proletariat, even if material conditions improve for at least a subset of those who make it in the commercialized countryside.

Heeding calls by the agronomist Wen Tiejun and others to find a “Third Way,” some villages have sought to return to collective farming. It is indeed the case that, at least in principle, the commodification of rural land need not result in a complete predominance of private actors. If a village chooses collectively not to sell the rights to the use of its land, it can replace cultivation by individual households with a scaled-up agricultural cooperative — one in which each household exchanges its land allotment for shares in a village-based enterprise.

The resulting shareholding cooperative is in some ways an agricultural version of the industrial collectives of rural China that marked the beginning of economic reforms in the 1980s, engaging in commercial farming rather than industrial production. As a form of self-development by the village, establishing such cooperatives is undoubtedly preferable to allowing outside commercial actors take over, yet by no means do they herald a return to the socialist collectives of the Maoist era. Even collectively owned farming enterprises are essentially commercial actors, subsumed by agrarian capitalism and relying on markets both for buying their inputs — including labor — and for selling their output.

I n recognition of increasing economic stratification throughout society, the state has sought to build at least a minimal safety net. In this respect, the evolution of Chinese welfare institutions has been broadly similar to the development of poor laws in England, initially enacted in response to the enclosure of the commons and the rising numbers of paupers without any means of subsistence.

At the same time, although the Elizabethan Poor Laws were motivated by an anxiety about the state of the realm as a whole, they continued to maintain a medieval commitment to territorially based charity, funded by local ratepayers and available only to paupers settled within a parish. Under the so-called settlement laws, it became as difficult for a pauper to change his official place of settlement as for a Chinese peasant under Maoism to change his hukou registration.

By obstructing mobility, both institutions thwarted the development of a national labor market even as land was increasingly transformed into private property. In the wake of revolutionary upheaval in France, the poor laws were further fortified in 1795 by indexing welfare to the price of bread — a reform that Prime Minister George Canning credited with having “saved England from a revolution” of its own.

In 1834, the New Poor Law finally abolished the centuries-old parish-based regime and replaced it with a centralized system that limited welfare strictly to the disabled and the ill. The able-bodied poor were left with no other option than the workhouse, so stigmatized and so horrific that only the truly desperate would enter it. Finally, a nationwide labor market emerged, leading to the proliferation of slums in England’s industrial cities.

In general outline, Xi’s urbanization policies and his restricted program of social welfare envision a similar transition — except for the state’s determination to prevent the emergence of slums. Even while calling for a more robust welfare system, Xi has consistently held back on public funding, preferring social security programs financed through employers and individual contributions, to prevent a fall into “the idleness-breeding trap of welfarism.” Welfare as such is for orphans, the disabled, and the very old, whereas the able-bodied indigent must find work, or else rely on family for support.

I n England, however, the abolition of the old poor laws coincided with major political agitation. It was preceded by the Reform Act of 1832, which expanded the franchise to the middle class and opened the way to the eventual inclusion of the working class. China, in contrast, has offered no democratic reforms, nor have they been at the top of protesters’ demands.

On the contrary, even as the state is making its citizens turn to the market for their economic needs, it continues to appeal to the political subject of Maoism, one that is expected to sacrifice for the collective good. At the same time, and somewhat improbably, the state has begun to cultivate neo-Confucian rhetoric as well. In lieu of waging class struggle, the people are called on to build a “harmonious society” ( hexie shehui ) — the less protest, the better.

In this vein, Xi has promoted the “Chinese dream” ( Zhongguo meng ) as the most urgent political desideratum of the millennium. This dream is not merely a Chinese rendering of its American counterpart. The American dream belongs to the individual, hearkening to the myth of Horatio Alger, whereas the Chinese dream is that of the nation.

Sublating socialism into nationalism and fed by an intensive cultivation of memories of the so-called century of humiliation that followed China’s defeat in the Opium Wars, it seeks to “rejuvenate” the nation and return it to its rightful place at the heart of a Sinocentric world. The realization of China’s long overdue dream — one that was once a reality and now must be restored — may entail personal sacrifice, including temporary economic inequality, but everyone must play his part. This is a deferral of equality now for the sake of a future dream.

The intensifying personality cult around Xi may be interpreted as an attempt to forge unity in the absence of a political consensus, much as Mao Zedong relied on charismatic leadership to overcome social and political fragmentation. The public promotion of “Xi Jinping Thought” — it has been enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution, along with Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, and Deng Xiaoping Theory — has a similar aim, although its ideological vitality remains questionable.

The anthropologist John Osburg characterizes China as “a post-belief” society. The People’s Republic of China officially remains, and must remain, a socialist state, but its credibility in claiming that label is eroding by the day. At the same time, the party is losing its ability to draw on its historical legitimacy. Mao Zedong and his comrades rightfully claimed credit for having unified the nation and secured its international autonomy. In contrast, the current generation of princelings in charge fought no revolutionary battles but rely on inherited credentials instead.

This is indeed why they appeal to a “rejuvenated” future rather than a revolutionary past. Ultimately the new social contract between the people and the party state is a pragmatic one: social stability in return for continued economic growth, a bargain that political scientists characterize as “performance legitimacy.”

This is an extract from The Unmaking of the Chinese Working Class: How Communism Built a Capitalist Superpower , now available from Verso Books.

Teemu Ruskola is a professor of law and East Asian languages and civilizations at the University of Pennsylvania. He is the author of The Unmaking of the Chinese Working Class and Legal Orientalism .

scraped.body_text:

In recent decades, the basis of US hegemony has shifted from domestic industrial strength to its ability to enforce the rules that organize global production, finance, and money. Today this imperial role is now increasingly under strain.

Donald Trump wants to restore domestic industry while also defending multinationals’ privileges. Understanding why these two goals can’t be reconciled is key to grasping the weaknesses of US capitalism today. (Annabelle Gordon / The Washington Post / Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

I mperialism is again at the forefront of world politics. Large-scale war has become a permanent feature of the present era, from Ukraine to Gaza. Donald Trump’s second term has added a tariff war, threats to annex Greenland, the abduction of Venezuela’s president, and, together with Israel, an unprovoked war on Iran. This is not the whim of one man, for the confrontation with China began under Trump’s first term and deepened under Joe Biden.

At the same time, politics across the mature capitalist countries is in deep turmoil. In the United States, the Left has become a force in mass politics, with a democratic socialist as mayor of New York and widespread opposition to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Israel’s genocide in Palestine, and the war on Iran. In France, governments have fallen one after the other, and social unrest is spreading. But the far right is also rising powerfully, from France’s Rassemblement National and Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland to Reform UK and Austria’s Freiheitliche Partei Österreichs, alongside the Trump White House.

Left and Right draw on the same realities of stagnant wages, industrial decline, and degraded public services. If the Left is to offer a credible political program to the working class and the poor, it must grasp what links resurgent imperialism to the decay of capitalist accumulation in the historic core of the world economy. With millions of people now looking for answers, this means offering a politics of class rupture.

T he starting point is the paradox at the heart of US capitalism, which is also the central paradox of contemporary imperialism. In 1945, the United States produced about half of world manufacturing output; today it produces roughly one-sixth . Productivity growth has been feeble since the great financial crisis of 2007–9, investment has remained weak, and real wages have stagnated for over a generation. Yet the dollar’s share of official reserves has slipped only slightly below 60 percent. US productive preeminence has declined, but the monetary hierarchy has hardened.

The United States alone settles its international obligations in its own liabilities. Everyone else must acquire dollars, manage dollar exposures, and adjust to the policy of the Federal Reserve. Foreign investors hold around $9 trillion of US Treasury bonds , about a third of the marketable stock, and central banks across the world are stuffed with US public paper.

The material basis of US hegemony has thus shifted from domestic industrial strength to the capacity to set and enforce the rules that organize global production, finance, and money. This is also where its imperial power truly lies.

US corporations have flourished within this structure. Among the largest globally active enterprises, US corporations take around 44 percent of profits and hold 34 percent of intellectual property, compared to 11 and 14 percent for their Chinese counterparts. US multinationals led the globalization of production from the 1980s onward, exporting productive capital and building the global chains that shifted industrial capacity abroad, while relying on the dollar to run them.

This was a triumph for private US capital, but it hollowed out industry within the United States and created the social wreckage that became Trump’s political raw material. Global monetary, financial, and corporate dominance has gone together with domestic deterioration.

This is why neither of the two main US parties has been able to reverse industrial decline. Trump’s 2018 tariffs brought little reshoring, since many corporations simply moved their supply chains to Vietnam and Mexico. Biden kept the tariffs and added the subsidies of the Inflation Reduction Act and the CHIPS Act but left US capital’s global strategy untouched.

Trump now wants to restore domestic industry while at the same time defending the privileges of multinationals. One of his first acts on returning to office was to withdraw from the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting framework of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which more than 130 countries had signed, including the Biden-era United States. It would have allowed states to tax a share of the profits generated by multinationals within their borders and to impose a minimum tax of 15 percent, curbing the transfer of profits to tax havens through intellectual property held offshore.

But Trump’s aims cannot be reconciled. To see why, we must look at how production and finance are organized around the world today.

V ladimir Lenin insisted in 1916 that imperialism must be grasped through the dominant mechanisms of accumulation of its time. Drawing primarily on Rudolf Hilferding , he identified these as the fusion of banking and industrial capital into finance capital, the export of capital, and the territorial division of the world among rival powers. His method remains indispensable, but the concrete forms of imperialism have changed profoundly.

Applied to contemporary capitalism, Lenin’s method reveals two structural foundations of imperialism: first, the pairing of globalized productive capital with internationalized financial capital; second, the dollar as world money, which turns that pairing into a hierarchy enforced ultimately by US military power. World money is a crucial element of imperialism today but a consideration that classical Marxist theory never developed.

Contemporary production is organized through global chains coordinated by multinationals — mostly US, European, and Japanese — that control design, intellectual property, logistics, and access to markets. Finance has become global alongside production, but the two have not fused as in Hilferding’s time. They form a pairing in which neither side simply commands the other. Productive capital generates value and surplus value; financial capital supplies the credit, liquidity, and means of payment without which global production could not run. US capital has led on both sides of the pairing: its multinationals built the chains, and its banks and asset managers globalized finance.

The pairing of capitals operates in a world market that has no world state, no world central bank, and no world court of justice. What holds it together is world money, which must serve across separate jurisdictions as unit of account, means of payment, and reserve of value, especially in a crisis. Only the dollar performs these functions.

A manufacturing supplier in Vietnam or Mexico ships components today and waits sixty or ninety days to be paid, but wages and inputs must be paid now. The gap has to be financed, and because the lead firm in the chain invoices in dollars, it is financed in dollars at rates priced off dollar benchmarks. This is not an economic choice but the price of admission to the chain. Between 1999 and 2019, about three-quarters of exports in the Asia-Pacific and virtually all exports in the Americas were invoiced in dollars. Through these chains, the monetary policy of the Federal Reserve reaches directly into workshops on the other side of the world.

The state that issues the necessary dollars is not just another power pursuing its interests abroad. It is the authority that ultimately guarantees settlement, liquidity, and enforceability for globally mobile capital, deciding whose liabilities count as money and whose balance sheets must adjust. Production remains the foundation, but the hegemon’s command over world money is the hinge of imperial power, the point at which the pairing of capitals is disciplined across the world.

The hierarchy becomes fully visible in a crisis. In 2008 and again in 2020, the Fed opened dollar swap lines to a select circle of fourteen central banks. Those inside stabilized their financial systems in days. Those outside, including India, Indonesia, and South Africa, faced currency depreciation, loss of reserves, and austerity. Sanctions and exclusion from payment systems complete the apparatus of coercion, as the freezing of approximately $300 billion of Russian central bank assets in 2022 showed. The fourteen account for roughly 55 percent of US imports and 60 percent of US exports. They also host more than 90 percent of US military personnel stationed abroad. The map of monetary privilege and the map of US military power largely coincide.

The dollar and the F-35 are two moments of a single structure of domination, and US air and naval power guards the choke points through which world trade moves. This is imperialism running through the balance sheets of firms, banks, and states, backed by military power. It does not need to plant a flag over a territory or to establish an expensive colonial administration.

C rucially, the financial side of the pairing has itself been transformed since the great financial crisis of 2007–9. Before the crash there was Financialization Mark I, centered on globally active commercial banks, which turned workers’ homes into a prime terrain of extraction through mortgages and consumer debt. At its peak, bank profits in the United States approached 40 percent of all corporate profits. The crash ended that regime.

It was replaced by Financialization Mark II, resting on shadow banks — above all, asset managers such as BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street. Research that I and colleagues have recently done on 426 major asset managers shows that the equity they manage rose from $13 trillion in 2013 to $46 trillion by mid-2025. That is roughly 40 percent of the equity of all billion-dollar listed companies in the world. In every region outside North America, US asset managers are the largest group of foreign investors. They represent imperial power exercised through balance sheets rather than territory.

Unlike commercial banks that draw their profits mostly from the spread between the lending and the borrowing rates of interest, asset managers depend on the gap between the rate of profit and the rate of interest — what Hilferding called founder’s profit. Such profits are realized primarily through rising asset prices. Stock market inflation has thus become a leading channel of financial accumulation.

The entire edifice of Mark II rests on the state. US gross public debt rose from just over 60 percent of GDP in 2007 to more than 120 percent by 2025. At the same time, the Federal Reserve absorbed public debt securities on a historic scale, created vast amounts of new dollars on its balance sheet, and became dealer of last resort for the shadow banks and others in the money markets. Whatever the neoliberal rhetoric of free markets might say, contemporary capitalism survives through state hyperinterventionism, but on behalf of finance, not to rebuild production.

Investment and productivity outside a narrow set of sectors have consequently stayed weak. The vast AI boom does not alter this picture; it confirms it. Spending on data centers and chips is concentrated in a handful of giant corporations, financed from their enormous cash holdings and increasingly by vast debt, while asset managers pour capital into the same few stocks. The promised productivity gains remain largely a matter of expectation, already priced into shares long before they appear in production. This is still primarily accumulation through asset price inflation, not yet a true transformation of production.

The historic core of the world economy thus continues to drift in an interregnum. The old order has lost its dynamism, but no new one has emerged.

S till, the reach of the Fed extends far beyond the borders of the United States, since the dollars it creates are world money. The dollar dependence created by global production chains accumulates into national pressures: dollar debts that must be serviced, profits that must be repatriated, technology payments that must flow abroad. The burden falls heaviest on the Global South, and the result is subordinate financialization. This is not an immature version of the financialization of the United States or Britain but a distinct form produced by subordination in both production and finance.

A peripheral central bank cannot expand its balance sheet at will or ignore the exchange rate when it forms monetary policy, since it operates in the highly precarious environment of loanable capital flowing in and out of the country. Much of that capital is managed by the same US asset managers that dominate Mark II.

In October 2025, the average policy interest rate in Brazil, India, Indonesia, Mexico, and South Africa stood 4 percentage points above the Fed’s. This is a liquidity tribute, levied by the monetary hierarchy itself. High rates choke domestic investment, attract speculative inflows, push up the exchange rate, and undermine domestic manufacturing. Peripheral states are forced to stockpile dollars as self-insurance and park them in US Treasuries, while their own governments and firms borrow at far higher rates. Resources that could build factories, railways, and hospitals are, in effect, lent to Washington.

Tribute on this scale needs local beneficiaries. Large firms in peripheral countries borrow cheaply in dollars and invest in domestic financial assets at high yields; banks profit from the public debt issued to absorb the inflows; and sections of the middle class enjoy cheap imports. In a peripheral country, the exchange rate is a class weapon as much as an economic variable. And the United States does not need a viceroy to collect the tribute, for it flows through the ordinary workings of the world market.

C hina presents the opposite picture to the United States. It accounts for close to 30 percent of world manufacturing value added and around 15 percent of world merchandise exports. State-owned enterprises dominate its strategic sectors, and it has built institutions that partly bypass the US-led order, such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.

Yet China is not attempting to construct a separate imperial bloc or to acquire territory. It seeks a determining voice in the rules that govern trade, technology, and investment, and, in the longer term, new arrangements for world money.

That is where it is at its weakest. The renminbi accounts for less than 3 percent of global reserves and international payments, and less than 5 percent of world trade is invoiced in it, against roughly half in dollars. Chinese public debt does not serve as global collateral, the People’s Bank of China offers no liquidity backstop to the world market, and China’s own payment system processes little more than 12 percent of the dollar volume handled by the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication.

The barrier is structural, not a matter of will. World money requires deep markets in safe public liabilities, legal protection for foreign creditors, and an open capital account. The capital controls and public command over finance that protected China’s industrialization are precisely what prevent the renminbi from becoming world money. China is a productive superpower obliged to settle its obligations in a currency it does not issue and to hold its reserves in its rival’s debt.

Nor is Chinese domestic accumulation free of contradictions. Since 2007–9, growth and profitability have fallen to a “ new normal .” China still invests roughly double the US share of GDP, but the returns on that investment have declined sharply. The rational course would be to lower investment and systematically raise the incomes and consumption of Chinese workers, but the economic, social, and political risks of doing so are enormous.

The result is an impasse. The hegemon cannot recover its productive foundations, and the challenger cannot issue world money. Neither can impose a resolution, and neither will accept permanent subordination. There is no orderly path of succession within a monetary hierarchy that is singular, coercive, and increasingly contested, and therein lies the danger for the world.

The United States has stopped acting as the hegemon, that is, as the power that presents its own interests as the general interest. It acts instead as the biggest and most aggressive contestant in an increasingly open field, treating even its allies as subordinates. When Washington demanded sanctions on Russian energy after 2022, Germany accepted them at severe cost to its own industrial base. Yet US military predominance is no longer uncontested, and the war on Iran has shown that even weaker opponents cannot simply be made to submit. The situation echoes the rivalries before 1914. World war is not inevitable, but proxy wars, reserve seizures, payment exclusion, and technology embargoes have become an embedded feature of world politics.

Should the Left, then, cheer for de-dollarization and the BRICS? Weakening the monopoly of the dollar would loosen a crucial mechanism of domination. But the putative challengers are neither a socialist bloc nor a new anti-colonial movement. They are states competing in the world market and seeking ways around the dollar, not a fairer world money. Multipolarity is not a class category. The Left should oppose sanctions, the liquidity tribute, and the forced accumulation of reserves without enlisting in anyone’s camp.

O ne of the most encouraging political developments in this gloomy conjuncture is the US left seriously debating how to win and use governing power. Max Elbaum has rightly argued here that it cannot limit its positive platform to domestic issues while saying only what it opposes in foreign policy.

The analysis above shows why. The domestic and the imperial are two sides of the same structure, and a left government would confront that structure from day one. Success is not possible without overturning the prevailing capitalist mechanisms of social, economic, and political power. This is precisely the politics of class rupture that the Left should be offering to the millions seeking change.

I saw what this means at close quarters in Greece in 2015. Syriza’s election win had little significance in itself — it was at best only the beginning. A left-wing government that truly sought to save Greece from the disaster of the bailouts had to break the established mechanisms of power. That could only be done by using the machinery of the state in conjunction with the mass movement. To deliver results, a left-wing government would be obliged to transform the state.

The challenge crystallized on one issue — as it typically does in times of a radical upheaval. That was, to stay in the European Monetary Union (EMU), or to exit? Breaking with the euro would have required capital controls, public command over the banks and money, and a far-reaching reorganization of the economy that could have shifted power toward workers and the poor. Inevitably, there would have been a profound rupture with the entrenched class and imperial interests stifling Greece, both of which threw their weight behind the policy of remaining with the EMU. The mere thought was enough to send shivers down the spine of the timid Syriza leadership. Abject surrender followed.

There is a lesson here for the US left — and beyond it — despite the vast difference between the preeminent imperial power and a small European power. If it seeks to offer a politics of rupture that tilts the balance decisively in favor of workers and the poor, it must use and transform the machinery of the state while drawing on the strength of the mass movement. It should also be clear that there will be fierce and violent opposition on all levels. Success will not come without decisively overturning the domestic and the imperial configuration of class power in the United States. Of that there can be no doubt. It is almost redundant to say that the task is of world-historic importance.

T here is, however, plenty of historical experience on which the US left can draw as it seeks a class politics that could bring success. The first step involves developing a program of reversing domestic US productive decline, with the working class in the lead, as has already been argued for other developed capitalist countries.

That means public investment on a scale not seen in generations, public banks directing credit to production, and a central bank brought within a democratic economic plan instead of serving as dealer of last resort for BlackRock. It also means restoring capital controls as a normal instrument of policy and extending public ownership in energy, infrastructure, and housing, where social need and private profit sharply diverge. And it further means democratic, worker-based control of corporations, since a bureaucratic state corporation run on the priorities of capital changes nothing essential.

Such a program would reverse the global accumulation strategy of US capital, subordinating multinational and financial capital to democratically determined priorities. In short, it would aim to deglobalize and definancialize the US economy. This is neither isolationism nor autarky. The aim is an open economy that continues to trade, invest, and cooperate across borders but on terms set democratically rather than by multinationals and footloose financial capital. Openness should serve the reconstruction of production at home and genuine cooperation abroad, not the global strategy of US capital.

A program of this kind ultimately rests on the issue of sovereignty. The problem is that this term has been appropriated by the Right, which uses it to assert the unrestrained power of the US state abroad while defending the interests of capital at home. But for the Left, sovereignty has a different and older content, that of popular sovereignty. If democracy is to have real meaning, workers and the poor ought to have both voice and power at the workplace, the neighborhood, the town, the city, and the country. Popular sovereignty does not mean only electing a government that spends more on social care, housing, and infrastructure while taxing the rich, necessary as that is. It requires building the organized power of working people — channeling the renewed strike militancy of the United Auto Workers and the drives to organize the nonunion factories of the South — alongside the communities and movements that have resisted ICE, the genocide in Palestine, and the war on Iran.

Since, moreover, there is no democratic space beyond the borders of the nation-state, a program of class rupture would also rest on national sovereignty. This is an even thornier issue for the Left to grasp. In a subordinate country, such as Greece in 2015, national sovereignty means breaking out of imperialist domination. But the United States sits at the top of the imperialist hierarchy, and the sovereignty of the US state is a lever through which other nations are subordinated.

For the United States, therefore, national sovereignty raises directly the question of what the nation is and which class constitutes it. For the Right, the nation is the imperial state and the capital it serves. For the Left, national sovereignty is anti-imperialist at its core and means fighting against the oppression of others. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels put it plainly , after stating that workers have no country: the proletariat must “rise to be the leading class of the nation, must constitute itself the nation,” and is in that sense “itself national, though not in the bourgeois sense of the word.”

This is the opposite of nationalism, which asks workers to line up behind their own ruling class. The task is then clear. The US working class can constitute itself as the nation only by taking command of the instruments of imperial power — the Fed, the sanctions machinery of the Treasury, the military budget — and ending their use to subordinate other nations. US workers gain nothing durable from the dollar order. The more Washington pursues imperial primacy, the more it hollows out the domestic economy.

Antiwar politics and anti-capitalist politics are one struggle. Opposition to war that leaves domestic property relations untouched is incomplete, and transformation at home that ignores the imperial order will be crushed by it. The system that extracts value from the periphery is the same system that hollows out the core. That is what gives working-class internationalism a material content, instead of leaving it a liberal slogan compatible with the free movement of capital. It is the ground on which a genuinely internationalist socialist politics can be built.

This article draws on a contribution to the internal programmatic discussions of the Communist Party of Austria (KPÖ).

Costas Lapavitsas is a professor of economics at SOAS, currently at the New School for Social Research, and former member of the Greek Parliament.

scraped.h1: How Milei Defused Argentina's Hyperinflation Bomb
scraped.body_text:

Inflation

Juan Ramón Rallo | From the December 2026 issue

The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.

Argentina was approaching monetary detonation. Its Treasury could not finance its deficits voluntarily, its central bank was effectively insolvent, and monthly inflation was accelerating above 12 percent.

That was just three years ago. Today, monthly inflation has fallen below 2 percent, sovereign spreads touched eight-year lows in July, and the central bank's gross reserves reached their highest level since 2019 in September. This is one of the most remarkable disinflations of the modern era to have occurred without dollarization, a currency board, or a new currency. Javier Milei did not merely slow the rate at which prices were rising; he dismantled the fiscal and monetary mechanism that was driving Argentina toward hyperinflation.

But as the events of late 2025 showed, that achievement remains vulnerable. A stabilization can be economically coherent and still be politically mortal. Argentina has restored a substantial degree of public sector solvency, but it has not yet made that solvency independent of the next election.

Deficits themselves do not make Argentina unique. What distinguished Argentina was how those deficits had to be financed. In a country with functioning capital markets and a credible government, the state sells bonds to domestic and foreign savers; it obtains command over present resources, while creditors receive claims on future tax revenues. Public borrowing may be undesirable or objectionable on other grounds, but so long as the government remains solvent in the long run, it is a financial operation that can be sustained over time without debt restructurings or bouts of high inflation.

Argentina had largely exhausted that option. After repeated inflationary crises and serial debt repudiations—nine sovereign defaults, most recently in 2020—investors would lend to the Treasury only at prohibitive rates. Borrowing at those rates would itself make the debt trajectory unsustainable, so creditors expected either another restructuring of dollar-denominated bonds or an inflationary liquidation of peso-denominated liabilities. Those expectations raised borrowing costs further, making the anticipated outcome more likely. The Argentine state had trapped itself in a doom loop.

So the government relied on the one creditor that couldn't refuse it: the central bank. Fiscal deficits were financed, directly or indirectly, by issuing pesos. But that brought it up against a second constraint. The inflationary effect of money creation depends not only on the quantity of money supplied but on the quantity people are willing to hold. And after decades of monetary abuse, Argentines wanted as few pesos as possible.

Every newly issued peso became a hot potato to be exchanged for goods, dollars, or inflation-protected assets. As the demand for real peso balances contracted, the government had to print ever larger quantities to extract the same real resources, which pushed prices up faster, which further reduced the willingness to hold pesos, which required still more issuance. That's the feedback loop of an economy approaching hyperinflation.

Rather than stop the process, the government tried to repress its visible symptoms—a task for which the country has a well-worn tool kit. Its most familiar instrument is the cepo cambiario , a web of capital and exchange controls with which the state prevents its citizens from freely satisfying their demand for dollars and hides the peso's depreciation behind an artificially strong official exchange rate. President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner imposed it in 2011; Mauricio Macri lifted it on taking the presidency, only to reinstate it amid the currency run of 2019; the leaders who followed tightened it further. Under the cepo, exchange rates multiplied. Exporters were forced to surrender their dollars below market value, while politically privileged importers bought them cheaply from the central bank. That arrangement punished exports, subsidized favored imports, invited corruption, and bled reserves.

The second instrument operated through the central bank's own balance sheet: extremely high nominal interest rates paid on short-term liabilities held mainly by commercial banks. These so-called remunerated liabilities were a standing bribe to the financial system to sit on its pesos rather than convert them into dollars or goods. Since those interest payments were themselves financed by creating new money for which there was no demand, they generated what Argentines call the quasi-fiscal deficit—a deficit produced not by the Treasury's spending programs but by the central bank's mounting interest bill. Paying interest to suppress monetary expansion today merely promised greater monetary expansion tomorrow.

By the end of 2023, the numbers had become grotesque. The Treasury's fiscal deficit stood at roughly 5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), while the central bank's quasi-fiscal deficit approached 10 percent. Sovereign spreads hovered near 2,500 basis points—meaning that when an equivalent U.S. Treasury bond yielded 5 percent a year, Argentina would have had to pay around 30 percent to borrow in dollars. Monthly inflation hit 12.8 percent in November and was accelerating. (For perspective: Americans were furious when inflation peaked at 9 percent a year under President Joe Biden.) The gap between the official exchange rate and parallel rates exceeded 100 percent and at times approached 200 percent, strangling foreign trade. And the central bank's net international reserves stood at roughly negative $11 billion, the lowest level in its recorded history.

That was the machine Milei inherited on December 10, 2023: an insolvent Treasury, a central bank buried under remunerated liabilities, a rapidly contracting demand for the national currency, and a regulatory apparatus built to disguise the consequences of all three.

Argentina was not yet in hyperinflation. But it had entered its antechamber.

Milei's strategy was to restore the solvency of the Treasury and the central bank so that the controls concealing their insolvency could safely be removed. The sequencing was important. If he had scrapped every exchange control while the government still ran large deficits, the central bank still printed pesos to cover them, and net reserves were deeply negative, that could have accelerated rather than stopped a speculative run.

The first front was fiscal. Milei cut government spending, and not just in inflation-adjusted terms. Some cuts were explicit: Public works were halted, discretionary transfers to provincial governments were slashed, subsidies were pared back, and government employment contracted. (Such changes struck at many of the mechanisms through which Argentina's political class distributed patronage.) Other cuts operated through inflation itself: The government declined to fully index some nominal expenditures to rising prices, shrinking the real value of public salaries and pensions. This was socially painful, particularly for pensioners, but it allowed the fiscal correction to proceed faster than Congress would otherwise have permitted.

National primary spending fell by roughly a quarter in real terms in Milei's first year—an adjustment with few peacetime precedents—which brought national spending, as a share of the economy, back toward levels last seen in 2007–08. Within weeks of taking office, the government was posting monthly primary surpluses; it closed 2024 with a fiscal surplus and has treated balanced budgets as the nonnegotiable anchor ever since. That change altered the monetary regime before any formal institutional reform. Once the Treasury stopped requiring net financing from the central bank, the primary source of fiscally driven peso creation disappeared.

Milei also devalued the official exchange rate within days of taking office, bringing it closer to the market rate. That produced an immediate price shock, with monthly inflation exceeding 25 percent in December 2023. Critics called the devaluation inflationary, and in an immediate accounting sense, it was. But much of the inflation it unleashed was already latent, repressed behind an official exchange rate that almost nobody could access and nobody believed. By recognizing the accumulated depreciation at once, the government sharply narrowed the gap between official and parallel markets, restored exporters' incentives, and began dismantling expectations of an uncontrolled adjustment. After a transitional period, most exchange restrictions were lifted in April 2025.

Skeptics will note—correctly—that the liberalization co-incided with a new $20 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and will be tempted to conclude that it was this that made it possible to lift the cepo: just another bailout in a long history of Argentine bailouts. That reading misses the difference between financing a flow (the deficit) and refinancing a stock (the inherited debt).

Earlier IMF programs had poured external resources into governments that were still generating new fiscal imbalances, so the money flowed in while the pile of public liabilities kept growing—most spectacularly in 2018, when the largest loan in the IMF's history stabilized nothing. This time, the Treasury was already in surplus, and the facility operated on the stock inherited from the past: Argentina's largest external creditor was rolling over its own exposure, thickening the central bank's liquidity buffers, and stretching the horizon over which the old debt would be serviced. That support undoubtedly reinforced the program's healing dynamics and probably brought the lifting of the cepo forward. But it was neither a sufficient condition for success nor, over the medium term, a necessary one. A Treasury running surpluses and a central bank no longer bleeding pesos would eventually have rebuilt reserves and regained market access on their own, though this would have happened more slowly.

The second front was the central bank itself. Once the Treasury stopped demanding monetary financing, the Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA) could sharply cut the interest rates paid on its remunerated liabilities. With lower expectations of inflation and depreciation, it was no longer necessary to pay enormous nominal rates to keep pesos from stampeding into goods and dollars.

The relationship ran in both directions. Falling inflation allowed lower nominal rates, lower rates shrank the central bank's interest bill, a smaller interest bill reduced future money creation, and reduced expected money creation further increased the demand for pesos. A virtuous circle began to replace the old doom loop.

The government then dismantled the central bank's stock of remunerated liabilities, shifting the job of absorbing excess pesos—and its cost—onto Treasury instruments. This did not make the debt disappear, but it lengthened maturities and placed the cost where it belonged: on the Treasury's accounts, under public and legislative scrutiny, rather than hidden within the central bank's balance sheet. The distinction matters. The quasi-fiscal deficit had allowed governments to claim more fiscal discipline than actually existed by parking part of the cost of stabilization outside the formal budget. Milei's consolidation made the state's liabilities transparent and stopped the central bank from autonomously compounding them through an escalating interest bill.

As confidence returned, sovereign spreads collapsed from roughly 2,500 basis points when Milei was elected to around 400 in July 2026, their lowest in eight years. That allowed the Treasury to roll over maturing debt at ever longer terms and lower cost. Argentina has not yet fully regained ordinary access to international capital markets; the government still leans on multilateral financing and domestic issuance to meet foreign-currency maturities, and spreads widened again, to above 600 by late September, as long-term U.S. rates rose and investors began to price the 2027 presidential election. But the probability of another restructuring has receded dramatically. The improvement shows on the central bank's balance sheet too: In 2026 alone, the BCRA has bought more than $14 billion in the foreign exchange market, and in early September gross reserves topped $50 billion, their highest level since 2019. Purchases have slowed sharply since the summer, and usable net reserves remain far smaller, but the direction of travel has reversed from the deeply negative position inherited in 2023.

All of this occurred alongside a modest but real reduction in taxes. The Impuesto PAIS, a major surcharge on foreign-currency transactions, was allowed to expire at the end of 2024. Export taxes were abolished for regional economies and thousands of industrial products and were cut for major agricultural exports on a declining schedule; tariffs, internal taxes on selected goods, and the wealth tax were also reduced, pushing the national tax burden to its lowest share of GDP in almost two decades. These cuts were modest relative to Milei's ambitions, but notable because they occurred without sacrificing the surplus. Milei did not balance the budget by raising taxes; he cut spending faster than revenue fell.

The macroeconomic result is hard to dispute. Monthly inflation, 25.5 percent in December 2023, was 1.7 percent in August 2026. Year-over-year inflation has fallen to 33.5 percent from 211 percent in 2023, and it is still declining.

Does all of this mean that Argentina is financially saved and that Milei has completed his task? No. The months before the October 2025 midterms show why.

When the opposition began climbing in the polls, and above all after it crushed the government's candidates in September's Buenos Aires provincial election, markets started pricing a scenario in which Milei lost the political capacity to defend his own agenda. The repricing was brutal. Country risk, which had been trading around 700 basis points in mid-August, doubled to nearly 1,500 by mid-September, and the peso depreciated by more than 20 percent over the episode, even though short-term interest rates soared and the authorities burned billions of scarce dollars trying to stabilize it.

Note what had not happened. The government had not abandoned the surplus, had not returned to monetary financing, and had not rebuilt the remunerated-liability machine. Milei's program had not secretly become insolvent; what triggered the crisis was the rising probability that its enemies might regain the power to make the state insolvent again. Nor was the panic irrational. Asset values depend on expected future policy, not just current policy. Savers who believe a future government will monetize deficits, impose controls, or restructure debt will sell pesos and Argentine bonds before that government takes office, and that means the anticipation of a regime reversal can generate, in advance, the very crisis the reversal would eventually have produced.

And this was not merely a panic among foreign fund managers. Ordinary Argentines know their political class too well and have learned to protect themselves by dollarizing; the threat of a fiscally irresponsible government had them fleeing the peso en masse. The central bank's statistics tell the story. Gross retail purchases of dollars reached some $5 billion in September and almost as much in October—double their previous monthly pace, and the heaviest retail dollarization since the eve of the election in 2019—before collapsing to barely a third of that rhythm the month after the vote.

The panic revealed a real weak point, though. Milei had fixed the flows but not yet the stocks: The state's liquid assets—its international reserves—still fell short of the bills coming due, whether pesos being dumped for dollars or hard-currency bonds maturing in the months ahead. Rebuilding a state's balance sheet takes years. Reserves accumulate purchase by purchase, and maturities lengthen only as fast as creditors' trust returns. Until that slow work is done, any rise in the perceived risk of a political reversal can abruptly close the state's access to refinancing, leaving it with maturing debts it cannot yet cover and a run on the peso it cannot stabilize with its own resources.

That was the gap the U.S. Treasury stepped in to fill. In October 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent set up a $20 billion swap line with Argentina's central bank and—in an operation American taxpayers had every reason to question—bought pesos outright in the days before the vote. Bessent was bridging, for a few weeks, a gap that political panic had blown open. The intervention contained the panic just long enough for the election to remove its immediate political cause. On October 26, Milei's coalition took more than 40 percent of the vote, expanded its bloc in Congress, and locked in enough votes to sustain the president's vetoes. Within days, the peso steadied, spreads resumed their slide, and the central bank was buying dollars again. By year's end, Argentina had repaid the $2.5 billion it had actually drawn on the swap.

Still, the lesson is uncomfortable. A stabilization is consolidated only when an election can no longer plausibly revive expectations of default and monetary collapse. Argentina isn't there yet.

Time, if politics allows, will close the balance sheet gap. Reserves are being rebuilt, and maturities stretch a little further with every successful auction. But some of Milei's central libertarian promises are still, for now, only promises.

Milei inherited a country with no voluntary creditors, almost no demand for its currency, a Treasury hooked on monetary financing, a central bank trapped by its own interest bill, deeply negative net reserves, and capital controls that strangled trade while failing to stop depreciation. In less than three years, his government produced sustained fiscal surpluses, dismantled the quasi-fiscal time bomb, cut monthly inflation from 25 percent to below 2 percent, compressed sovereign spreads to eight-year lows, liberalized the exchange market, rebuilt reserves, and reduced taxes. And it did that without confiscating deposits, without a new default, and without raising the overall tax burden.

Hyperinflation is no natural disaster. It is the political consequence of a state that loses solvency and finances itself through a currency its citizens no longer wish to hold. Milei has stopped that process. Whether he has changed Argentina's institutions enough to prevent its return is a verdict that will arrive only after he leaves office.

Juan Ramón Rallo is dean and professor of economics at the Universidad de las Hespérides in Spain.

scraped.title: How the GOP Can Win Back Latinos
scraped.description: Voters in South Florida shared their frustrations with The American Conservative.
scraped.author: Juan Rojas
scraped.body_text:
Voters in South Florida shared their frustrations with The American Conservative .

It was Election Day in neoconservative South Florida. The torrential rains briefly subsided as I made my way to the local polling station in suburban Fort Lauderdale. A handwritten sign made the following plea to voters: “We didn’t fight terrorists abroad just to come home and watch DEMOCRATS elect them into office.”

The state’s younger generations, however, see matters differently. One 20-something Latino I spoke with described himself as a socialist and said that Republicans had nothing to offer young people. Conversely, a young mother of Peruvian heritage told me she typically voted for Republicans but felt Trump needed a wake-up call over broken promises.

In the end, Republicans avoided a bloodbath in Florida despite voters—and especially Latinos—swinging hard to the Democrats. The Republican gubernatorial and senatorial candidates Byron Donalds and Ashley Moody narrowly prevailed over Democratic challengers Angie Nixon—who was endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)—and David Jolly. The Miami neocon trio of GOP Reps. Carlos Gimenez, Maria Elvira Salazar, and Mario Diaz-Balart also appear to have survived, though Salazar and Diaz-Balart’s races were still too close to call at the time of writing.

Elsewhere in the country, Latinos drove historic Democratic victories, including all statewide races in Texas. All told, the group swung 29 points away from Republicans after Trump’s performance in 2024. What lessons, then, should the GOP draw from this Latino backlash?

One thing to note is that there are important differences between Latinos of different backgrounds. Voters of South American and Cuban origin, for example, tend to lean neoconservative when it comes to foreign policy. And second- and third-generation Latinos are often indifferent to political developments south of the border.

In Florida, Moody won Cuban-Americans by seven points, mitigating losses among Hispanics. One Cuban-American millennial, a venue promoter in Wynwood, Miami, told me he split his vote, explaining that he couldn’t vote for Nixon due to her inability to call Cuba a dictatorship. And in the Cuban-American stronghold of Hialeah, the neoconservative faithful held firm in their support for the GOP. “We have to let Trump work”, said Marcos, a middle-aged mechanic, originally from Havana. The president “knows what he’s doing,” he added, referring to both the Iran War and the sanctions-induced crisis in Cuba.

Yet among Venezuelan-Americans in South Florida, MAGA neoconservativism has shown considerable cracks over a range of issues, including the administration’s policy towards Caracas. In the wake of the January kidnapping of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro, concern over Trump’s cozy relationship with the regime successor Delcy Rodríguez was largely confined to media and intellectual circles. Ten months later, many grassroots Venezuelan-Americans continue to give the president the benefit of the doubt. Some, however, have become frustrated with the prospect that the regime in Caracas may ultimately survive Trump’s term.

In suburban Fort Lauderdale, José—a 2024 Trump voter—told me he had been ecstatic following the Maduro raid but since then has soured on the administration. “Things are worse than ever, not just here but also for my relatives that are still in Venezuela,” he said. “They were supposed to arrest the Chavistas , not sign all these deals with them!” José added, referring to Venezuelans who subscribe to the socialist ideology of former President Hugo Chávez.

Then, of course, there’s the elephant in the room of the administration’s approach towards immigration enforcement. At a watch party close to the Trump National Doral hotel for a local Miami-Dade official, some invitees panicked at Florida Republicans’ tight margins on election night. “How could Miami vote for a socialist for senator?” said one Venezuelan-American realtor. “It’s the immigration issue,” another attendee responded. “They’ve gone too far with ICE. A lot of people are just staying home,” he added. Indeed, turnout in majority Hispanic precincts throughout the state fell to 44 percent even as overall turnout stood at 60 percent.

The remarkably accurate pollster Atlas-Intel found that 40 percent of Latinos listed “immigration policy, deportations, and ICE” as one of their top three electoral issues, putting it ahead of “combating corruption” and “economic policy and taxes.”

It’s not hard to see why Hispanics are deeply concerned about immigration enforcement. Around 60 people have died under ICE custody since Trump returned to office. Many of the voters I spoke with told stories of friends and family members—some of whom were U.S. citizens —who suffered abuse under ICE detention. Notably, Salazar has drawn ire from immigration hardliners for criticizing enforcement excesses and championing a pathway to citizenship for certain illegal immigrants.

Nonetheless, it’s foolish to presume that Democrats will dominate among Latinos for the foreseeable future, including when it comes to immigration. In a seeming paradox, Atlas-Intel also found that 45 percent of the demographic still favored mass deportation of illegal immigrants, compared to 40 percent who were opposed. The truth is that Latinos—much like the broader population—remain broadly against illegal immigration even as a slim majority also favor abolishing ICE.

Many of the Latino Trump voters I previously spoke with in 2024 expressed frustration over having migrated legally to the U.S. while millions of illegal immigrants and fraudulent asylum seekers “jumped the line” at the border under President Joe Biden. Progressives are profoundly mistaken if they think that they can avoid renewed border chaos by only deporting criminals, while also allowing anyone to claim persecution and solicit asylum inside the U.S.

If a future Democratic administration reopens the border, it’s quite likely voters—Latinos included—will swing back to the GOP in subsequent elections; as of this writing, voters continue to prefer Republicans by 13 points over Democrats on immigration. If Republicans are truly serious about delivering lasting results on the border while also avoiding endless backlash, there is a conservative but also populist path forward for the party.

In 2008, current Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, a Republican, made a compelling case against an ICE police state, arguing it would be both less costly and more effective to punish employers of illegal labor under a rigorous, national regime of E-Verify . That program, which verifies the immigration status of employees, has been repeatedly sabotaged at the state and national level by carveouts and selective enforcement, due mainly to employer lobbying.

Much to his credit, Vice President J.D. Vance stated in his post-election autopsy that he was open to changing enforcement “by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor.” At present, worksite investigations and prosecutions of employers of illegal labor sit at or near record lows. Actually deterring illegal immigration by cracking down on employers ultimately depends on achieving sufficient scale and consistency of enforcement. In Canada, hiring illegal workers is nearly impossible due to a rigorously enforced equivalent of E-Verify.

In 2023, Gov. Ron DeSantis passed a law mandating that private firms subject employees to E-Verify. The mandate, however, features a carveout for companies with fewer than 25 employees and has been poorly enforced. And even that has been too much for some: The Wall Street Journal , for example, decried the piecemeal mandate in February, claiming that it was “ killing growth ” (the paper also expressed panic at Republican efforts to broaden the mandate).

Given sufficient political will, Kobach estimated his proposal could be implemented at a cost of around $600 million over five years, a trivial expense (compare this to the $85 billion currently devoted to ICE). Illegal immigration by economic migrants—as in Canada—would collapse, and large numbers of recent arrivals would self-deport for lack of employment options. It remains to be seen whether the Trump administration—or Democrats for that matter—will eventually embrace such a proposal.

Foreign policy will be another tricky issue for the administration with Latinos moving forward. So long as the Iran War continues to fuel higher prices at the pump and grocery store checkout, voters of all stripes are likely to deliver another gut punch to the GOP in 2028. Latino neoconservatives—in Miami or elsewhere—will probably continue to prefer Republicans, but some may opt to stay home if they perceive limited progress on regime change in Cuba or Venezuela before Trump leaves office.

There are, however, areas where Republicans will continue to reap dividends with Latinos in the long term. Hispanics are overwhelmingly Catholic or evangelical and generally conservative on issues like crime, family, and energy abundance. In addition to backing mass deportation, Latinos approved of federal recognition of two biological genders and increased fossil fuel production under Trump by margins of 10 and 20 points, respectively; they likewise back Republicans over Democrats on crime by nearly 12 points.

For the GOP, winning back Latinos who defected to the Democratic Party or who sat out this election will remain crucial for the foreseeable future. Republicans can start by embracing the vice president’s four-point plan for reestablishing trust with voters: 1) end the war; 2) focus on cost of living/inflation; 3) put America First; and 4) change our relationship to Israel.

Juan David Rojas is a columnist at UnHerd covering Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula.

scraped.title: The Midterms Prove Left-Populism Is Rising
scraped.description: To save the GOP, the Trump admin should end wars, purge corruption, and deliver wins for working people.
scraped.author: The American Conservative
scraped.body_text:
To save the GOP, the Trump admin should end wars, purge corruption, and deliver wins for working people.

The midterms were a bloodbath. Democrats took both chambers of the U.S. Congress and red-state governorships. The hardest part for Republicans to swallow is how familiar the winning pitch sounded: In 2016, Donald Trump addressed Americans’ concerns regarding the cost of living, Middle East wars, and government corruption. The painful truth is that this year, Democrats addressed those concerns better.

The exit polls tell an interesting story. When asked about their top issues, 39 percent of voters said the economy (46 percent for Republicans and 52 percent for Democrats), 33 percent said the state of democracy (20 percent for Republicans and 79 percent for Democrats), and only 14 percent said immigration (89 percent for Republicans and 10 percent for Democrats). Other questions reveal that the cost of living, the Iran War, and corruption were all critical factors in motivating voters to support the Democrats.

To be clear, President Donald Trump has done excellent work on immigration, anti-white discrimination, and censorship—arguably the three main issues for the online or “dissident right.” But by launching the Iran War, going overboard with tariffs (which much of the online right in principle supports), and allowing widespread corruption throughout the administration, Trump dropped the ball on issues everyday Americans care about. Not the wisest move.

Just look at Gina Hinojosa, a relative nobody who unseated the longtime Texas Governor Greg Abbot on Tuesday. Her campaign was defined by the conscious decision to set aside traditional liberal concerns over identity issues to embrace economic populism. “There is just no winning the culture war,” Hinojosa told the New Yorker . “My agenda is not a Democratic agenda. It’s a populist agenda.”

On the campaign trail, Hinojosa railed against billionaires, corporations, and AI data centers. She called for more school funding, a one-time $1,500 check to every Texas household, and better healthcare access. She framed the incumbent Abbot as a corrupt politician who sold out Texas to wealthy elites. Evidently, Texans loved what they heard, winning her 5.2 million votes (53 percent) to Abbot’s 4.5 million (46 percent).

The Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who easily brushed off Mike Collins’s attempt to unseat him, is another Democrat who embodies this rising tide of left-wing populism. Osoff has lambasted the Trump administration for failing to deliver for the working class. He has decried this administration as “a government of, by, and for the ultra-rich.” Like many elected Democrats, he hasn’t shied away from indulging some of the dumber populist tendencies by invoking “the Epstein class” to bash Trump and his friends.

Many believe Ossoff has a shot at securing the 2028 Democratic nomination. It’s anyone’s guess. But whoever does cinch the nomination will probably sound a lot like him. If midterms proved one thing, it’s that left-wing populism, like it or not, is popular.

The new populist formula appears to eschew some of the more radical economic policies favored by the likes of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Those policies appeal to many working-class voters but can alienate white-collar professionals who don’t have to worry much about their own health insurance. But the populism of Hinojosa and Ossoff demands little sacrifice from the professional managerial class. After all, who could say no to lower prices, fewer wars, and less corruption?

That, sadly, was pretty close to Trump’s winning formula in 2016 and 2024. Of course, Trump hit on other issues like immigration and left-wing cultural insanity, which Democrats most certainly will not adopt. But they don’t need to. While mass immigration and race preferences remain unpopular, the midterms reveal that enough Americans are willing to support Democrats so long as they are promising to deliver on basic everyday concerns.

But will they deliver? It should be self-evident that the Democrats, once in power, will resume their real agenda: crushing their political enemies, discriminating against whites, censoring your conservative grandma on Facebook, and reopening the immigration spigot. Sure, they might implement some pro-working-class policies, but I doubt most Americans’ lives will dramatically improve.

The Democrats’ control of Congress will cause endless headaches and stymie Trump’s agenda for the next two years. Fortunately, their ability to fully enact vengeance and resume the destruction of our country will be limited at least until 2029, when a new president, possibly a Democrat, enters the White House. The Oversight Committee can issue subpoenas and haul people into televised hearings, but given that Trump’s personal lawyer is running the DOJ, criminal referrals will go nowhere—at least for now.

So although Trump has delivered on issues the online right cares about—not entirely, of course, but the wins are there—he neglected the median voter, who, however capricious and uninformed, must be placated. Any Republican running for office in 2028 will face an uphill battle, especially those who served in this administration.

What matters most now is that the remaining two years are spent delivering wins to Americans and repairing the shattered coalition: ramp up deportations and debank illegals (Dems rarely hit on immigration in their midterm ads for a reason); get us out of Iran; do whatever necessary to get costs down; publicly purge the administration of corrupt officials.

Failure to do so will doom Republicans in 2028. But that’s not all. Such a failure would solidify the GOP’s brand as the party of rich and corrupt old people with horrible Botox jobs who care more about waging distant wars than tending to the needs of their American compatriots. That was the legacy of the George W. Bush era, which in turn gave us Barack Obama. Should Trump fail, expect whatever comes after to be far worse.

Patrick Casey is a writer and editor based in Washington, D.C. He is also the host of the “Restoring Order” podcast.
