scraped.title: Eating Ourselves Alive
scraped.description: I have only once been asked to be a witness in a libel trial in which the plaintiff denied that he was a cannibal, contrary to the allegation made in
scraped.author: Andrew Day
scraped.body_text:
The destructive urge goes beyond politics and even war.

I have only once been asked to be a witness in a libel trial in which the plaintiff denied that he was a cannibal, contrary to the allegation made in print by the defendant, but I suppose that that is infinitely more times than the great majority of people have ever been asked to be such a witness. (I should add that I was to be a witness for the defendant, though my knowledge of the plaintiff’s cannibalism was distinctly limited.)

The plaintiff was Charles Taylor, the president of Liberia at the time. He dropped the case against Stephen Ellis, the author of the brilliant and definitive book about the Liberian Civil War. Taylor did so, he said, because of the cost involved, though no one believed this, as he was by then a very rich man. He would have had to testify in London, and in a libel trial all manner of evidence is allowed; it would not have been too difficult to prove that he had no reputation to lose, which is to say, good reputation. What was hardly beyond dispute was that he had used drugged-up children to fight in his guerrilla army in his determination to become president.

Memories of Liberia returned to me when I read recently an article in the Spectator about Miatta Fahnbulleh, daughter of a Liberian refugee to Britain, Henry Boima Fahnbulleh. She is now secretary of energy security and net zero in the current British government, and as such, as her very title suggests, almost certainly destined to assist and be partly responsible for the further impoverishment of the country. According to the article , not yet and perhaps never to be the subject of an action for defamation, her father:

was indeed foreign minister in Liberia in the 1980s, and latterly a national security adviser to President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. But he is also a Marxist radical who dedicated himself over a long career to the violent overthrow of those who got in his way.

Unsurprisingly, this took me back to the time during a short lull in the civil war back in 1991 when I visited Monrovia, the capital of Liberia. You could reach the city at that time only by sea, for it was besieged by Charles Taylor’s forces. I travelled on the Steel Trader under Captain Monty Jones, an estimable Welsh sea captain and entrepreneur who was almost solely (and heroically) responsible for the revictualling of the city under siege. He died, alas, in 2019, having been a staunch opponent of the pirates who operated in his West African theater of operations. I had the highest admiration for him and found an article about piracy in the area in which he was quoted:

“They [pirates] spray the wheelhouse with machine gun fire before trying to board. It is a normal military tactic: intimidate your enemy,” said sea captain Jones, who has been hijacked several times.

Many pirates are armed with handguns and long guns, he said, and are often high on drugs. ‘There is no way to reason with them.”

The pirates had evidently turned on, tuned in and dropped out, à la Timothy Leary.

The destruction of Monrovia was complete and very thorough. This destruction was not merely the consequence of war or bombardment. That could not have explained why the medical records of the Maternity Hospital had been used as lavatory paper, why the books of the library of the University of Liberia had been pulled from the shelves on to the ground and trampled upon, or why the castor wheels had been carefully sawn off every single piece of hospital furniture of the now deserted, dark, and echoing John F. Kennedy Hospital (where open-heart surgery had once been performed), all at a considerable expense of effort.

In the Centennial Hall, where national events such as the inauguration of presidents took place, the body of what was possibly the only Steinway grand piano in the country rested on the floor, its legs sawn off, surrounded by a necklace of human faeces. Again, this could hardly be interpreted as destruction wrought by war: There was surely something more to it than that. The destruction was symbolic, as iconoclasm always has been symbolic. Iconoclasm speaks to a hatred of whatever is destroyed, in this case a civilization felt to be both alien and probably superior, or at any rate that regarded itself as superior.

This was not what appalled me most, however. It was when I spoke to two young British journalists about what I had seen, recommending that they went to see it for themselves, that I was most shocked.

They could not see any symbolic significance in the destruction of the piano, or for that matter of the hospital. Why was I worried about a few, ultimately replaceable inanimate objects when a quarter of a million people, something like a 12th to an eighth of the population, had been slaughtered in the war? What was the destruction of a mere piano to that?

They could see no connection between the slaughter and the iconoclasm. This astounded and alarmed me. And I now see this obliviousness as a forerunner of what we now see in Europe, that is to say, a widespread iconoclasm masquerading as political purpose.

The love of or respect for civilization is not universal or automatic. Insofar as the achievements of civilization are not equally accessible to all, it is often, and by many, as much hated as it is loved. It confronts people with their own insignificance or nullity, and they seek to take their revenge upon it. Of course, giving vent to their hatred can easily be given a patina of political virtue, such as the desire for equality or social justice, and demagogues are gifted precisely at the provision of this patina to masses of humanity. There are few joys greater than destruction in the name of higher purpose. Man is a destroyer almost as much as he is a creator.

The Russian anarchist, Mikhail Bakunin, an opponent of Karl Marx, said that the destructive urge is also a creative urge. No: This is not the creative destruction of capitalism as described by Schumpeter. This is destruction for the joy of destruction of what is hated.

Theodore Dalrymple is a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute and a contributing editor of City Journal . He is a retired physician who, most recently, practiced in a British inner-city hospital and prison.

scraped.title: Chaos In Riyadh: Aramco Skyscraper Hit By Missile Strike
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Chaos In Riyadh: Aramco Skyscraper Hit By Missile Strike
scraped.body_text:
Three troubling developments emerged from the Gulf region on Sunday morning:

Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry confirmed that an attempted attack on the Aramco administrative building in King Abdullah Financial District occurred earlier.

The Saudi Press Agency reported that falling shrapnel caused minor damage, with no injuries or fatalities reported. Videos posted on X show blown-out windows and damage across several floors.

A Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District sustained minor damage from fallen debris after a Houthi missile attack, according to Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry. No casualties have been reported. https://t.co/ZzEQoDSmjc pic.twitter.com/wnX9smTDiE

"An administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was subjected to an attempted attack," the official Saudi news agency reported earlier today, citing a source at the Saudi Energy Ministry.

🛑شاهد برج ارامكو في مركز الملك عبدالله المالي في الرياض . pic.twitter.com/FkTNZvzzkf

"The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported," the agency reported.

The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles over Riyadh and the southern region. The damage to Aramco's office tower raises questions about the effectiveness of the kingdom's $83 billion in defense spending last year and its ability to safeguard both the financial district and critical oil and gas infrastructure.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X that the kingdom's air defenses also "intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh."

In the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three oil tankers were ablaze. Iran has threatened vessels transiting the critical waterway without Iranian authorization. Tehran did not say whether it had targeted the three tankers.

"Since the early hours of this morning, three non-compliant tankers have exploded and caught fire while they were sailing in the illegal channel in the Strait of Hormuz," the IRGC wrote in a statement.

Separately, US Central Command said US forces disabled the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman after it attempted to breach the blockade of Iran.

Following the Democratic Party's sweep in the US midterms, fears have mounted that the Trump administration could target Kharg Island and/or Pickaxe Mountain to figuratively "finish the job" and weaken the regime by striking its oil and gas exports or nuclear program, despite positive diplomatic signaling.

Last week, Brent crude fell by more than $20 as traders unwound its war-risk premium amid expectations that the Democratic sweep would force the Trump administration to wind down operations against Iran and pursue a peace agreement.

"The more than $20 decline in Brent over the last week reflects bearish sentiment and a rapid unwind of the geopolitical risk premium in the price rather than a change in supply/demand fundamentals. I'd guess there is still $10-15 of risk premium reflected in the current $95 level, and while there is risk of an ongoing unwind if the Iran-US narrative continues to trend towards de-escalation, it is worth reflecting on what has really changed," UBS analyst Dominic Ellis wrote in a note to clients.

However, Ellis warned that even with the path toward de-escalation seemingly "opening a new era of diplomatic outreach, a new Iran deal and a clear path back towards the normalization of energy exports, the near 700 mn drawdown in global inventories as a result of the conflict so far and the at least 40-50mb ongoing monthly inventory draw if the conflict continues will drive incremental demand that keeps a floor on oil for the next 18-24 months."

items.title: Ex-MAHA Insider Tells Rogan What Trump Didn't Know About His Own White House
items.summary: Ex-MAHA Insider Tells Rogan What Trump Didn't Know About His Own White House Former senior White House advisor Calley Means says he had full White House approval for a federal look at how much sugar American children eat - until Trump's former Chief-of-Staff Susie Wiles killed it. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles listens as President Donald Trump speaks to reporters after signing an executive order reclassifying marijuana as a less dangerous drug in the Oval Office of the White House, D...

scraped.title: Ex-MAHA Insider Tells Rogan What Trump Didn't Know About His Own White House
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Ex-MAHA Insider Tells Rogan What Trump Didn't Know About His Own White House
scraped.body_text:
Former senior White House advisor Calley Means says he had full White House approval for a federal look at how much sugar American children eat - until Trump's former Chief-of-Staff Susie Wiles killed it.

"And that's where Susie told me, we can't do that. I need the sugar industry money. I need the money for the midterms," Means told Joe Rogan in an episode published Friday. In fact, according to Means, Wiles was up to all sorts of bad stuff.

Means, who quit on Oct. 22 without giving a reason and says he connected Robert F. Kennedy Jr. with Donald Trump in 2024, spent more than two hours naming the people he says stood between MAHA voters and what they voted for. He said a Wiles aide put an executive order on his desk declaring glyphosate, the weed killer in Bayer's Roundup, a national security issue, told him it was "final," and said Kennedy "should not be calling the president or calling anyone." Trump, he said, didn't know his own Justice Department then pushed the Supreme Court to take the case Bayer went on to win.

" There is a very concentrated group of people in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for and are frankly, I think it's very clear, doing things for other reasons, particularly in many cases to enrich their families," Means said near the top of the episode.

The episode went up the same day Trump announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff on Monday, with Wiles moving to the Trump political operation after Republicans' midterm wipeout . Means taped it before the shakeup, and Wiles is who he spent most of the first hour on. He marked the news on X:

Susie Wiles is out as chief of staff.

— Calley Means (@calleymeans) November 6, 2026

"Susie Wiles is the most powerful chief of staff in modern American history. And she has taken a stranglehold on any policy decision," Means said, adding that cabinet secretaries spend meetings "constantly worrying about how to get on Susie's good side."

He then walked Rogan through the people around her. Wiles, he said, was one of the country's top lobbyists before the White House , and "her career has been taking money from the industries and foreign governments who would pay her the most money" - including, in his account, as a top consultant to Benjamin Netanyahu and to the pharmaceutical and pesticide industries. James Blair, the head of political operations and "her friend from Florida," he said "has taken a lot of money from industries like the sugar industry."

Tony Fabrizio, Trump's chief pollster, is the one every policy "goes through," Means said, because his polling tells the team what is politically worth doing, while he takes money from "almost every single industry we're fighting against right now to this day." Later in the episode the show pulled up what Means said was the client list on Fabrizio's website: Pfizer, PhRMA, Philip Morris, Procter & Gamble, R.J. Reynolds and Dow Chemical among them. On school lunch reform, Means said, Fabrizio was "getting paid by Pepsi and giving political analysis that the juice isn't worth the squeeze."

When Means pitched healthier school meals to Fabrizio, citing Rogan's listeners, the pollster brushed it off, he said: "[MAHA] is not really a big part of our strategy." The strategy, by Means' account, was gerrymandering ("they were obsessed with redistricting") and campaign gimmicks like no tax on tips, all justified by the need for campaign cash.

Richard Walters, who joined the White House from FGS Global, came from a firm that "lobbied for pesticides, lobbied for pharma" and was paid by the pesticide trade group CropLife right before he left, Means said. While Wiles was "out getting cancer treatment," he added, "Richard was effectively chief of staff." Trump disclosed Wiles' breast cancer diagnosis in March, saying she would keep working through treatment.

Then the family business. Wiles' daughter Katie is a lobbyist at Continental Strategy , and Means said that was an open channel. "If a company hired Susie's daughter, then that was getting a high priority," he said, calling it "an open discussion in the White House." By his account the firm had "almost zero in revenue" before Trump's return and shot up to "30-ish million dollars a year in revenue." Florida filings already put Continental's lobbying pay near $5 million in 2023.

Ballard Partners, where Wiles worked before the campaign, was the other route. "If you hire Ballard, you get a meeting with Susie and you can get things done," Means said, calling the firm's reported $98 million "the down payment." Later in the episode he laid out the whole menu:

"If any special interest is watching, and you're trying to rig the system, unless it changes, pay Ballard, pay Continental, Susie's daughter, pay Checkmate, Chris [LaCivita's] son. That's another one that shot up. And, you know, pound Susie with donations and calls. Everyone knows this playbook. It's an open secret in DC."

Chris LaCivita ran Trump's 2024 campaign with Wiles. His son, Chris LaCivita Jr., joined Checkmate Government Relations after the election and registered to lobby for more than 40 clients in 2025.

Means stressed it isn't a Trump problem alone. "This is how DC works," he said, and he said he doesn't think Trump "knows about most of this."

Means' most detailed account was glyphosate, the herbicide in Bayer's Roundup. He said getting the word into the first MAHA report was "the biggest policy battle I had seen up to that time," and that as Bayer's push for legal immunity stalled in the states and in Congress, he warned Wiles' team and USDA leadership that the administration should stay out of it.

Then, he said, a Wiles aide called him into a room and put an executive order on the desk. "And it was the glyphosate EO that says it's a national security issue," Means said. "And he said, this is final. It's national security. It's coming out tomorrow." The aide told him to "please inform Bobby" and that Kennedy "should not be calling the president or calling anyone," Means said. Wiles then called Kennedy's office, and the order came out the next day.

That was February's "Promoting the National Defense by Ensuring an Adequate Supply of Elemental Phosphorus and Glyphosate-Based Herbicides," published in the Federal Register on Feb. 23, which Kennedy publicly defended at the time. "I will tell you, the Secretary of War, the major generals, they don't see our lack of glyphosate on US farms as a national security issue," Means said. He said the order was driven by Courtney Knupp, then a National Security Council staffer - "she, with Susie, drove the E.O." - who has since been named CEO of the United Soybean Board.

The Supreme Court came next. Means said Heidi Overton, then a White House aide and now Trump's pick for FDA commissioner, worked with the Justice Department, without consulting Kennedy, on the argument for the Court to take up the Roundup case, and that the solicitor general's office brought in Sarah Harris, who he said came from Bayer's main law firm. The solicitor general urged the justices to take the case, and the Court ruled for Bayer's Monsanto in June.

Trump himself didn't know his Justice Department had pushed for it, Means said. When a regenerative farmer raised the ruling at a meeting with Trump and Kennedy, he said, the president called it "a terrible idea." "And the people around him, I think treat him horribly. They treat him like they talk about him like a baby," Means said.

The single most prioritized health issue for Blair, Means said, was "to get a better pathway for fruit flavored vapes" - ahead of Medicare, health access or food. Blair argued that approving vapes "was a core midterm issue," aimed at young men, Means said.

Then-FDA Commissioner Marty Makary was pressed on it "meeting after meeting" in the West Wing and held his ground, Means said. Makary was pushed out in May. Overton then "wrote up a policy to relax standards" on fruit-flavored vapes, Means said, and public health groups sued over the FDA's flavored e-cigarette policy in July.

When Means pushed the other way on food, he said, Blair told him "the food industry, we don't want to beat up on them too much."

Asked by Rogan what was stopping Trump, Means pointed at the bureaucracy. Kennedy, "my hero," runs a 90,000-person department, and "he's surrounded by demons who want him out and want him just destroyed," Means said. "They were sending around a memo, a CIA manual, about how to be a bad bureaucrat and subvert an institution from within. That's like sent around by all the career officials."

Means appeared to be describing the Simple Sabotage Field Manual, a 1944 guide from the CIA's wartime predecessor, the OSS, which the CIA publishes on its website. It tells saboteurs inside an organization to insist on going through channels, refer everything to committees and haggle over the wording of communications.

Means also pointed to Moderna's mRNA flu shot, which the FDA refused to review in February. He said the trial compared it against an outdated flu vaccine and showed "a 0.8% absolute risk reduction." Asked about side effects, he said, "it can't be definitively said, but there were deaths," in the trial group.

Overton, a Makary protege from Johns Hopkins, told the two of them the corporate pressure had grown too much, Means said. "And I'm like, okay, this place turns you into demons," he said. The shot was approved in August after what Means called a "sham advisory committee." After Makary's exit, he added, the FDA told Pfizer it no longer has to run the new COVID vaccine study that had been a condition of the shot's reapproval.

Kratom's concentrated opioid compound 7-OH, which Means called "gas station heroin," followed the same path. He said regulators set a strict 0.05% limit early in the term, then, after "unrelenting lobbying," raised the allowed concentration 20-fold. "Again, I don't think Trump even knows about this," he said.

The line Means said he heard most from Wiles was about the midterms. "Susie said to me many times, we need money for the midterms, [Calley]. We need money for the midterms," he said.

The sharpest example came when David Kessler, the 1990s FDA commissioner who took on Big Tobacco, petitioned the FDA to examine sugar and refined carbohydrates in children's diets. Means said the initiative had a 60 Minutes segment behind it, full White House approval and a pass through the interagency process before Wiles told him she needed the sugar industry money. Earlier in the episode he gave it as a "direct quote": "I need the money from the sugar people to win the midterms."

"Okay. The midterms are over. Now what?" Rogan asked. Whatever the strategy was, he added, "they got destroyed." Means pinned the loss on "the strategy of James Blair and Tony Fabrizio and Susie," and said the point now is "why the hell aren't we doing these now?"

Rogan didn't let Trump off the hook. "Don't you think he takes some responsibility?" he asked, pointing to the Iran war and "the cryptocurrency thing." "Of course he's the ultimate responsibility," Means said, while arguing that senior staffers are now working to throw the president under the bus for the loss.

What finally pushed him out, Means said, was a federal definition of ultra-processed food that was "simply a definition, not even tied to regulation." He said he had Harvard, Tufts, the American Heart Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Medical Association lined up behind it. A Mondelez lobbyist told him "we don't want it done. This will hurt our business," and said he would call Wiles. "He talked about these people at the White House like they were extensions of him," Means said.

In a meeting with Means and Kennedy, Wiles said they were "doing great" and that she didn't know "about any special interest concerns," Means said, adding that she "lied to us to our face." Afterward, he said, he heard her saying "we need to do something about [MAHA]."

School meals were the other casualty. Means spent six months on an interagency rule to end donuts and sugary pastries at school breakfast, the most common breakfast for American schoolchildren in his telling, and to add a protein requirement. "There was dozens of meetings and calls saying that taking junk food out of school lunches would hurt the companies," he said. "And when I left, the day I left, the stocks of the major junk food companies went up 8 percent."

The market data back up the size of the move. General Mills closed up 8.0% on Oct. 22, the day Means resigned, and Kraft Heinz gained 6.8%, though it was a strong day for consumer staples broadly, with the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF up 3.3%.

When he left, Means said, Wiles texted him "saying how much she admired me" and asked him "not to speak negatively of her." Asked what he would tell Trump now, he said, "I would recommend that he clears house," and that the president should "go to war with Congress" and stop "trying to make friends with John [Thune] anymore, who's a demon."

The fight moved to X on Saturday. Means posted what he called "a formal request" for Wiles and Blair to stop "harassing" him with texts and calls, and offered to "vigorously correct and apologize" for any factual error sent to him in writing:

This is a formal request for Susie Wiles and James Blair to stop harassing me with texts and calls. If there is a factual inaccuracy in what I said, send it to me in writing and I will vigorously correct and apologize for any misstatements. I will note that everything I said is...

— Calley Means (@calleymeans) November 7, 2026

Blair answered 42 minutes later, saying he had called Means the night before and told him he would consider suing if Means defamed him. "Calley, your poor me act is tiring and embarrassing for a grown man who launched a smear campaign," Blair wrote. "I've been called worse things by better people than you. And I haven't even gotten started."

Again not true. Called Calley last night. He didn't answer or return my call. He messaged me this morning. After a few messages and telling him I'd consider suing him if he defamed me, I told him was done responding to him privately. And haven't since. Calley, your poor... https://t.co/FRjj32Ojj7

— James Blair (@JamesBlairUSA) November 7, 2026

Kennedy, whom Means called "a hero," didn't name him. Within two hours of the episode going up on Friday, he posted that "draining the swamp is a mandate" - and then thanked Wiles, crediting her, not Means, with his partnership with Trump:

Draining the swamp is a mandate, and we have an obligation to deliver. Entrenched interests have exercised power in Washington under both parties for decades. President Trump and I intend to keep fighting until the American people - not corporate influence - drive our health...

— Secretary Kennedy (@SecKennedy) November 6, 2026

I'm grateful to Susie Wiles for her calm and inspiring leadership and wisdom. Susie brokered my partnership with President Trump in July 2024 and then spearheaded the campaign to get our team elected. She oversaw the transition process and helped me bring an extraordinary cadre... https://t.co/hZ9JC5WRyH

— Secretary Kennedy (@SecKennedy) November 6, 2026

"After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster told the Daily Caller News Foundation , which could not reach Wiles.

Meanwhile:

The Calley Means - Joe Rogan episode this week should be required listening in every high school civics class

— Mike Benz (@MikeBenzCyber) November 8, 2026

scraped.title: The Incoming Democrat Governor Of Texas Is Already Going After Elon Musk
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: The Incoming Democrat Governor Of Texas Is Already Going After Elon Musk
scraped.body_text:
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D-TX) has asked the state's parks department to hold off on a proposed sale of state land to SpaceX until she takes office, contacting the department's executive director before she is sworn in this January. The move puts part of Elon Musk's expansion plans in South Texas on hold.

Hinojosa won the governorship this week as Democrats swept the statewide races in Texas , a result that put the state's relationship with Musk and his companies in question . Musk relocated several of his businesses to Texas in recent years, and he has close ties to President Donald Trump and outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott (R-TX).

Investors reacted the morning after the vote. Tesla and SpaceX each fell nearly 6% in premarket trading on Wednesday. Musk had spent heavily to prevent that outcome. The billionaire, one of the Republican Party's largest donors, had given more than $445 million to Republican candidates and causes this cycle and urged his followers on X to vote against Democrats. About $190 million of it went into Ken Paxton's (R-TX) race for the U.S. Senate, most of it through the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate Republican leaders.

The sale under discussion covers about 1,300 acres of public land in Cameron County, including Boca Chica State Park , which covers about 1,055 acres and sits next to SpaceX's Starbase rocket facility. Acquiring the land would allow SpaceX to expand its operations at the site, which serves as the company's main launch and production hub for its Starship program.

A draft agenda for the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission's Thursday meeting included the sale, according to the Texas Tribune . The item came off the agenda at Hinojosa's request, she said , though the department had already said in October that the commission was not considering the sale at its November meeting. Hinojosa did not say whether the department agreed to wait until she takes office, and the commission did not announce a new date for the discussion. Texas Monthly first reported the proposed deal last month, and environmental groups opposed it after the news became public.

Hinojosa tied her intervention to her personal connection to the area. The park lies in the Rio Grande Valley, where she grew up.

"It's such an important resource," Hinojosa said of the park. "The Valley is so important to me as the place I am from, and I will never forget it."

The Boca Chica pause is the first concrete action Hinojosa has taken against Musk, one of Texas's largest employers, and it arrives before she holds any formal authority over state agencies. Abbott remains governor until January, and the Parks and Wildlife Commission's members serve under his appointments.

Musk's companies came to Texas largely on the strength of the state's business climate. He moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX, X, and The Boring Company to the state, citing in part his opposition to Democratic policies in California. Tesla relocated its headquarters to Austin in 2021, and Musk announced in 2024 that SpaceX and X would follow after California enacted a law he publicly opposed. Starbase incorporated as its own city in 2025.

Hinojosa's election also raises questions beyond Musk's holdings. During the campaign, she promised a temporary moratorium on data centers in Texas , a pledge that bears on the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout the Trump administration has promoted as part of its push to reindustrialize the American economy. Texas has become one of the country's leading destinations for large-scale data center construction.

CNN's Jake Tapper pressed Hinojosa on that issue in an interview on Thursday.

"Your victory, in particular, is one that we're told AI investors are worried about, given your promises of a temporary data center moratorium ," Tapper said.

Hinojosa said she intends to change the terms on which Texas deals with major companies.

"We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans ," she said.

Tapper also asked about Boca Chica, and whether Musk might move his companies out of Texas. "Selling our beach to Elon Musk is just something that is almost unimaginable. It's unacceptable," Hinojosa said. "Our beaches are enshrined in our Texas Constitution as being free and open to the people of Texas."

Hinojosa claims she remains open to working with Musk , though she placed conditions on that relationship.

"We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms ," Hinojosa told Tapper. "It cannot be just running over the people of Texas, and that's what changes now that I will be governor."

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa: "We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms" Jake Tapper asked her about blocking the sale of a Texas state park to SpaceX, and whether Musk might leave the state over it. Her... https://t.co/owsQCmw5iW pic.twitter.com/Zzl8At5X2J

— Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) November 6, 2026

Hinojosa did not say in the interview what terms she would require of Musk's companies. On data centers, she said Texas needs to "stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," new state laws she did not spell out.

Hinojosa takes office in January, and the fate of the Boca Chica land sale, and the working relationship between Musk's companies and the state of Texas, now rests with her administration.

scraped.title: U.S. Strikes Iran’s Air Defenses as Tehran Seeks Russian Weapons * The Gateway Pundit * by Antonio Graceffo
scraped.description: U.S.
scraped.author: https://www.thegatewaypundit.com/author/antoniog/
scraped.h1: U.S. Strikes Iran’s Air Defenses as Tehran Seeks Russian Weapons
scraped.body_text:
U.S. forces struck Iranian air defense systems early on Nov. 7, hours after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed it had shot down another American drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz . President Donald Trump told reporters Saturday that the strikes were “minor” and that U.S. forces knocked out an Iranian anti-aircraft device “in about 15 minutes, maybe five.” Washington has not confirmed the loss of any drone.

Trump also said talks through mediators were continuing. “We are talking to Iran. We have been,” he said.

According to Iranian state media , Iran is doing well in the war. However, no outside source has confirmed the IRGC’s claims of drone shootdowns and tanker damage. The IRGC said it shot down MQ-1 drones over Qeshm on Nov. 4 and Nov. 6, counting them as its 15th and 16th of the war. It also claimed to have downed an MQ-9 Reaper over the Strait on Nov. 4. As of that date, it put its combined total at 68 MQ-1 and MQ-9 drones since the war began.

The IRGC also said naval mines destroyed four tankers on Nov. 4 along a route it had declared prohibited, that it had seized two vessels , and that two more tankers struck mines on Nov. 6. CBS News reported “no confirmation of any of these incidents from maritime officials .” U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), which says U.S. forces cleared the main shipping lanes of mines, has called earlier IRGC mine claims “FALSE” .

On Nov. 5, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center, which reports attacks on commercial shipping, said a tanker had been hit by two unidentified projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal , Qatar.

The United States is enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports and oil terminals with more than 10,000 personnel. CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said on Oct. 30 that Iran had exported no oil since the blockade was reimposed in mid-July and that IRGC naval forces were absent from the Strait. “I didn’t see the IRGC out there, at all,” he said. “Iran’s navy is all at the bottom of the sea.”

During an Oct. 25 visit to the Strait, Cooper said, “This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.” CENTCOM said U.S. forces had helped Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer and supported the passage of more than 3,000 commercial vessels through the Strait over the previous six months.

Iran has continued buying military goods despite the blockade. A Reuters investigation found that Iran had imported at least $2 billion in military equipment, explosives and heavy trucks since January 2025 through a network of more than 5,000 entities.

On Nov. 4, the State Department sanctioned two individuals and one entity based in Belarus, Russia and Nigeria for their roles in Iran’s efforts to obtain shoulder-fired air-defense missiles.

Iran is also seeking more weapons from Russia. On Nov. 5, the Financial Times reported that Russia had agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles. According to UNITED24 Media , the launchers are APU-L models designed for Mi-28 attack helicopters. Each carries two LMUR missiles, which Russia has used against Ukraine since 2022.

Russian defense industry documents obtained by the Ukrainian group Dallas Analytics show a 2024–2025 production schedule listing China and a customer coded “K-10” as foreign buyers. A source told the FT that “K-10” is the designation Russia’s state arms agency uses for Iran .

On Nov. 5, Vladimir Putin received Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, at the Kremlin . The two discussed a gas pipeline from Russia to Iran. Although Iran holds the world’s second-largest natural gas reserves, it is turning to Russia for supplies as war damage and underinvestment threaten to deepen its energy crisis . Iran International reported that Rezaei had been sent to Moscow to seek S-400 air defenses .

Iran also faces accusations of directing the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthis seized Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb area in September, and Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging the escalation.

On Nov. 3, Yemeni Interior Minister Maj. Gen. Ibrahim Haidan said 21 foreign experts, 14 from the IRGC and seven from Hezbollah, were helping the Houthis plan and direct military operations from Hodeidah, Sanaa, Saada, Hajjah, Amran and Khokha.

He said their specialties included ballistic missiles , drones, electronic warfare, selecting commercial ships as targets, explosive-laden boats, autonomous submarines and mine-laying. Their work, he said, threatens shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea. Al Jazeera’s report does not describe evidence supporting the claims.

Hezbollah’s Media Relations Office denied the accusations on Nov. 4. The following day, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei “strongly rejected claims about the presence of Iranian military advisers in Yemen.” He was also responding to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who had accused Tehran of interfering there.

On Nov. 4, Iran marked 13 Aban, the anniversary of the 1979 U.S. embassy takeover, with rallies at more than 900 locations , including a march in Tehran from Palestine Square toward the former U.S. embassy. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said a change in Washington’s political leadership following the U.S. midterm elections would not alter U.S. policy toward Iran. He warned that Iran would respond on a much broader scale to any new U.S. attack

scraped.description: Kansas Democratic Senator-elect Adam Hamilton has warned his party against spending the next two years investigating President Donald Trump.
scraped.author: https://www.thegatewaypundit.com/author/benk/
scraped.h1: Incoming Dem Senator Urges His Party Not to Spend Two Years Investigating Trump — Wants Them to Focus on Cost of Living Instead (VIDEO)
scraped.body_text:
Kansas Democratic Senator-elect Adam Hamilton has warned his party against spending the next two years investigating President Donald Trump .

Appearing on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Hamilton, who flipped the deep red state of Kansas in last week’s midterm elections, said he would be “deeply disappointed” if his first two years in the Senate were dominated by investigations into the Trump administration.

He instead argued that lawmakers should instead focus on lowering the cost of living for ordinary Americans.

“The bigger priority for me, and I think for most people in America, especially people living paycheck to paycheck, is ‘please help us with the cost of living,’” Hamilton said.

Hamilton addedthat the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress should prioritize ending the war with Iran and reversing Trump’s tariff policies.

“If I spent the next two years, my first two years in the Senate, in investigations, I’d be deeply disappointed,” he continued.

“I want to get to work helping the people in my state and helping the people across the country.”

Watch the clip below:

Adam Hamilton:

If I spent the next two years, my first two years in the Senate, in investigations, I’d be deeply disappointed.

I want to get to work helping the people in my state and helping people across the country.

Yes, let’s get guardrails put in place so that we don’t… pic.twitter.com/RE0VyrNOkG

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 8, 2026

His remarks come as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress following their sweeping midterm victories.

Several prominent Democrats have already made clear that they will begin their lawfare campaign on day one of the next Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer declared Wednesday that Democrats would launch investigations and pursue legal action at the earliest possible opportunity.

The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, has told the administration to “lawyer up.”

‘LAWYER UP’: Jubilant Dems Warn Lawfare Campaign Will Begin the Moment They Take Office

Hamilton, however, warned that Democrats risk squandering their electoral gains if they fail to focus on what really matters.

“Let’s focus on helping the American people,” he said.

“And I’ll tell you, the Democrats, if they don’t, if we don’t figure that out and get to work on helping people, this is going to be a one and done, kind of, you know, kind of blue wave.”

scraped.h1: Trump Orders Justice Department to Investigate Democrats Over Impeachment Threats
scraped.body_text:
President Trump says he has ordered the Justice Department to investigate Democrats who have threatened to impeach Attorney General Todd Blanche and other members of his administration.

Trump made the announcement Saturday afternoon in a post on Truth Social , days after Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate.

“The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States,” Trump wrote, adding that they were also threatening others with impeachment and “many other forms of punishment.” He said Democrats admit they have “no reason to do so” and described the conduct as criminal.

Since Election Day, at least two House Democrats, Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia and Rep. Deborah Ross of North Carolina, have publicly said they would support impeaching Blanche, according to Fox News.

Trump also said Democrats have threatened Republican donors with prison, though he did not name any donors.

The president’s order sets up battle with the incoming Democratic majority, which has made clear it plans to use its new power to launch investigations and possibly impeachment proceedings against administration officials. Trump’s supporters see the talk of impeachment as political retaliation dressed up as oversight, and the president appears determined to push back before Democrats are even sworn in.

scraped.h1: New Migrant Caravan Heads North After Democrats Win Midterms
scraped.body_text:
A new caravan of as many as 500 migrants has crossed into Mexico and is heading toward the U.S. border, just days after Democrats won control of the House, the Senate and the Texas governor’s office, Breitbart Texas reported.

Between 300 and 500 migrants, most of them from Central America, crossed the Rodolfo Robles International Bridge from Guatemala into Ciudad Hidalgo, Mexico, on Friday, according to reports out of Mexico. The group then began moving north toward the municipality of Suchiate.

Independent journalist Julio Rosas, who shared a report on the crossing from the Mexican newspaper Diario del Sur, linked the timing to the election. “With Dems winning the midterms, migrants will start making their way to the U.S.-Mexico border,” he wrote on X.

Oh look, exactly as I predicted after reporting on a different caravan before the midterms.

With Dems winning the midterms, migrants will start making their way to the U.S.-Mexico border and wait until Trump’s policies go away. Whether that happens after 2028 is up to American voters.

— Julio Rosas (@Julio_Rosas11) November 7, 2026

It is the second caravan in recent weeks. An earlier group left Mexico’s southern border in mid-October under the name “Caravana Sin Fronteras” before renaming itself “Fe y Esperanza #2,” or “Faith and Hope #2.” Rosas reported that members of that caravan said they hoped Democrats would win the midterms. Some were reportedly migrants who had already been deported from the United States.

Illegally reentering the country after deportation is a federal crime, punishable by fines and up to two years in prison for a first offense, or up to 20 years for those with an aggravated felony conviction.

The Department of Homeland Security responded bluntly to the earlier caravan. “There is absolutely ZERO chance this caravan will be allowed into the United States,” the department said.

scraped.description: The secretary of state says Washington wants a “presence agreement” allowing American troops to operate jointly with Venezuela less than a year after Maduro’s…
scraped.h1: Rubio Says U.S. in Talks to Establish Military Presence in Venezuela
scraped.body_text:
The United States is negotiating with Venezuela to establish an American military presence in the country, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.

In an interview with the New York Times , Rubio said the U.S. wants a “presence agreement” that would allow American troops to operate “jointly” with Venezuelan forces. There are currently no U.S. military bases in South America.

The talks come less than a year after the U.S. operation that led to the arrest of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro and his wife at the start of the year. Under Maduro, Venezuela hosted military drills with Russia, China and Iran in 2022.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signaled the shift weeks ago. Asked by The Center Square in early October about bases in the region, he said the U.S. is expanding its footprint in Central and South America with partners. “We are at war with the drug cartels, with DTOs,” Hegseth said.

President Trump has also pointed to the economic benefits of the new relationship. “We’re taking a lot of oil, and we have a great relationship,” he told The Center Square, adding, “We’re going to start filling up our national strategic reserves with the Venezuelan oil for very little money.”

The administration has targeted narco-terrorists across the Caribbean and South America for more than a year, an approach some have nicknamed the “Donroe Doctrine,” a play on the Monroe Doctrine. Trump-backed candidates have also won elections across South America.

The Venezuela talks are part of a reshuffling of America’s military footprint. The U.S. has reached an agreement to build two bases in Greenland, confirmed a troop drawdown in Germany and floated moving more forces out of Italy and Spain.

scraped.h1: Why New Age practices are more dangerous than they look, according to a former psychic
scraped.body_text:
Jenn Nizza tells Rick Burgess it’s Christians’ job to expose the lies about witchcraft that modern culture keeps normalizing.

Rick Burgess, BlazeTV host of “Strange Encounters,” wants his audience to be equipped but never paranoid when it comes to spiritual warfare.

“We've tried to be good stewards of this podcast, and just to warn you — not to have you looking for demons around every corner, but also not to send you out into this fallen creation where there's spiritual war raging for you not to be prepared,” he says.

That’s why he had former psychic Jenn Nizza on the show. Deeply involved in the occult and New Age for roughly 25 years before becoming a Christian, Nizza now warns believers about the spiritual dangers of mainstream New Age practices — tarot cards, astrology, crystals, numerology, and the like.

On this episode, Nizza joins Burgess for an honest conversation about the New Age pitfalls ensnaring Christians.

Mainstream occultism doesn’t look like black robes, blood rituals, and devil worship. Rather it presents itself as “light,” which is why people are so drawn to it, Nizza explains.

“The counterfeit is very manipulative. ... It's really darkness in disguise presenting as a false light,” she says, highlighting how the messaging often revolves around “healing, solutions, [and] wisdom.”

She explains how Satan, who the Bible says disguises himself as an angel of light, offers “cheap [imitations] intended to deceive” — things that “look so close” to the truth and seem “so convincing” that even Christians will sometimes take the bait.

Modern culture has played a pivotal role in normalizing New Age beliefs and practices through “social media, cinema, [and] the music industry,” says Nizza.

“‘Wicked’ with Ariana Grande ... the movie ‘Tarot,’ ‘Practical Magic,’ ‘Hocus Pocus’ ... that's the devil defining a very real, spiritually dangerous practice: witchcraft,” she tells Burgess.

“This is glamorizing witchcraft and desensitizing the masses. So we as Christians need to step in and share the truth about what it is, and rather than glamorize, expose it and point to the light of Christ.”

She gives the example of the popular, long-running TLC show “Long Island Medium,” which documented the life of psychic medium Theresa Caputo.

“She's just like how I used to be — want to help people and seemingly innocuous, right?” says Nizza but, “You don't go home with her. You don't know what the demonic oppression she is facing, and I can assure you that she is because when you do these things, you will face the side effects.”

“[Christians] need to be the ones to go in there and tell the truth about this and not shy away from this because otherwise you're letting these secular movies that are run by devils disciple your congregants, disciple your children, and certainly at the very least, educate them falsely.”

To hear more, watch the episode above.

To enjoy more bold talk and big laughs, subscribe to BlazeTV — the largest multi-platform network of voices who love America, defend the Constitution, and live the American dream.

BlazeTV Staff

items.summary: Thanks to the loud noises of a few boldface names on the left, Americans are getting the impression that the Democrats of 2026 are the anti-technology party. With the blue team surging into Congress this election cycle, the logical inference is that the tech industry lost big — a huge deal for the many voters who had just about resigned themselves to the idea that technology is the one thing that can’t be stopped in America.Drawing this conclusion would be a colossal misread of reality, no ma...

scraped.title: Don’t be fooled by Bernie Sanders — tech won the midterms | Blaze Media
scraped.description: Its power is irresistible. Its importance is irreversible.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: Don’t be fooled by Bernie Sanders — tech won the midterms
scraped.body_text:
Its power is irresistible. Its importance is irreversible.

Thanks to the loud noises of a few boldface names on the left, Americans are getting the impression that the Democrats of 2026 are the anti-technology party. With the blue team surging into Congress this election cycle, the logical inference is that the tech industry lost big — a huge deal for the many voters who had just about resigned themselves to the idea that technology is the one thing that can’t be stopped in America.

Drawing this conclusion would be a colossal misread of reality, no matter how sensationalist the headlines about draconian tech crackdown plans coming from Bernie Sanders and company.

The left elites do not want to de-technologize our economy, our government, or anything else. They simply want to control the technology — the better to control everything downstream of it.

At the tactical level, Democrats did not win because they ran against tech. At the strategic level, the domestic and international left is more convinced than ever that the only way it can end the Trump era and re-establish itself as the ruling elite is by wielding technology with renewed force.

First, the ground truth. As observed by Adam Kovacevich, the tech-optimist Democrat who founded the Chamber of Progress and came from Google’s public policy shop, AI and data centers ranked a distant 19th among issues in a New York Times/Siena survey. Democrats in gubernatorial contests who didn’t support data center bans performed better than those who did. And almost all Democrats Kovacevich defines as “pro-innovation” have won their races. (So far.)

The exit polls tell the same story. Almost 40% cited the economy as their top concern; nearly a third cited the “state of democracy.” The rest prioritized immigration, health care, foreign policy, and crime.

Now, one could argue that all these priorities have to do with tech in some sense. Tech has largely eaten the economy. Tech is reworking our form of government. Tech is what’s behind the intense push to fill out well-paying jobs with skilled immigrants. Health care is rapidly being technologized. Foreign policy is already dominated by the race to technologically transform the global battlefield — a dynamic that has focused unprecedented controversy around Israel, a country that has rapidly vaulted to cyber-superpower status. Crime? Seen any headlines about cyberattacks lately …?

Yes, in a very real sense, as Donald Trump so memorably put it, everything is computer now.

RELATED: America’s ‘AI czar’ could revolutionize our form of government

Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

But the left elite has no qualms about the force of these transformative technological changes. It only opposes the vector, which has arrowed in a nominally rightward direction ever since the most influential faction of Silicon Valley decided they could only remain masters of their own destiny if they threw in with Trump.

The left elites do not want to de-technologize our economy, our government, our immigration policy, our health care industry, our foreign policy, or anything else. They simply want to control the technology — the better to control everything downstream of it.

Right-wingers may look at that fact and see within it a darkly pulsating evil. Because they share little religious unity, many on the right insist on seeing that menace in ideological, not religious terms — not demonic but communist, socialist, or third-worldist.

Yet whatever kernels of insight may lurk therein, the truth is that the right is even more desperate to control the tech than the left is, and that tortured desire defines the political battle space far more than any of the hoary modern “isms” that Americans keep being told to conform our transformed postmodern reality to. It’s not going to work.

Everyone — left, right, center, white, brown, or purple — fears erasure, defeat, and destruction at the hands of adversaries who have aced them out for control of godlike tech.

RELATED: Sorry, Bill Gates. We’re sitting out this apocalypse.

BAY ISMOYO/AFP/Getty Images

That’s why the midterms weren’t a referendum on the breakneck advancement of technology to an even greater position of dominance over our country and our way of life. And yet despite real defeats for data centers in local elections, tech’s commanding position remains intact. Those setbacks may turn out to be Tootsie Roll-sized speed bumps. (Think stopping data centers stops AI? Think again. )

Tech elites who embraced Trump — Elon Musk first among them — may worry about reprisals from Democrats looking to throw bloody beefsteaks to the slavering mob. But at a time when almost nothing but tech has consequential energy behind it, it is technology that was the victor on Tuesday and technology that will define the fateful choices America’s elites will make — with or without public support — about just what our country and our people are to become.

James Poulos

BlazeTV Host

scraped.title: The best caregiver support may come with terrible coffee | Blaze Media
scraped.description: At a weekly gathering in Montana, the coffee is ferocious, the cookies disappear, and the tissues get passed around. Nobody has to explain a burden everyone at the table recognizes.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: The best caregiver support may come with terrible coffee
scraped.body_text:
At a weekly gathering in Montana, the coffee is ferocious, the cookies disappear, and the tissues get passed around. Nobody has to explain a burden everyone at the table recognizes.

The election is over. People will spend weeks picking apart the results. Meanwhile, family caregivers are sorting medications, helping someone get dressed, and having late-night conversations with the ceiling fan.

November is National Family Caregivers Month. As the holidays approach, expectations pile up even when a caregiver’s strength is running low.

If you’re a caregiver who’s frazzled, stressed, heartbroken, or weary, you’re in the right place.

You can be surrounded by people who love you and still feel lonely. I often tell pastors that caregivers can feel lonely on a crowded pew.

Family caregivers know what it means to disappear into someone else’s story. People ask how your loved one is doing. You explain the latest procedure or what the doctor said. Somewhere in the conversation, what you’re carrying disappears beneath the details of the person you’re caring for.

When I started this column for Blaze News, I wanted caregivers to find a little respite and something solid to stand on while they caught their breath. Whatever else I write about, I keep coming back to the caregiver who wonders whether anyone understands.

That’s also why I started a caregiver group at our church here in Montana.

Every Thursday morning, we gather around a table. First-timers sometimes arrive nervous, sometimes already teary-eyed. Walking into a room of strangers to talk about caring for someone you love takes courage.

The church has committed to keeping us supplied with tissues.

The pastor or his assistant sometimes has coffee waiting. When neither is there, that responsibility falls to me.

I’m accustomed to making coffee for Gracie. She likes coffee that reaches out and slaps you. Most attendees have learned to politely decline when I’m handling the brewing.

One fellow brought a tin of cookies from Costco. We’ve made a sizable dent in them.

Well, let’s be honest. I’ve made a sizable dent. I keep passing the tin around, but somehow it makes its way back to me. I need to be careful, or I’ll get so big the bears will have to start hiding their food.

RELATED: Would you trust this politician with your wallet?

Sonmez karakurt/Getty Images

We go around the table and check in. Sometimes the circumstances are dire, and the tissues get passed along with the cookies. Sometimes we talk about ordinary things. Even amid the tears, laughter has surprised us at every meeting.

You see, each of us speaks fluent caregiver. Nobody needs a lengthy explanation of why someone is exhausted, frightened, or struggling to make one more decision. We recognize the language because we live it.

This week, one man whose wife lives with dementia told us he can no longer have a rational conversation with her. Around our table, he said, he felt heard for the first time in a long time.

How many more caregivers feel the same way he does?

Sometimes, speaking fluent caregiver sounds like this: “Pull up a chair. Have a cookie. Or three. Sign this waiver before drinking the coffee.”

I can’t offer bad coffee and a tin of cookies to readers. You’ll have to supply your own tissues. If you run out, use toilet paper. We’ve all done it.

But I can bring four decades of caring for someone I love to this page. I can speak honestly about the weariness, the fear, the resentment we’re reluctant to admit, and the laughter that still catches us by surprise.

RELATED: There is a place sin cannot molest

Wwing/Getty Images

I can also remind you of something I regularly need to hear myself: You don’t have to feel better in order to be better.

Making your own doctor’s appointment, accepting help, or sitting with people who understand can be a good decision even when you still feel worn out afterward.

If you’re struggling to find the words to say to a caregiver, try these: “I see you, and I see the magnitude of what you’re carrying, and I hurt with you.”

If tears come, you don’t have to find something profound to say. Stay and listen.

If you’re a caregiver who’s frazzled, stressed, heartbroken, or weary, you’re in the right place. Tell me how you’re doing in the comments. I try to read them all and respond when I can.

If you’re none of those things, you’re still in the right place. Because if you love someone, you’ll most likely become a caregiver.

If you live long enough, you’ll need one.

Friends don’t let friends caregive alone.

Peter Rosenberger

scraped.title: Indonesia Might Be Heading into a Deep Political Crisis - Left Voice
scraped.description: The largest country in Southeast Asia has been rocked by a wiretapping scandal as Indonesians are souring on Prabowo’s administration.
scraped.author: Samuel Karlin
scraped.body_text:
The largest country in Southeast Asia has been rocked by a wiretapping scandal as Indonesians are souring on Prabowo’s administration.

Samuel Karlin

Indonesia, which in recent years has risen to the status of a middle power, might soon be rocked by a significant political crisis. Following news of a wiretapping scandal which targeted the country’s president, Prabowo Subianto, the government deployed tens of thousands of military personnel to Jakarta. The government also detained three senior police generals including former national police chief, Listyo Sigit Prabowo (unrelated to president Prabowo).

Despite the massive military deployment, a report by Bloomberg suggests that on the ground in Jakarta, things appear to be functioning as usual, and the military presence isn’t noticeable. But the same report also explains that behind these developments is a larger conflict between President Prabowo and the former president Joko Widodo who had appointed Listyo as national police chief. The conflict between the current president and former president embodies a deeper conflict between the country’s military, of which Prabowo was a top general, and the country’s police, an institution which remains close to Widodo.

The conflict at the level of the regime comes as Indonesians are souring on Prabowo’s presidency. In recent weeks students and civil society groups have been protesting in Jakarta against the government’s handling of ongoing forest fires in the country. Protesters have denounced that these fires were caused by the clearing out of sensitive lands for palm oil plantations.

Hundreds of Indonesian students and civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against President Prabowo Subianto's policies, including the handling of ongoing forest fires and government spending priorities. pic.twitter.com/E5BrXBQDtf

Additionally, mineworkers have begun a sit-in at the largest nickel-mine in the world to demand a fair contract. A pillar of Indonesia’s geopolitical significance is that it is home to the largest nickel reserves in the world. Along with nickel being used in many everyday goods, it is a key component to rechargeable batteries, giving Indonesia strategic leverage in the EV industry. This also makes Indonesian miners a strategic sector of Asia’s working class, and it will be important that workers of the world show solidarity with their struggle.

Mineworkers at the largest nickel-mining site in the world (100k+ workers) in Indonesia are staging protests and now a sit-in demanding a fair contract. Workers say at least one worker a month dies due to the lack of safety equipment and the wages are unlivable. pic.twitter.com/3hRBimgyQS

Most protests in Indonesia have remained modest in size, especially compared to student-led demonstrations which have spread across Europe and even emerged in countries in Asia and Latin America. But they speak to larger disapproval of Prabowo. After two years in power, Prabowo’s approval rating currently sits at a low of 44.5 percent, the lowest any president has received in the time that Indonesia has conducted polling. This comes as the country’s economy is stagnating, and its stock market is at risk of being downgraded, which could result in a currency crisis.

Indonesians have also turned on Prabowo due to the failure of his multi-billion dollar meals program, a flagship policy which had been meant to address malnutrition. The program, which was popular as a campaign point, has been roiled by allegations of corruption and thousands of cases of young people being poisoned or being served rice with glass and maggots. The administration has also received backlash for strengthening the role of the military in the government and restricting civil liberties.

In his time as a general, Prabowo led the violent persecution of pro-democracy activists under the country’s brutal military dictatorship which ended in 1998. However, Prabowo successfully branded himself as a cuddly, grandpa-like figure during his 2024 presidential campaign.

Another key to his electoral victory was the support he received from Widodo. The former president left office as one of Indonesia’s most popular leaders, having played a key role in elevating Indonesia to middle power prestige. While the country’s constitution barred him from running for another term, he made a deal to back Prabowo in exchange for cabinet positions for his political allies. This agreement is now falling apart amid the wiretapping scandal, spelling deeper crisis for Prabowo’s regime.

However the different factions in Indonesia’s government choose to maneuver, neither political block represents Indonesia’s students and workers who are beginning to take action against air pollution, exploitation, and attacks on democratic rights, among other issues. What role the workers and popular sectors in the country play in the event of greater political instability is to be seen.

Originally published on Novemer 6 in CRP News .

Protest

Samuel Karlin is a socialist with a background in journalism. He mainly writes for Left Voice about U.S. imperialism and international class struggle.

U.S. Marine Devin Jacob Ballard is suspected of robbing and killing a 39-year-old woman in Okinawa. This is another episode in a long history of the U.S. military presence in Okinawa fueling violence against Okinawa residents.

Samuel Karlin

The latest Trump-Xi summit produced no major breakthrough, instead establishing a fragile “managed stability” amid continuing tensions over trade, technology, Taiwan, and China’s global influence.

André Barbieri

The Lee Jae-Myung government is pushing for the deployment of South Korean troops to the Strait of Hormuz. Korean workers must oppose the deployment and the expansion of the war industry.

March to Socialism

HD Hyundai workers are demanding the end of unfair contracts, wage cuts, and discriminatory treatment. Their voices echoed far and wide across Seoul at the 2nd National Joint Action Rally of Migrant Workers.

Bae Ye-ju

Out now in English from 34 Press and Left Voice --- "Socialist Strategy and Military Art" by Emilio Albamonte and Matías Maiello draws on Clausewitz, Lenin, Trotsky, and Gramsci, rethinking revolutionary strategy and working-class hegemony for the 21st century.

Adrien Masson

November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike.

Damien Bernard

The Berlin Left Party's state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue.

Ari Aalto

October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis.

Juan Chingo

scraped.h1: Native News Weekly (November 8, 2026): D.C. Briefs
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

WASHINGTON — In addition to articles already covered by Native News Online, here is a roundup of other news released from Washington, D.C. that impacts Indian Country recently:

The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) will hold two Tribal consultation sessions Nov. 9-10, 2026, to gather input on proposed revisions to Title 2 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), which governs federal awards, including grant administration, cost principles and audit requirements.

The first session will be held in person on Monday, Nov. 9, followed by a virtual session on Tuesday, Nov. 10. Tribal leaders and finance professionals are encouraged to participate and provide feedback on how the proposed changes could affect critical funding resources for Tribal governments.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Participants will have up to three minutes to deliver oral comments. Written comments may also be submitted for up to five business days following the consultations, within the 45-day public comment period.

The Native American Finance Officers Association (NAFOA) is urging Tribal leaders to weigh in to ensure the final rule respects the government-to-government relationship between Tribal Nations and the federal government, as well as the federal trust responsibility.

The proposed revisions are intended to increase transparency, accountability and oversight while reducing administrative burdens on federal agencies and grant recipients. OMB will consider Tribal input before taking final action.

To RSVP or request additional information, contact OMB’s Office of Federal Financial Management at MBX.OMB.Grants@omb.eop.gov . NAFOA has also provided a template letter for submitting written comments.

The National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) is calling on the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) to initiate formal Tribal consultation on the federal rescheduling of cannabis.

During its 83rd Annual Convention & Marketplace, Tribal leaders adopted Resolution PSC-26-048, urging DOJ to consult with Tribal Nations about the implications of cannabis rescheduling for Tribally regulated cannabis products.

NCAI said the DOJ’s order addressed certain U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved and state-regulated medical cannabis products but did not address products regulated by Tribal Nations. The organization maintains that federal policy must respect the sovereignty of Tribal Nations that choose to regulate cannabis within their territories.

NCAI has forwarded the resolution and a formal letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche requesting consultation.

NCAI also encouraged Tribal leaders to attend the Indigenous Cannabis Industry & Policy Summit, scheduled for Nov. 9-11, 2026, at the Washington Plaza Hotel in Washington, D.C.

scraped.author: Chuck Hoskin Jr
scraped.h1: The Affordability Crisis is Hitting Low-income Cherokee Elders. We are Taking Action on the Rez.
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Cherokee Nation is investing $4.5 million in expanded financial assistance, nutritious meals and senior nutrition sites to help thousands of Cherokee elders address rising costs, improve their quality of life and remain connected to their communities using tribally generated funds.

Cherokee values teach us to respect our elders, listen to their wisdom and honor the sacrifices they’ve made for us and for our future. But honoring our elders takes more than words. It means making sure they have what they need to live healthy, secure and fulfilling lives.

Across our 7,000-square-mile Cherokee Nation Reservation, too many elders are feeling the squeeze of rising costs. Groceries, utilities and other basic needs keep taking a bigger bite out of monthly budgets. For elders living on fixed incomes, even a modest increase in expenses can force difficult choices.

Deputy Chief Bryan Warner and I believe our elders deserve better. That’s why we’re putting more tribal resources directly into their hands and expanding access to nutritious food and fellowship.

Your contribution is appreciated.

At our recent pair of Cherokee Nation Elders Summits, we announced a major expansion of our Elders in Need program , which helps low-income Cherokee elders pay their utility bills. Chief Bill John Baker established EIN in 2012. Inflation — topping 32% just in the last decade — has eroded that initial benefit at a time when we have more tribal funding to bring to bear. So, we are increasing the annual EIN benefit by 50%, from $400 to $600, while tripling the number of eligible elders from about 1,400 to 4,200.

That will be significant relief for thousands of Cherokee households. More money for groceries, medications and everyday needs means less worry about keeping the lights on and homes comfortable. We’re making this possible through a $2 million annual investment from our historic Public Health and Wellness Fund Act. The expanded program will reach more elders living on the reservation, aged 60 and older, who participate in Cherokee Nation’s energy-assistance and food-distribution programs. It will also reach eligible elders in urban portions of the reservation.

Additionally, we’re building on another commitment, making nutritious meals and fellowship more accessible to our elders.

Last year, after launching our first new site in over a decade in Stilwell , we tapped PHWFA to expand nutrition services to Bowlin Springs, Dewey and Tulsa and began an effort to improve services and facilities at all sites.

In 2027, we’ll open new elder nutrition sites in Tahlequah, Salina, Catoosa and Locust Grove, while renovating existing sites in Oaks, Foyil and Porum. That’s another $2.5 million investment in our elders.

With these latest commitments, we’re moving closer to a goal outlined in my State of the Nation address: putting an elder nutrition site within reach of every Cherokee elder on our reservation. These sites are about more than a good, hot meal. They’re places where senior citizens are able visit with friends, stay connected to their communities and find the interpersonal interactions that are so vital to our physical and mental well-being.

Our Public Health and Wellness Fund Act was created to improve Cherokee lives, and supporting our elders sits at the very heart of that mission. Good health isn’t just medical care — it’s having enough to eat, a safe home, and knowing your tribal government is there to assist you.

PHWFA also reflects something powerful for all of us: sovereignty, self-governance and tribal self sufficiency. As with all of the more than $50 million invested annually in PHWFA programs, grants, projects and services, our $4.5 million investment in elders uses zero federal dollars.

While the country waits on states and the federal government to address the affordability crisis for elders, Cherokee Nation is making a bold move using the tribally funded PHWFA. As our resources grow under PHWFA, we can expand investments under that law and help more elders — and all citizens — in the future without waiting on a federal grant.

Deputy Chief Warner and I, along with the Council of the Cherokee Nation, will continue to ensure Cherokee elders are a primary consideration in every community effort. We know that each elder is the living embodiment of who we are as a people, and when we take care of our elders, we honor our past as we build a brighter future. Cherokee elders spent their lives caring for families, building up communities and carrying forward our culture and values. We owe them that same care in return.

Chuck Hoskin, Jr. is the principal chief of the Cherokee Nation
