scraped.title: Tribal Leaders Oppose Senate Permitting Bill Despite Changes in Substitute Amendment
scraped.description: Overview: National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro says revisions to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 fail to address fundamental concerns about tribal sovereignty and consultation. A bipartisan group of U.S. senators has released a substitute amendment to legislation intended to streamline federal permitting, lower energy costs and create jobs. […]
scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Tribal Leaders Oppose Senate Permitting Bill Despite Changes in Substitute Amendment
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro says revisions to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 fail to address fundamental concerns about tribal sovereignty and consultation.

A bipartisan group of U.S. senators has released a substitute amendment to legislation intended to streamline federal permitting, lower energy costs and create jobs.

However, the proposed changes have done little to ease concerns among tribal leaders who say the legislation threatens tribal sovereignty and diminishes the role of Tribal Nations in federal decision-making.

U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee; Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), chairwoman of the EPW Committee; and Mike Lee (R-Utah), chairman of the ENR Committee, released the substitute amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on Saturday.

The amendment includes clarifying, conforming and technical changes intended to reflect feedback received since the legislation’s introduction in September. The legislation is designated S. 5653.

The bill’s amendment comes on the heels of a virtual press conference Friday, during which tribal leaders voiced their opposition to the passage of BAAJA.

Despite the revisions, National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) President Mark Macarro told Native News Online that the changes do not adequately address Tribal Nations’ concerns.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Macarro strongly criticized both the substance of the legislation and the process being used to advance it during the lame-duck session of Congress.

“First, the premise that Tribes, Tribal sovereignty, and Tribal decision-making are impediments to federal permitting is a fallacy. Tribal Nations, when at the table early in the planning and design process, are key to successful project outcomes.

“Any amendments to S. 5653 merely puts lipstick on a pig. This bill is rotten from the inside and there is no fixing the rot. Tribal sovereignty continues to be diminished in this bill.

“An amendment of this magnitude demands regular order, which would allow deliberation and meaningful consultation with Tribes. But the process of 5653 in this lame duck session is a rush job and insulting to sovereign Tribal Nations. They are selling out the Tribal Nations for green energy,” Macarro said in an email to Native News Online on Saturday.

Heinrich defended the revised legislation, saying the substitute amendment incorporates feedback from Tribal Nations and New Mexicans while addressing energy affordability.

“I’ve worked hard to incorporate the feedback we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into this Substitute Amendment, and I’m proud to join my colleagues in releasing it today. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help lower energy costs, strengthen Tribal consultation, and create more good-paying jobs,” Heinrich said.

He added that the legislation would require data centers to pay for the electricity they consume and the grid upgrades needed to support their operations, rather than shifting those expenses to households.

“It also makes sure data centers pay for the energy they use and the grid upgrades they cause, instead of passing those costs on to New Mexico families. Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” Heinrich said.

Whitehouse also emphasized the bipartisan effort behind the legislation and the feedback received from lawmakers, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves BAAJA and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Whitehouse said.

“Now’s it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs,” he added.

The disagreement highlights a fundamental divide over federal permitting reform: while the legislation’s supporters argue that changes are needed to accelerate energy development, lower costs and expand infrastructure, tribal leaders continue to question whether the proposed approach adequately protects Tribal Nations’ sovereign authority.

For Macarro and NCAI, the issue extends beyond technical changes to permitting requirements. It is about whether Tribal Nations will have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their lands, resources and communities.

NCAI maintains that Tribal Nations must be engaged early in the planning and development of projects, with their sovereignty and decision-making authority respected throughout the federal permitting process.

Levi “Calm Before the Storm” Rickert (Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation) is the founder, publisher, and editor of Native News Online. Rickert was awarded the Best Column Award in the print/online category... More by Levi Rickert

scraped.title: Distant polls, spotty mail obstruct Native American voting 6 years after law meant to help them - ICT
scraped.description: California never formed a committee to improve Native American voting, leaving barriers like distant polls unaddressed.
scraped.author: Melanie Henshaw
scraped.h1: Distant polls, spotty mail obstruct Native American voting 6 years after law meant to help them
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Melanie Henshaw ICT + CalMatters

Six years after California passed a law requiring the secretary of state to form an advisory committee to help improve voting access for Native Americans, the committee still has not been formed, the secretary of state’s office confirmed to CalMatters/ICT.

Advocates from the California Native Vote Project said they received some reports of problems at polling sites on Election Day, and say the underlying barriers the committee was meant to address, including distant polling places and unreliable mail service, remain.

A spokesperson for Secretary of State Shirley Weber who declined to provide their name said in an email that the office plans to begin recruiting members “after the November election.”

“It’s really frustrating,” said Calvin Hedrick, director of policy for the project, an advocacy group promoting voting rights for Native American peoples in California. “It’s a bummer to have to fight for something again after it was already promised by statute.”

The law, Assembly Bill 2314 , which called for a Native American Voting Accessibility Advisory Committee, was authored by Assemblymember James Ramos and sponsored by then-Secretary of State Alex Padilla .

“California’s nearly three-quarters of a million Native Americans deserve to have their voices heard in our democracy,” Padilla said in an August 2020 statement released by Ramos’ office.

Anthony Roberts, Chairman of the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation, which supports the law, said in 2020 that a lack of polling places and the rejection of certain types of identification remained obstacles. “Until those obstacles are addressed, California’s Native Americans remain at risk of being excluded, with no voice in government, the education of their children and other vital services.”

The law required the committee to set guidelines for reaching Native American voters, recommend public service announcements at least 45 days before elections, suggest ways to improve Native American poll worker recruitment, and advise on language assistance and plain-language materials. But the committee’s recommendations would be nonbinding. The secretary of state was required only to consider them.

The law set no deadline for forming the committee, provided no funding and did not require input from tribal governments or groups.

Members, who are to be chosen by the secretary of state, would have to have experience with voting rights or be county elections officials. The law also set no meeting schedule. By contrast, the state’s separate Language Accessibility Advisory Committee , which is supposed to ensure voters can understand the voting process, must meet at least four times a year.

“Lacking those things, it’s pretty clear it’s just going to end up in the dustbin,” said Allison Neswood, senior staff attorney for the Native American Rights Fund, an advocacy group promoting the interests of Indigenous communities. Neswood is Diné.

Ramos, who is Serrano/Cahuilla and a lifelong resident of the San Manuel Indian Reservation, was not available after multiple requests from CalMatters/ICT. “It’s been difficult finding a time, but still working on it,” wrote a spokeswoman in his office, in October. A Democrat from San Bernardino, he is the first and only Native American from a California tribe elected to the Legislature.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

A spokesperson for Weber acknowledged the committee does not exist, in response to questions from CalMatters/ICT in October. The office said it has been “working closely with Native American advocates to review our committee-related documents” and is planning to recruit members.

The secretary of state’s office did not respond to additional questions about why it had not done anything for six years, who it had contacted for recruitment, whether it had requested any funding and whether it had any documents available for review.

Hedrick said his organization, which promotes voter registration and provides nonpartisan voting information in California Native communities across the state, has been doing its own voter outreach without support from the secretary of state’s office. With only two employees to cover all of Northern California, he said, his team is “stretched really thin.”

Resources from a committee would be an important boost to his group’s efforts, Hedrick said.

“It’s something we need to really be pushing for over the next few years — and we can’t allow them to rest and forget about it,” said Hedrick. “We can’t allow them to promise us it’s something they’re going to do next year, we need to hold their feet to the fire and make sure it gets done.”

In California, the state’s broader responsibilities for ensuring voter access sit mostly with the secretary of state, who is the chief elections officer and must make reasonable efforts to promote voter registration and encourage eligible voters to cast ballots. But when it comes to where people vote, the state points to the counties.

The state sets guidelines for drop boxes, including the minimum number per county. But county election officials decide where they go, whether to add any beyond the minimum and when they’re open. Unlike some states, California, which shares geography with 109 federally recognized tribal nations, does not mandate that there be polling locations on tribal lands.

In Shasta County, a monitor for the Native Vote Project saw a citizen of the Redding Rancheria turned away from the polls on election day. He later reported he was able to vote.

On the Hoopa Valley Indian Reservation, the largest reservation in the state, advocates coordinated a vehicle caravan to transport elders from rural areas of the tribe’s lands to reach the only polling site on the reservation.

The Native American Rights Fund produced reports in 2020 and 2026 that found significant barriers to political participation for Native Americans and Alaska Natives. The 2020 report drew on testimony at nine hearings, including two in California. The 2026 report analyzed federal election data from 2020 to 2024, but did not study any California counties specifically. Hedrick said that he continues to hear complaints from Native Americans, especially those in rural communities, about the time and resource costs of voting.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“For people who live in a city where their ballot box is often a 10-minute drive or less, it’s unfathomable to think someone would have to drive an hour or more to vote — but that’s the reality in many of our communities,” said Hedrick, who is Mountain Maidu. Since 2021, California has mailed a ballot to every active registered voter. Advocates say that doesn’t fully address the gaps, because tribal communities, particularly in rural areas, often lack reliable, timely mail service. Some reservations lack even a single polling place or ballot box, forcing tribal citizens to take time off work and drive miles out of their way to cast their ballots.

A 2024 article in the Harvard Civil Rights-Civil Liberties Law Review found that voting by mail in Indian Country was “plagued” by overlapping barriers, including a lack of post offices.

“The inadequate postal infrastructure in Indian Country immediately impacts the ability of voters to receive and cast a ballot via mail,” wrote Torey Dolan, a Choctaw citizen and associate law professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

Native Americans were not granted automatic U.S. citizenship until 1924 and were not able to vote in all states until 1962. According to Ramos, they often live long distances from post offices: About 89 percent of current post offices were established before 1920, research has found.

Registering is also difficult. Many Native people who live on tribal lands in California have no permanent address, which makes it hard to place them in a voting precinct. Tribal communities in California have also historically had less access to internet and broadband services.

At least one California tribe successfully brought voter services closer to its citizens in recent years. In September 2023, the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians accepted a designation from the secretary of state making its tribally run health center a voter registration agency under the National Voter Registration Act. Weber said at the time it was the first such designation of a tribal medical facility in the country.

Hedrick and his colleagues at the California Native Vote Project travel to tribal communities across the state, engaging with voters and educating them about the electoral process. He also meets with people who haven’t registered to vote and works to better understand what’s keeping them from doing so.

If the committee were established it could not require counties to open voting sites. But Hedrick said if the committee existed, it could do similar work and could play an important role in building trust between the state and communities that have long felt ignored.

That trust is thin, Neswood said, in part because Native peoples rarely see themselves reflected in government.

“If Native people consistently see that their voices and their priorities and their people aren’t represented in these institutions, it just reinforces the lack of trust,” Neswood said. “We’re fighting an uphill battle.”

Hedrick said rebuilding that trust starts with showing up in tribal communities.

“We need people out in tribal communities listening to voters and talking to people who aren’t registered — I think that’s something this committee could be doing,” Hedrick said. “It became statute in 2020, we’re talking in 2026, and (the committee) still hasn’t happened yet and it’s not happening now.”

scraped.author: Source New Mexico
scraped.h1: New Mexico public schools see decline in Native certified teachers, state education data says
scraped.body_text:
ICT

This story was originally published by Source New Mexico.

Matt Mondschein Source New Mexico

New Mexico’s public education system saw a steep decrease in Native language and culture teachers over the past year, according to data presented to state lawmakers on Friday, Oct. 30.

The state’s certification program for Native American language and culture allows experts in those fields to teach in New Mexico public and charter schools without a college degree and, if full-time, earn the annual salary of a Level 1 teacher at $55,000.

Teachers certified in the 520 Native American Language and Culture Certification program play a role in the New Mexico Public Education Department’s action plan to address the landmark Yazzie/Martinez education equity lawsuit by expanding Native language education and increasing the number of students who graduate with proficiency in English and another language , including Native languages.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

KatieAnn Juanico, assistant secretary for PED’s Indian Education division, highlighted the importance of Native-certified teachers to the interim Indian Affairs Committee, saying: “I was raised on the reservation — without our language, we lose a sense of self, a sense of respect.”

But recent PED data she presented shows a decline in the overall number of 520-certified teachers in public and charter schools statewide. In July 2025, PED reported 234 Native language and culture teachers in public and charter schools, new PED data shows there are now 147— a 37 percent decline in just over a year.

Juanico explained that based on feedback she’s received, many 520-certified teachers struggle with the requirements once they enter a public or charter classroom, particularly with classroom loads and developing lesson plans.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

The 520-certified Native teachers realize, according to Juanico, “‘Whoa, what did I sign up for?’ with all these students that I have to watch, manage and build lesson plans for.” She added that, “Oftentimes, our 520 teachers, our tribal community members, don’t come to the classroom knowing all those things.”

Juanico added that PED only tracks 520-certified teachers in public and charter schools and the decrease may also be due to Native teachers with the 520 certification returning to a tribal school after teaching at a public or charter school. Collecting that data “is an opportunity to understand why those teachers are leaving the district and charter schools,” Juanico said.

To support 520-certified Native teachers, Juanico said the Indian Education Division wants to develop classes for Tribes, Pueblos and Nations to boost Native-teacher success after receiving the 520 certificate, and to work with districts and charter schools to recruit and hire more certificate holders.

State Rep. Patricia Royal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) highlighted the need for the PED Indian Education Division to collect more information on 520-certified teachers and how they’re addressing gaps articulated in the Yazzie/Martinez case.

“It is important to have that information because we should be modeling and showcasing our tribes as leading the charge in this,” Roybal Caballero said.

Democrats successfully flipped control of both the House and Senate following historic wins in the 2026 midterm elections, shifting the ba...

scraped.title: 'We can't let the party off the hook': Black voters demand results after Democrats' midterm wins
scraped.description: After delivering major midterm victories for Democrats, Black voters are demanding affordability, economic opportunity, and voting rights.
scraped.author: Gerren Keith Gaynor
scraped.h1: ‘We can’t let the party off the hook’: Black voters demand results after Democrats’ midterm wins
scraped.body_text:
Political strategists say the Black-lash is shifting from electoral victories to demands for action on affordability, economic opportunity and voting rights.

Black voters are again rightfully getting their flowers for delivering what has been described as a “ Blue Tsunami ” in last week’s midterm election. Exit polls show Black voters, who had near-historically high turnout rates in key states, overwhelmingly backed Democrats over Republicans, 90% to 9%.

But as Democrats celebrate the consequential and historic wins on Nov. 3 that gave them huge majorities in the U.S. Congress and governorships, the “Black-lash” isn’t over simply because Black voters delivered at the ballot box. Now, Democrats must do what Black voters expect of them.

“The Black-lash was never about electing Democrats, and so the Black-lash does not end just because Democrats won,” Terrance Woodbury, a Democratic pollster and founding partner of HIT Strategies who coined the term, told theGrio. “The Black-lash is going to force Democrats to deliver.”

Woodbury’s warning reflects a broader sentiment among Black political strategists and organizers who say the next Congress must turn electoral victories into tangible results for Black communities, particularly in economic opportunity, affordability, and the protection of voting rights.

The pollster told theGrio that while Democrats won 90% of Black votes on election night, less than half said they believe that Democrats will make their lives better. It reflects a reality that the so-called backbone of the Democratic Party isn’t guaranteed to show up at the polls for them in future elections.

Democratic leaders also recognize the marching orders from Black voters.

“This election wasn’t some mandate for Democrats. It was an opportunity,” said Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear , who chairs the Democratic Governors Association and is a potential 2028 presidential candidate. Beshear told theGrio, “Now we’ve got to seize that opportunity and make sure we don’t squander it.”

Melanie Campbell, president and CEO of the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation, said Black voters expect action from the newly elected Congress, even as Democrats face the challenges of governing with President Donald Trump in the White House.

“I’m looking for y’all to get some stuff done, and also make sure that if you can’t get it done, you better be caught trying,” Campbell told theGrio.

Exit poll data from the National Coalition for Black Civic Participation showed that a little more than 71% of Black voters said they backed Democrats who they believed would protect voting rights and combat racism and hate.

Campbell is among several Black-led organizations already developing policy agendas and plans for the first 100 days of the new Congress, focusing on voting rights, economic opportunity, and other priorities affecting Black communities. The State of the People, for example, is releasing a comprehensive policy book called “ The Black Papers .”

Maryland Governor Wes Moore , who was overwhelmingly re-elected on Tuesday for a second term and is also rumored to run for president in 2028, told theGrio that he believes Congress should act even more urgently.

“I think we need to be aggressive and fast. I don’t think we need a 100-day plan. I think we need a 100-hour plan,” said Moore.

The Maryland governor and former Rhodes Scholar called on Congress to take immediate action to end Trump’s war in Iran and reverse his tariffs and federal cuts to health care. However, he also called for more specific policies to boost economic opportunity for Black communities, such as expanding access to government contracts for Black-owned businesses and expanding trade and apprenticeship programs for Black young adults.

Democratic strategist Ashley Etienne, who previously served as communications director for Vice President Kamala Harris , said the midterm elections demonstrated the political leverage Black voters now possess and the importance of using it to demand meaningful policy changes.

“We now are in a power position. We now have leverage,” Etienne told theGrio. “My advice to them would be become very clear-eyed about what the expectation is for those votes, and the expectation is that you legislate, lead in a way that has demonstrable impact on our lives.”

Etienne also challenged the notion that addressing the specific economic challenges facing Black Americans amounts to “identity politics,” arguing that Democrats must develop policies that reflect the needs of the communities that helped elect them.

“If you’ve got an economic agenda, you should have an agenda that is reflective of the unique challenges of all of these communities,” she said.

The political leverage of Black voters in the midterm elections wasn’t built overnight.

Campbell said much of that groundwork was laid long before the midterms, with Black women helping to organize not only themselves but also their families and communities.

The organizing was particularly visible among HBCU students, Black churches, and grassroots organizations that mobilized voters in states like Georgia, Mississippi, and North Carolina.

“That’s our culture,” said Campbell.

Woodbury of HIT Strategies said the midterm results showed renewed support for Democrats among Black men, some of whom shifted toward Trump during the 2024 presidential election. But he cautioned against interpreting that shift as a permanent return to the Democratic Party.

“My warning to Democrats is just to not wave a mission accomplished flag,” Woodbury told theGrio. “They didn’t just come home; they remain swing voters.”

The pollster said Democrats must recognize that Black voters were motivated not simply by party loyalty but by a desire to protect their rights, improve their communities and prevent further harm.

For Etienne, the message is that Black voters must continue organizing around their demands, rather than relying on electoral victories alone to produce change.

“We can’t let the party off the hook,” she said.

scraped.title: Democrats’ midterm victory puts Supreme Court’s conservative majority under new pressure
scraped.description: Democratic midterm victories have renewed questions about Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito retiring and the future of the Supreme Court's
scraped.author: Bolarinwa Oladeji
scraped.h1: Democrats’ midterm victory puts Supreme Court’s conservative majority under new pressure
scraped.body_text:
Democratic midterm victories have renewed questions about Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito retiring and the future of the Supreme Court's conservative majority.

The political consequences of the 2026 midterm elections may reach beyond Congress and into the Supreme Court , where the future of its conservative majority is becoming a renewed concern for Republicans.

Democrats’ victories have changed the calculations surrounding two of the court’s most senior conservative members, Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito.

At 78 and 76 respectively, both are approaching an age at which retirement decisions carry significant political implications, particularly because Supreme Court appointments can influence American law for decades.

The Associated Press has called Democratic control of both the House and Senate , with the new Congress expected to take office in January 2027. That leaves Republicans with a narrow window to confirm another Supreme Court nominee before the Senate changes hands.

The situation has prompted discussion of what some legal commentators describe as a possible “reverse Ginsburg” scenario. The comparison refers to the decision by the late Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg to remain on the bench during Barack Obama’s presidency. After her death in September 2020, President Trump nominated Amy Coney Barrett , whose confirmation strengthened the court’s conservative majority.

An opinion piece published by The Hill on November 7 explores the possibility that Thomas and Alito could face a similar legacy question from the opposite ideological direction. If either justice leaves the court during a future Democratic administration, a Democratic president could have the opportunity to appoint a liberal successor, potentially changing the court’s current 6-3 conservative balance.

The timing is central to the argument. Trump remains president until January 2029, but Democrats will control the Senate from the start of the next Congress. That could make confirmation of conservative nominees considerably more difficult if a vacancy occurs before the next presidential election.

The Washington Post reported November 5 that Alito had said he had no plans to retire during the current lame-duck session. He also indicated that he intended to remain on the court through its current term. Thomas, meanwhile, has previously indicated that he has no plans to step down.

There are competing considerations. Supreme Court justices hold lifetime appointments and are not obligated to retire according to party advantage. Pressuring judges to leave simply to preserve an ideological majority could also deepen concerns about political influence over the judiciary.

The possibility of a shift is therefore not an immediate outcome of the election. It would depend on vacancies arising, the presidency and Senate being controlled by Democrats, and the confirmation of replacement justices.

Still, the midterm results have made succession at the Supreme Court a more urgent political question. The conservative majority built through years of Republican appointments could ultimately depend not only on the justices’ judicial records, but also on when they choose to leave the bench.

scraped.title: Ms. Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean launch Fugees hotline offering fans a first listen to new music
scraped.description: Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean launch Fugees Hopeline, letting fans preview a new medley and share messages of hope ahead of a December release.
scraped.author: Odafe Oghen
scraped.h1: Ms. Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean launch Fugees hotline offering fans a first listen to new music
scraped.body_text:
As they celebrate 30 years of “The Score,” the musicians are inviting fans around the world to share their stories and messages of hope.

Ms. Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean are giving Fugees fans something they’ve been waiting more than two decades to hear: new music.

The musicians have teamed up with international public art platform CIRCA to launch Fugees Hopeline, an interactive phone experience that offers a preview of a forthcoming Fugees medley while inviting fans around the world to share their own messages of hope.

Launched Nov. 5 as part of the 30th-anniversary celebration of the group’s landmark album, “The Score,” the hotline features personal messages from Hill and Jean. Hill’s daughter, Selah Marley, narrates the experience, guiding callers through the options, including listening to the new music and recording their own reflections.

Fans in the United States can participate by calling +1 (424) 7-FUGEES (738-4337), while international listeners can access the hotline through WhatsApp. Voice submissions will be accepted through Dec. 31, after which the line will remain available for listening.

The recordings will become part of a growing international audio archive, with selected contributions featured at Miami Beach’s Faena Forum on Dec. 4 and 5 during Art Basel Miami Beach. Hill is curating the exhibition alongside Saint & Citizen.

Inspired by artist John Giorno’s 1968 “Dial-A-Poem” project, Fugees Hopeline also includes three original collages created by Hill using photography, typography and archival images from the group’s history. Limited-edition prints are available through CIRCA, with larger versions signed by both Hill and Jean.

The collaboration follows the musicians’ surprise reunion performance in the Hamptons in July and an appearance at Hill’s Diaspora Calling Festival in the United Kingdom in August.

Hill and Jean kicked off their U.S. anniversary performances Nov. 4 at Berkeley’s Greek Theatre, with upcoming stops at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles on Nov. 8 and Seattle’s Climate Pledge Arena on Nov. 10.

Three decades after “The Score” helped cement the Fugees’ place in hip-hop history, Hill and Jean are celebrating their legacy by inviting fans to become part of the story.

items.title: The NBA’s Greatest Villains of All Time
items.summary: We're looking at the enforcers, instigators, and heartbreakers who mastered the art of basketball villainy.Read more...

scraped.title: The NBA’s Greatest Villains of All Time – The Root
scraped.h1: The NBA’s Greatest Villains of All Time
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

We’re looking at the enforcers, instigators, and heartbreakers who mastered the art of basketball villainy.

By

Rashad Grove

Published

SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 23: Draymond Green #23 of the Golden State Warriors complains about a call during the first half of their game against the Memphis Grizzlies at Chase Center on October 23, 2026 in San Francisco, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images)

While the NBA is full of crowd favorites, there’s nothing quite like rooting for a villain. From cold-blooded players who loved nothing more than silencing 20,000 screaming fans to ruthless enforcers who treated the hardwood like a battleground, the league has a long history of players who thrived on boos. Here is a look back at the 20 biggest villains in NBA history—the instigators and enforcers who made playing the bad guy an absolute art form.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

The epitome of the 1970s enforcer, Maurice Lucas was a legit tough guy who would not hesitate to put his hands on you. Standing 6’9 with all muscle, Lucas put up major numbers and made his presence felt with his intense physicality. His legendary toughness was cemented in Game 2 of the 1977 NBA Finals when he fearlessly confronted Darryl Dawkins after the 300-pound center punched a teammate, slapping Dawkins and squaring up with fists raised to alter the physical tone of the series.

Rick Mahorn’s role on the “Bad Boy” Detroit Pistons was to inflict physical pain on opponents, and he did so with pleasure. Dubbed the “Chairman of the Board” by teammate John Salley, Mahorn anchored the Pistons’ frontcourt with pure physicality. What made Mahorn such a great villain was that he never apologized for his brutal style. While his opponents complained, Mahorn went about his business of protecting the lane by any means necessary.

Standing 6’4’ and weighing over 250 pounds, Charles Barkley was a “one of one” and as tough as they come. Along with his Hall of Fame resume, Barkley was never one to shy away from a confrontation. Over the years, Barkley went head-to-head with Charles Oakley, Bill Laimbeer, Patrick Ewing, and, in his classic duel, Shaquille O’Neal, his current co-host of ESPN’s Inside the NBA.

Over his 19-year NBA career, Charles Oakley gained a well-earned reputation as a brother you don’t want to mess with. Standing 6’8″ and built out of solid muscle, Oakley was the gold standard of NBA enforcers—a throwback power forward whose physical presence was felt in every game. Whether insulating Michael Jordan during his early years in Chicago, defining the brutal defense of the 1990s New York Knicks, or taking on security guards at Madison Square Garden, Oakley was not to be messed with.

RELATED: Can’t-Miss NBA Drama: Top 5 Storylines to Watch This Season

No team has embodied the villain character like the Bad Boy Pistons. Led by Isaiah Thomas, the squad featured some of the most physical and dirty players of all time, such as Bill Laimbeer, Joe Dumars, Rick Mahorn, Dennis Rodman, and John Salley. Winning back-to-back championships in 1989 and 1990, the Pistons did it with brutal physicality that hasn’t been seen since in the league.

The 1990s New York Knicks ruled Madison Square Garden with physical intimidation and hard-hitting defense. Led by Patrick Ewing, Charles Oakley, Anthony Mason, and Xavier McDaniel, and coached first by Pat Riley and later by Jeff Van Gundy, the Knicks played bully ball instead of being a finesse squad. When you entered MSG during this era, you had to be ready for some real physical punishment.

Embracing his villainy, Reggie Miller’s sharpshooting and trash-talking more than fit the bill. Miller didn’t just accept road hostility; he courted it. His status as basketball’s ultimate villain was forever forged at MSG when he took on the New York Knicks. Scoring 8 points in 9 seconds during Game 1 of the 1995 Eastern Conference Semifinals, Miller flashed his iconic “choke” gesture at celebrity fan Spike Lee. What an epic villain moment by Miller.

Learning the tricks of the trade from the “Bad Boy” Pistons, Dennis Rodman took villainy to another level. A master of psychological warfare, Rodman was a floor-crashing, instigating force who turned relentless hustle and boundary-pushing mind games into an elite basketball weapon. Known as “The Worm, ” he specialized in baiting opponents into technicals and ejections while maintaining total composure himself.

Rasheed Wallace accumulated an incredible 317 regular-season technical fouls and was ejected 29 times—both all-time NBA records. Wallace was an undeniable talent, but his legacy as an antagonist was defined by his running war with NBA officials. He was the face of Portland’s volatile “Jail Blazers” squad. Whether barking at referees or talking trash to the opposing team’s fans, Wallace was right at home in hostile environments.

Whether he’s going by Metta Sandiford-Artest, Metta World Peace, or Ron Artest, he was always ready for some action. In his 17-year career, Artest was one of the most unpredictable and physically terrifying perimeter defenders in NBA history. His status as a villain came on November 19, 2004, during the infamous “Malice at the Palace” brawl in Detroit. After charging into the stands to confront a fan who threw a drink at him, Artest sparked the most explosive riot in American sports history, resulting in a landmark 86-game suspension.

A modern-day ticking time bomb, Draymond Green is liable to go off at any minute and has the track record to prove it. No one in the game today has more flagrant fouls, technical fouls, and ejections than Green. As enforcer of the Golden State Warriors dynasty, Green uses psychological warfare to bait opponents into technical fouls and plays with an aggressive edge that constantly toes the line of being dirty. He’s something else!

Trae Young has an “ice-cold” aura with his villain status. His villain origin story began during the 2021 Eastern Conference playoffs, cementing his status as the premier visitor enemy at Madison Square Garden. Facing the energized NYC crowd, Young embraced his role as public enemy number one in MSG. After nailing the game-winner in Game 1, he put his finger to his lips to silence the arena and took a theatrical bow on the Knicks’ home floor. A villain was born.

Dillion Brooks is always looking for a problem. A relentless perimeter defensive specialist, he actively seeks out hostility and feeds off arena boos. As petty as they come, Brooks turns every matchup into psychological warfare, routinely poking the NBA’s biggest superstars, such as LeBron James, with brazen trash talk and physical play. Without question, Brooks enjoys being a villain.

scraped.h1: First Look: Who’s Who in the Upcoming Snoop Dogg Biopic
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

We’re breaking down who’s playing who in the new Snoop Dogg biopic. Trust us, this list will give you plenty to talk about!

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

Snoop Dogg at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Festival held at T-Mobile Arena on September 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Christopher Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)

The forthcoming Snoop Dogg biopic is rounding out its cast. And now, we have a pretty full picture of which stars will help bring the film to life!

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

While the recent news of Cynthia Erivo’s casting may have been met with online disdain this week, some of the other casting choices may inspire a bit more confidence. We’re breaking down who’s playing who so you can get your mind right by the time the film hits screens in August 2027.

Daviss is taking on the lead role of Snoop Dogg in the film. His previous credits include “Outer Banks,” “Do Revenge,” and “Age of Summer.”

Related: Is Snoop Dogg About to Get His Very Own Biopic? For Shizzle, My Nizzle

London will portray Snoop’s mother, Beverly Tate, in the film. Her previous credits include “This Christmas,” “ATL,” and “You People.”

Erivo was cast as Afeni Shakur, mother of the late Tupac Shakur, in the film. Her previous credits include “Wicked,” “Harriet,” and “Widows.”

“Bel-Air” star Sholotan will portray rapper Kurupt in the film, one of Death Row Records’ first signees. His previous credits include “It’s A Sin” and “Run Hide Fight.”

Smith is taking on the role of rapper Warren G in the film. His previous credits include “The Gates,” “The New Edition Story,” and “Young. Wild. Free.”

Bullock will play rapper, producer and entrepreneur Dr. Dre in the film. His previous credits include “BMF,” “White Men Can’t Jump,” and “The Vince Staples Show.”

Booth was cast as rapper The Lady of Rage in the film. Her previous credits include “Rap Sh!t,” “Bad Girls Club: Chicago,” and “Discovering Brooklynn.”

Champagne will portray Snoop’s older cousin, the late Nate Dogg, in the film. His previous credits include “Seven Seconds,” “A Jazzman’s Blues,” and “Brown on Blue.”

Twain, legally Michael Archer Jr. (the son of the late D’Angelo and Angie Stone), is taking on the role of the late rapper The Notorious B.I.G. in the film. Archer, who lost his parents in 2025, will make his acting debut.

Hale plays Suge Knight in the film. His previous credits include “Nemesis,” “Platonic,” and “National Champions.”

Jones was cast as the late Tupac Shakur, one of Death Row Records’ biggest artists, in the film. His previous credits include “Panic,” “The Purge,” and “Shameless.”

Hayes will play Snoop’s wife, Shante Broadus, in the film. Her previous credits include “The Equalizer,” “The Angry Black Girl and Her Monster,” and “Raven’s Home.”

Miller is taking on a massive role – playing his own father, Percy Miller, a.k.a. Master P, in the film. This will mark his acting debut after playing basketball at LSU.

Rogers was cast as Snoop’s mentor, The D.O.C. in the film. His previous credits include “P-Valley,” “My Next Sweet Day,” and “Music and Murder.”

scraped.title: The Most Unforgettable Moments From HBCU Homecoming 2026 – The Root
scraped.h1: The Most Unforgettable Moments From HBCU Homecoming 2026
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

From viral Greek strolls and celebrity appearances to historic milestones and unforgettable victories, HBCU homecoming culture delivered moments worth celebrating.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

JACKSON, MISSISSIPPI – OCTOBER 17: Jackson State Tigers fans cheer during the homecoming game against the Florida A&M Rattlers at Mississippi Veterans Memorial Stadium on October 17, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi. (Photo by Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images)

If 2026 proved anything, it’s that nobody does homecoming quite like an HBCU! From celebrity sightings and showstopping marching bands to Divine Nine pride, campus royalty and edge-of-your-seat football finishes, this season delivered plenty of headline-worthy moments. Many historically Black colleges and universities celebrated major milestones, while students and alumni created new memories across their campuses.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

We’ve rounded up the people, places and moments that made HBCU Homecoming 2026 one for the books. The culture was on full display, and the world was watching!

Love was in the air at NCCU! Beloved eagle mascots Eddie and Annie made it official, exchanging vows during the university’s iconic 10:40 Break on Oct. 6, according to HBCU Gameday. Complete with a wedding dress, a tuxedo, and a cheering eagle family, this was one unforgettable homecoming union!

The yard is always serving looks, but Homecoming certainly turned up the heat. From head-turning ensembles to effortlessly fly street style, Howard students and alumni transformed homecoming into a showcase of Black fashion, creativity and individuality. At Howard, the fashion is always the main event.

RELATED : We Found the Freshest Street Style From HBCU Homecoming 2026

Never count the Bulldogs out! Alabama A&M erased an early 14-point deficit against Grambling State before unleashing 44 unanswered points across the second and third quarters. The final score? A commanding 61-31 victory and a homecoming crowd that had plenty to celebrate!

Hampton University’s own Ebony Fire alumni brought the energy, elegance and unmistakable school pride, reminding everyone that the bonds built on campus don’t end at graduation. The years may pass, but the fire of HBCU sisterhood never fades.

One year away from a century of Tiger pride! Texas Southern marked its final homecoming before its centennial with “Mission 99,” celebrating 99 years of legacy, Greek life, royal court traditions and Maroon-and-Gray spirit. The countdown to 100 is officially on!

Grambling State’s World-Famed Tiger Marching Band celebrated 100 years of musical excellence, honoring generations of musicians who helped make its signature performances a cornerstone of HBCU culture.

Gospel icon Kirk Franklin joined North Carolina A&T’s 100th Greatest Homecoming on Earth (GHOE) celebration, bringing generations together through music, faith and the unmistakable spirit of Aggie pride.

We previously told you about Aleem “The Dream,” who is proving that he has talent, discipline and showmanship beyond his years. The 10-year-old drum major captured hearts at Virginia State University’s homecoming football game. He’s reminding HBCU band culture that the next generation is already leading the way!

Purple and gold energy filled the yard! Brothers of Omega Psi Phi Fraternity, Inc. showed up and showed out at North Carolina A&T’s 100th GHOE, turning Greek unity, signature stepping and fraternity pride into a homecoming moment to remember!

Brandy and Kirk Franklin received a special musical welcome from Alabama A&M’s Marching Maroon and White, proving that nothing says homecoming quite like a marching band salute!

HISTORY MADE ✨ Five generations of former Johnson C. Smith University queens came together for homecoming to celebrate the crowning of its 100th Miss Johnson C. Smith University! 🎥: @jcsustudentlife1867/IG pic.twitter.com/IdUr3WV7gt

Johnson C. Smith University celebrated its 100th Miss JCSU, honoring a milestone in campus history and the legacy of queens who have represented the university with grace, leadership and Golden Bull pride.

100 years of Aggie excellence, and the celebration was everything! North Carolina A&T marked the centennial of its legendary Greatest Homecoming on Earth with a milestone weekend honoring a century of tradition, culture, music and unforgettable Aggie pride.

The Morgan State Bears battled back from a 14-point deficit against Robert Morris, securing a dramatic 28–27 victory with a touchdown in the closing seconds. Baltimore had every reason to celebrate!

Members of Alpha Phi Alpha Fraternity, Inc. have been going viral this season while strolling to their take on “Wipe Me Down.” If you haven’t seen it, these men are bringing signature moves, infectious energy and Greek pride to SpelHouse. The moment was a reminder that HBCU culture always sets the tempo!

scraped.title: Stephen Miller’s Unsettling Video About Cutting Off Fingers Resurfaces as Trump Names Him Chief of Staff, and Insiders Say He’s Done Playing Nice
scraped.description: A resurfaced video of Stephen Miller calling torture “a celebration of life and human dignity” is casting a disturbing shadow over President Donald
scraped.author: Nyamekye Daniel
scraped.h1: Stephen Miller’s Unsettling Video About Cutting Off Fingers Resurfaces as Trump Names Him Chief of Staff, and Insiders Say He’s Done Playing Nice
scraped.body_text:
A resurfaced video of Stephen Miller calling torture “a celebration of life and human dignity” is casting a disturbing shadow over President Donald Trump’s decision to hand him one of the most powerful jobs in Washington.

The footage shows a 17-year-old Miller sitting backward on a school bus, discussing cutting off Saddam Hussein’s fingers as other teenagers laugh. More than two decades later, Trump has chosen the architect of his immigration crackdown to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

The appointment has horrified critics and even drawn backlash from Republicans, with one lawmaker calling it a “horrible decision” and another describing Miller as a “megalomaniac.”

Coming just days after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress, the shake-up raises questions about how far Trump intends to push his agenda. Elevating one of his most aggressive advisers suggests the president is preparing to dig in as Democrats gain the power to investigate his administration and block legislation.

‘Go Apologize!’: Man Accused of Throwing Soda at Fast-Food Worker Gets Confronted in Parking Lot, Then Does the Unthinkable to Avoid the Heat

Florida Man’s Gun-Fueled Meltdown Over Kids’ Ding-Dong Ditch Prank Leaves Boy Needing Stitches

The old video offers an unsettling backdrop to that promotion.

Recorded around the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the footage has resurfaced publicly before, including in July 2025 . In the video, Miller initially says Iraqi civilians should be spared before turning his attention to Hussein and his associates.

“But as for Saddam Hussein and his henchmen, I think the ideal solution would be to cut off their fingers,” he says.

He then argues that keeping people alive while torturing them demonstrates respect for life.

“I don’t think it’s necessary to kill them entirely; we’re not a barbaric people, we respect life. Therefore, torture is the way to go. Because tortured people can live. Torture is a celebration of life and human dignity,” Miller says, as laughter erupts off camera.

He closes by expressing hope that his peers and future leaders will appreciate the supposed respect torture shows other cultures.

The White House previously defended the recording as teenage comedy.

Responding to Vice in 2017, then-White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders dismissed the footage as a video-yearbook sketch. She said the performance did not reflect any past or present policy positions held by Miller. Her defense centered on the context of the remarks, not on disputing the video’s authenticity.

But criticism of Miller’s promotion extends well beyond comments he made as a teenager.

Several Republican lawmakers questioned Trump’s judgment in a Saturday report by Fox News Digital’s Elizabeth Elkind. One unnamed congressman expressed “utter disbelief,” while Rep. Marlin Stutzman, a Republican from Indiana, called the appointment a “horrible decision.”

“Stephen is a megalomaniac who should have never been given the keys to the Ferrari,” another unnamed Republican told the outlet.

That lawmaker nevertheless disputed blaming Miller for the party’s election losses, arguing that voters in their districts did not know him.

Outgoing Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon offered a different assessment. Before Trump announced the promotion, Bacon told Elkind that Miller had “greatly hurt the administration” and “cost us many seats on Tuesday.”

“He took an immigration policy that favored the president 2:1 in the public, overreached and made it 2:1 unfavorable,” Bacon said. “Many Republicans don’t like him.”

The White House defended Miller, telling Fox News Digital that he had been a key figure in carrying out Trump’s agenda.

Trump announced Friday that Miller would take over Monday, and Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, would move to the president’s political operation, according to Trump’s announcement.

The change gives Miller broader authority over the White House staff and the machinery used to carry out the president’s priorities. For an adviser already closely associated with Trump’s immigration agenda, the promotion expands his reach at a moment when passing legislation is about to become more difficult.

Reuters reported that administration officials viewed the appointment as a signal that Trump intends to pursue confrontation and rely more heavily on executive power.

Miller’s influence over the president’s message was already a concern before he landed the top staff job.

Critics have viewed him as a mouthpiece for Trump’s harshest positions, with some suspecting his fingerprints were on the president’s Truth Social posts. Authorship of those posts has not been established, but reporting has documented how Miller feeds material directly to Trump.

The Independent, citing The Wall Street Journal, reported that Miller used dramatic imagery and direct communications to push his priorities. In one instance, he showed Trump a photograph of an injured administration staffer while arguing that Washington’s crime problem was worsening. Trump subsequently posted the image and announced a National Guard deployment.

The reporting illustrates Miller’s influence over the information and imagery reaching the president. However, it does not establish that Miller personally wrote any particular social media posts.

Miller, meanwhile, greeted his promotion with praise for Trump and a promise to fight.

He called the president “the most transformative political leader in American History” and said he was “honored beyond words” to become chief of staff. He also thanked Wiles for her service and friendship.

“The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic,” Miller wrote.

scraped.title: 'No Way': Countess Vaughn Adds a Plot Twist No One Saw Coming After Gabourey Sidibe and Raven-Symoné’s Awkward Interview
scraped.description: Gabourey Sidibe may have uncovered deeper, unspoken consequences of body-shaming in the entertainment industry. While celebrities face constant scrutiny
scraped.author: Sharmaine Johnson
scraped.h1: ‘No Way’: Countess Vaughn Adds a Plot Twist No One Saw Coming After Gabourey Sidibe and Raven-Symoné’s Awkward Interview
scraped.body_text:
Gabourey Sidibe may have uncovered deeper, unspoken consequences of body-shaming in the entertainment industry.

While celebrities face constant scrutiny over their appearances, the criticism can leave lasting emotional scars that extend far beyond the headlines.

Sidibe’s experience highlights how years of judgment, unsolicited comments and public ridicule can shape the way someone views themselves.

During the Nov. 5 appearance on “ Tea Time with Raven & Miranda ,” Sidibe acknowledged that she had never felt particularly liked by Raven-Symoné.

Sidibe did not hold her tongue during a discussion in which Raven-Symoné candidly admitted that Sidibe’s acceptance as a plus-sized woman frustrated her.

‘I Didn’t Even Recognize Her’: Raven Symoné Loses More Weight and Fans Say She Looks Like ‘Her Old Self’

‘I Fired Everybody’: Lee Daniels and Gabourey Sidibe Emotionally Recall His Firing of ‘Disrespectful’ White Crew Members on the Set of ‘Precious’

“I’m jealous. When I was growing up in the industry, no one dressed me. I wasn’t able to really do fashion icons like you,” she explained. “I remember when you came on the scene, and you were embraced, and I was like, wow, I’m not; she is .”

Raven-Symoné admitted she had mixed feelings about it saying, “[I thought], Congratulations, thank you for knocking down doors, and I’m also, like, angry.”

Sidibe then replied, saying repeated experiences led her to believe Symoné didn’t like her. “Girl, I didn’t think you liked me,” she said. “I was here like, what’s up.”

When Symoné asked why, Sidibe explained, “You treated me like you didn’t like me!”

“My bad,” Symoné apologized. She then speculated that Sidibe was referring to an interaction while working “at Empire,” the Fox drama series where Symoné guest-starred in 2015.

Sidibe portrayed Becky Williams, a personal assistant who later became an A&R executive at Empire Records, working under Lucious Lyon (Terrence Howard).

She then dropped a bombshell about something she was told on set.

“I was told that you made some people promise to not be friends with me,” Sidibe said to the “Cosby Show” star. The podcast censored the names she mentioned.

Sidibe then recalled an encounter at a Chicago restaurant, where she “felt like [Raven was] put off by me.”

Raven said she did not know the “Precious” star Sidibe at the time. The three agreed to discuss the behind-the-scenes details further, but privately and off camera.

But she wasn’t the only one with a story about Raven-Symoné’s chilly treatment. Miranda described her as someone “shady” and “cold” to people she doesn’t know.

“The Parkers” star Countess Vaughn seemed to recognize that behavior, claiming, “Raven did me the same way” under a TikTok video. Vaughn never gave more details about what took place.

“Omg no way,” replied one person in the comments. Another said, “Countess’ comment just proves my point raven is like that because she resented the other ‘plus size’ girls because she felt competition.”

Also, during the interview, Symoné admitted that she felt frustrated by the lack of opportunities and acceptance she received throughout her acting career.

Despite understanding the emotions behind the Disney child star’s explanation, Sidibe challenged her perspective, arguing that their body-image experiences were not necessarily comparable.

“You’ve never been fat, and that is what bugs me. Because you had big boobs, that’s different than being plus [size],” Sidibe exclaimed.

Symoné rebutted that her weight changed during her teen years, and the industry pressured her to get a breast reduction to land a television role.

“Gabby didn’t come to play But i still find it interesting that Raven released that interview for everyone to watch. Knowing, that she’s gonna look bad. But whatever. Make that money lmao,” said one viewer.

Another noted, “Had them stuttering lmaooo like, let’s get it out the way, why were you telling people not to be cook with me?”

Their exchange explains why Sidibe and Raven rarely filmed together on “Empire.” It also shows how deeply beauty standards can affect women, especially in an industry where appearance often influences professional opportunities.

The distinction also highlights how Hollywood treats curvy women, women with larger chests, and plus-sized women differently. Although both groups of women experienced insecurities and pressures surrounding their bodies, those experiences don’t carry the same social or professional consequences.

Ultimately, unrealistic beauty standards create competition and resentment among women seeking acceptance.

Hollywood’s ongoing conversations about body image have brought renewed attention to how women experience appearance-based criticism and the importance of representation across different body types. The issue also raises questions about how beauty standards influence opportunities and visibility in the entertainment industry.

The discussion extends beyond Hollywood, reflecting broader conversations about beauty standards, body diversity and the pressure women face to meet expectations about their appearance.

scraped.author: Grace Jidoun
scraped.h1: ‘Go Apologize!’: Man Accused of Throwing Soda at Fast-Food Worker Gets Confronted in Parking Lot, Then Does the Unthinkable to Avoid the Heat
scraped.body_text:
A fired-up fast food customer has gone viral for calling out a white man’s alleged treatment of an employee.

TikToker @vaultedthoughts shared the drama in a video that’s racked up nearly 700,000 views.

He accused an unidentified man of throwing a tantrum — and a soda — at a woman cashier over an issue with his Big Buford burger at Checkers & Rally’s in Toledo, Ohio.

As @vaultedthoughts put it in a caption, a dispute over an order is “never that deep.”

In the clip, the TikToker follows the man to his vehicle in the parking lot, then takes him to task, demanding he march back into the restaurant and apologize to the worker he allegedly doused with soda.

Viewers cheered him on, calling him “goated” and a “stand-up man” in the comments for his no-holds-barred approach.

Family Tried Everything to Get 10-Year-Old Out of Foster Care, Now Foster Mom Faces Murder Charges for Her Death

Boost Mobile Employee Screams ‘Rape’ at Black Customer Who Keeps Telling Her Not to Touch Him

“Say your name, say it. If you wanna throw it at a woman, throw it at a man,” he shouted, referring to the customer’s refilled drink. “Toss it at me. Toss it at me.”

The man initially denied the incident, responding with “Excuse me?” and “Pardon me?” Then he claimed he had already apologized to the worker, which @vaultedthoughts didn’t buy.

“Go apologize to her,” he persisted. “You’re a grown-ass man; go apologize.”

What happened next had viewers “cracking up,” as one put it.

The man seemed to be ready to leave in his Subaru SUV, but then he suddenly opened the hatchback, crawled in, and hid.

From the safety of the vehicle’s cargo area, he said, “F–k you, man,” and slammed the hatch.

“The fear in his eyes while literally climbing into his trunk had me cracking up,” exclaimed one person in the comments on TikTok.

Echoing several others, another person said, “You know how scared you gotta be to crawl through the trunk?”

One commenter joked that the man climbed through his trunk to avoid apologizing.

Another had a different theory: “No, he did it to avoid an a– whooping.”

scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

A Brazilian biologist and a team of volunteer divers are killing coral to save a marine protected area just off the famous Ipanema beach.

They’re manually removing sun coral, an invasive species first seen in Brazil more than 40 years ago, from an offshore oil platform.

The coral has no natural predators in the region and it has spread along the coast, where it could suffocate Brazil’s marine wildlife.

So Adriana Gomes and her team are using a simple but effective technique to solve this problem: Their own hands. Watch the full video to see if they succeed.

items.summary: The new award comes after the administration cut human rights funding to nations in crisis. scraped.title: Trump Admin Giving $1M to Group Studying Crime Against White South Africans
scraped.description: The new award comes after the administration cut human rights funding to nations in crisis.
scraped.author: Sharon Lerner
scraped.h1: Trump Admin Giving $1M to Group Studying Crime Against White South Africans
scraped.body_text:
The new award comes after the administration cut human rights funding to nations in crisis.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

After slashing funding for programs that documented atrocities and protected human rights abroad, President Donald Trump’s State Department is now granting one of its first new human rights awards to a controversial South African organization that promotes the disputed notion that white farmers are a violently targeted, persecuted group, according to multiple sources knowledgeable about the funding.

The group expected to receive the nearly $1 million award, AfriForum, is a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners, a subset of South Africa’s white population. The organization says its members, who have a “ God-given calling ,” fight for Afrikaner interests and self-governance. The money will be used to “ document hateful rhetoric and violent acts ” against Afrikaners and other minority populations in the country.

The new award comes from a State Department bureau tasked with promoting democracy and human rights internationally. Until last year, those funds were mainly spent in poor and authoritarian nations — to fight corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, or combat child exploitation and sexual abuse in Afghanistan. Since Trump returned to office, his appointees have transformed the bureau, gutting its staff, canceling programs and reorienting some of its funding toward conservative causes in Europe.

Samuel Samson, who was appointed as a deputy assistant secretary to the State Department bureau by Trump, has claimed the U.S. has a “civilizational” connection to Afrikaners, who descend primarily from Dutch migrants and predominantly speak Afrikaans. Samson, who has met with far-right leaders in Europe since joining the administration last year, has framed the U.S. government’s financial support for Afrikaners as grounded in “a common heritage, a common culture, a common way of life, shared history and ultimately a common anthropology.”

There’s a long shared political history between Afrikaner groups and white nationalists in the U.S., said Audie Klotz, a political science professor at Syracuse University who has studied those connections. But, she said, “There’s no heritage connection here. It’s pure scientific racism. In the history of U.S. immigration, there’s no direct connection between South Africa and the United States.”

AfriForum met with the Trump administration in February 2025 to plead for help. The group told officials that Afrikaners are subject to racial discrimination and murders that are more frequent and asked the administration to “act strongly against hate speech that incites violence” against them, according to a statement .

South Africa is plagued by high rates of violence, and some Afrikaners have been tortured and murdered. But independent researchers have found those killings represent a tiny fraction of murders across the country, whose victims are disproportionately people living in poor urban areas, where residents are predominantly Black. Official government statistics , and two formal inquiries into the matter, do not reveal a pattern of targeted violence against Afrikaners.

But Trump subscribes to the idea that white farmers face a “genocide” and has cited disproportionate violence against them as a reason for punishing Africa’s wealthiest nation. In February 2025, he issued an executive order that cut off hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to South Africa and welcomed Afrikaners to the U.S. as refugees. Since then, the administration has opened the doors to more than 16,000 white South Africans while halting virtually all other immigration. Officials recently told Congress they plan to invite as many as 17,500 Afrikaner refugees to the U.S. in 2027.

AfriForum did not respond to specific questions for this story but said that “our understanding is that the allocation has not yet been finalised. Should the allocation indeed be awarded to AfriForum, we will make a public announcement in this regard.”

The new award is the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause. The white South African group governed the nation for decades under a brutal system of segregation known as apartheid, which kept the Black majority an impoverished underclass until the system was dismantled in 1994. Now, with Black South Africans governing the country, white people — of which Afrikaners are the majority — remain one of the wealthiest segments of the population.

The support has caused dismay among several former high-level diplomats, who spoke to ProPublica anonymously because they fear retribution from the administration.

Two former senior U.S. officials responsible for Africa policy said that they would never have met with AfriForum, let alone funded the group, because it was considered to be politically extreme and not credible. They described the organization as cherry-picking crime statistics to create a misleading narrative. “We would certainly not have funded what we would see as a racially incendiary initiative,” said one of the officials.

The decision to direct money toward the group comes after the Trump administration halted programs that advocated for the end of violence in African countries such as Sudan, where the Biden administration determined in 2025 that there was a genocide , calling it “the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe.”

“It’s offensive to provide funding solely to this one group after we’ve cut off funding in countries undergoing real documented crises,” said David Jandura, who managed the Africa portfolio for the State Department’s human rights bureau for several years and lost his job during the mass layoffs in 2025.

Congress has also raised questions about how the award was made. A Senate aide to Democrats told ProPublica that despite repeated requests to State Department officials, they had not received a briefing outlining the recipients of funds earmarked for democracy and human rights, which they described as “highly unusual.”

“The Trump Administration proceeded with funding fringe right-wing causes internationally despite objections from Congress,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a New Hampshire Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, who described the lack of transparency as “unacceptable.”

In response to a series of questions about the AfriForum funding, a senior State Department official wrote in an email that the department does not comment on funding deliberations and that they routinely keep Congress informed of their actions, consulting extensively on this year’s programming. “The Administration has been clear about its concern about the abhorrent race-based discrimination and violence in South Africa,” the unnamed official wrote. “Human rights protections do not depend on a person’s income or ethnicity.”

In July, ProPublica revealed that the State Department originally intended to give the $1 million research award to Lex Libertas, a small organization founded last year by a former AfriForum executive named Ernst Roets. Trump officials later expanded the potential awardees to a small pool of handpicked organizations. The plan drew outrage from Congress over the content of the award as well as plans to bypass the typical competitive bidding process. After ProPublica ’s reporting, the State Department released an open call for the funding opportunity , offering $986,500 to a nonprofit organization to “create a comprehensive record of violence affecting Afrikaner and other South African minority populations.” It’s this grant that is now being awarded to AfriForum.

Both AfriForum and Lex Libertas advocate for Afrikaner rights and have developed relationships with the Trump administration. Trump’s ambassador to South Africa, L. Brent Bozell III, visited AfriForum’s headquarters in September, praising the organization for its neighborhood watch programs while criticizing the South African government for not enacting policies requested by the Trump administration. AfriForum has also met with Trump officials in Washington, D.C. , drawing public criticism from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. And in September, Roets met with administration officials.

AfriForum was founded 20 years ago and, with some 300,000 members, claims to be the biggest civil rights organization in South Africa. It says it aims to “establish self-dependence and growing self-governance” and provides some local civic services, such as garbage collection and systems for reporting pot holes and broken traffic lights . The group has said it distances itself from “white supremacist and extremist groups” and that it disagrees with Trump’s assertion that white South African farmers are experiencing a “white genocide.” But it has also said the South African government is “ targeting the continued existence of Afrikaners ” through racial legislation and the downplaying of farm murders, among other things. Academics and former U.S. diplomats have repudiated some of the ideas the group promotes as racist.

It unsuccessfully challenged a ban on the “gratuitous display” of the national flag flown during apartheid, which a South African court has found to be a form of hate speech. And while the group’s leader, Kallie Kriel, has said apartheid “ was wrong ,” he has also said it did not constitute “ a crime against humanity ” as the U.N. has determined , on the grounds that not enough people were killed during that time.

AfriForum has been focusing on farm attacks since at least 2009. In 2018, during Trump’s first presidency, Kriel and Roets, who was then his deputy, met with government officials in Washington, D.C., about the issue, and Roets spoke about it with Tucker Carlson on Fox News , as the chyron below him announced in all caps, “White farmers brutally murdered every week in SouthAfrica.”

Additional research on crimes against white South Africans is an unnecessary and confusing use of U.S. taxpayer dollars, said Carolyn Holmes, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who studies democracy in southern Africa. Holmes noted that AfriForum already produces annual reports on crimes against farming communities. “These data already exist,” she said. “You don’t need a new study. You don’t even need a far-right study, we have those.”

The U.S. support offers more than a financial boost to the organization. “For some time, AfriForum has been campaigning for recognition of their claim that white people face discrimination and persecution,” said Alex Dyzenhaus, a lecturer in international relations and African politics at the University of St. Andrews. “Before, they were only getting the Tucker Carlsons and the far right of the news ecosystem. Now they have the U.S. government on their side.”

The Trump administration has made the plight of white, rural South Africans a key foreign policy issue. In addition to the early executive order, Trump held a contentious meeting with Ramaphosa in the White House last year where Trump claimed white farmers were being executed. The administration has also considered an ad campaign focused on encouraging more Afrikaners to come to the U.S.

In September, Roets of Lex Libertas met with the White House to discuss what he sees as the crisis facing the Afrikaner community and, along with the New York Young Republican Club, placed 3,000 white crosses on the National Mall to commemorate South African farm murders.

Roets declined to answer specific questions from ProPublica but, in a text message, described the murders of several Afrikaners that he knew personally. He also wrote, “I see the suffering of black people in South Africa, I am deeply moved by it, and I spend every day of my life campaigning to make things better for us all.”

Appearing at a press conference for the Lex Libertas event, Samson, the State Department official, showcased the sharp shift the administration has made in U.S. relations with South Africa. While apartheid has been understood globally as a symbol of racist oppression, Samson described the current South African government as having discriminatory “race-based” policies and a cautionary tale for the rest of the world.

At the end of apartheid, in 1994, South Africa was a “flourishing, prosperous society,” Samson said. Since then, the country has gone to “ruin.” He blamed the fall on a “radical ideological leftist movement that wears human rights, that wears tolerance and inclusivity, as a skin suit to advance their Marxist communist worldview.”

Part of the Trump administration’s solution to this perceived crisis, he said, was to provide the research funding.
