scraped.title: Mississippi Ballot Monitors Say They’re Being Shut Out of Vote Counting
scraped.description: Volunteers say they are navigating confusion and obstacles while trying to ensure a transparent counting process.
scraped.author: Aallyah Wright
scraped.h1: Mississippi Ballot Monitors Say They’re Being Shut Out of Vote Counting
scraped.body_text:
Volunteers say they are navigating confusion and obstacles while trying to ensure a transparent counting process.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

This story was originally published by Capital B .

It took Natt Offiah an hour to realize he had arrived at the wrong location to monitor the provisional and absentee ballots in the Mississippi U.S. Senate race. He drove to Madison County Circuit Clerk’s Office on Wednesday, but the building was under construction.

After a phone call, Offiah, director of organizing for the People’s Advocacy Institute, and his colleague finally reached the temporary clerk’s office. They were redirected again, shared Offiah, still unable to locate officials.

At the next building, one woman said, “I haven’t seen them in an hour or so,” before directing the organizers down a hallway.

Offiah said he banged on the door, to no avail. The duo sat outside the room for 45 minutes before heading back to the front desk. A receptionist then told Offiah about two dozen staffers had left 15 minutes before his initial arrival.

No one could provide him any information on when they would return to continue counting votes.

“There is no standardized process for counting. Each county can pick and choose when they want to start counting. So, we’re running into this runaround issue,” Offiah said.

His experience mirrors the dozens of other volunteers who say they didn’t sign up for chaos and confusion, but to protect the democratic process. Some — who reported their concerns in group chats shared with Capital B — say they’ve been denied a seat to observe the process, while others struggle to find information.

With the nation’s close eye on Mississippi, advocates say it’s even more critical to ensure election officials “do the right thing.” Voters have been on edge since Election Day, waiting to see who will become the state’s next U.S. senator.

Despite no early voting or online registration, turnout and absentee ballots have surged. As of Nov. 6, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.

Yet, there are still thousands of mail-in and affidavit ballots outstanding .

Issues like voter ID laws and inoperable machines have fueled delays, said Lydia Grizzell, policy and advocacy manager of ACLU of Mississippi.

“It is appalling the number of issues that we’ve seen and we had on Election Day, and now we’re seeing the extension of that post-Election Day in a way that is not great,” she said.

The Mississippi secretary of state’s office did not address the monitors’ allegations of being shut out of the vote counting process, but told Capital B the public is entitled to be present for the counting of ballots, the process where election commissioners announce which affidavit ballots are accepted or rejected, according to state statute. This does not include the preliminary work commissioners do to determine a voter’s eligibility.

There is no uniform process on how officials conduct affidavit ballot counting. In some counties, where ACLU dispatched attorneys, election officials had a closed door process, Grizell added.

“The best thing that we can do is have people watching, witnessing, and doing their best to gather as much information as possible as to what is happening,” she said.

Volunteers across the state are being deployed in a widespread effort prompted by several grassroots organizations. The NAACP has also deployed national legal, policy, and field staff to the state to make sure every vote is counted.

Both candidates sent their own groups to monitor the process and assembled a group of lawyers who are prepared to take legal action if necessary. Lawyers for Hyde-Smith sent a letter to election commissioners requesting “immediate separation, secure custody and preservation of all affidavit ballots.” Following Hyde-Smith’s legal team’s response, Colom’s legal counsel sent a letter to all 82 counties, calling the GOP senator’s demand unlawful.

Ahead of the election, thousands of Mississippians were moved to inactive status because the secretary of state’s office paid $50,000 to use unverified data from credit bureau Experian to clean out voter rolls. Secretary of State Michael Watson told Mississippi Today that the rollout of the commercial data was “wildly successful.”

This unprecedented number of inactive voters led to more affidavit ballots, prolonging the count, Tarekegn said. These ballots must be “cured”, meaning to correct issues with voter identification or mail-in ballots, by Nov. 10.

Organizers also pointed out that Mississippi’s outdated voting system exacerbated the counting issues. With no early voting, most ballots come in on Election Day. This overwhelms the system. Still, Tarekegn praised Mississippians for the high turnout.

“Mississippi is one of the hardest, if not the hardest, state to vote in,” she said. “We’re truly talking about probably more than 90% of the people having to show up on Election Day between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. to cast their vote.”

On Election Day, Rachel Madden was the 20th person in line at her precinct in DeSoto County. After an hour’s wait, she was told she had been made inactive and needed to vote by affidavit.

“She just told me that my name wasn’t in the system, and I was like, ‘Well, that doesn’t make any sense,’” Madden said.

She hadn’t changed her address, so she was confused why she had been flagged as inactive. The poll worker assured her, “It’s not a big deal, you’re like the second person this has happened to,” she said.

She said she was instructed by the poll worker to go to the courthouse to “cure” her ballot after being given a form. She made the 25-minute drive to the courthouse, where the employee informed her she had been inactive since May by District 1 Election Commissioner Laura Edler because of Madden’s supposed move to nearby Memphis, Tennessee.

Madden says she never moved anywhere. Her address was corrected in the system and she received a new voter card.

She recalls she then called to ensure her ballot was accepted. She said that an employee told her they would not be taking any more calls about affidavit ballots for the next 10 days, which would put Madden outside the deadline of ballot curing.

“I was like, in 10 days, it’s not gonna matter,” Madden said. “Even in person that day, they were not helpful. If I had not insisted, I don’t think they would have done it. I just don’t think that’s fair or right.”

Edler did not speak to any individual’s standing, but told Capital B that when the commission receives a change of address from the secretary of state’s office, then the voter will be notified and must rectify the issue or remain inactive.

Ballot monitors say it’s also been difficult to do their jobs.

In DeSoto County, Kelly Jacobs, a local organizer, said District 4 Election Commissioner Sissie Ferguson prevented her from watching as election officials presorted ballots and checked names.

The day after the election, Jacobs said she stopped by the election’s commissioner office, but learned they had changed locations. She then traveled to the police department, which directed her to the new location.

After being barred from entry, Jacobs called an attorney, who affirmed her rights, but officials continued to block her from observing, she said, which she captured on video. Commenters on the video state that they were allowed access to observe vote counting in other counties.

On Nov. 5, around noon, the public was able to monitor the process, but by then, the process had already started, she said. Jacobs is not confident officials will follow the law.

“Why did I have to go and complain? If not for my complaint, they would still be all locked up [in the room],” she said. “There’s five election commissioners. Why would none of them know the open meetings law?”

Ferguson did not respond to Capital B ’s request for comment. However, commissioner Edler said no one has been denied access. As of the afternoon of Nov. 6, she said there’s “a room full of people” who were actively watching the process.

In Lee County, about 100 miles away, a monitor reported that an official told them a count wouldn’t happen until “later this week or early next week,” according to a group chat shared with Capital B . Another volunteer was told it would occur on “Thursday morning” with no additional details.

Offiah, although still battling frustration and confusion, said he is looking forward to continuing the good work with the community.

“As a lifelong Mississippian, I am used to us living in a legacy of constantly fighting back, and this is just in alignment with our legacy,” he said. “And people ask folks from Mississippi, why do we live down here? Why do we stay out here with everything that we’re facing?”

He added: “But we’re fighters, and we won’t ever stop fighting.”

scraped.title: Flooding in Gaza Destroys 70,000 Tents as Israel Continues to Block Aid
scraped.description: The Palestinian Health Minister warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions” in Gaza.
scraped.author: Jon Queally
scraped.h1: Flooding in Gaza Destroys 70,000 Tents as Israel Continues to Block Aid
scraped.body_text:
The Palestinian Health Minister warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions” in Gaza.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

The suffering of the people of Gaza went from horrific and beyond comprehension to something worse on Saturday after storm waters overnight destroyed tens of thousands of tents and flooded tens of thousands of people into further desperation, all while the US and Israeli governments continue to maintain a cruel blockade on life-saving supplies despite a fast-approaching winter and a military occupation with no end in sight.

“At least 70,000 tents have been flooded & blown away by the torrential downpour and tempestuous wind in Gaza since last night,” reported Palestinian journalist Abubaker Abed, citing statements from health and media officials. “Families are shelterless. Food prices are soaring. Children are starving and shivering with cold. Caravans and mobile homes must enter Gaza now to avert this cataclysm.”

Gaza’s Government Media Office on Saturday, holding Israel wholly responsible for the disaster, said initial losses from flooded and destroyed tents were estimated at $3 million and that dozens of walls of homes had collapsed, resulting in injuries, while the threat of broader building collapse remained a serious risk.

In a statement, Palestinian Health Minister Dr. Majed Abu Ramadan said, “What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis. I urgently call on the international community, the United Nations , and health, humanitarian, and relief organizations to intervene immediately to save the lives of hundreds of thousands of displaced people in the Gaza Strip, following the flooding of thousands of tents with rainwater and the absence of basic safe shelter conditions.”

Al Jazeera reports :

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.

About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.

Ramadan further warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions, alongside growing risks of the spread of diseases and epidemics” if an emergency response was not rapidly and comprehensively deployed.

This is the worst morning ever. No one in Gaza City slept last night. The rain completely flooded the tents, soaking mattresses and destroying families' belongings. We are underwater. Thousands of families have been trying for hours to save what little they have left, with…

Video footage and eye witness accounts offered a heartbreaking picture of the suffering by those hit by the floods.

“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water ,” a man named Mansour al-Sakni, 33, told the Middle East Eye . “The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too.”

“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room,” he said. “We are poor people in Gaza. We want to live. We do not want to die from the bombing or the cold. Enough. Have mercy on us.”

According to NBC News :

The territory’s civil defence service said it had received 1,500 distress calls from displaced residents. Three abandoned houses collapsed without causing injuries, it added.

At a tent encampment in Gaza City, some people tried to repair their tents, ⁠while others used sand to reinforce them and prevent water from entering. ⁠Some were busy getting their children out of flooded tents.

Olfat Magdoub, a Gaza resident, tried in vain to sweep water away from her tent.

“This is the first day of rain, and of course ⁠we are already flooded. What will happen if it rains again the next day? This is only the first day and ⁠we’re already overwhelmed,” said the woman.

“Two weeks ago when it rained, I swear to God, I spent four days sleeping on blankets spread on the floor because the rainwater had flooded the bedding. Same now, the mattresses are wet so we sleep on the ground.”

While the flooding devastated the people and families trapped by the blockade of life-saving aid and shelter, fresh ire was pointed at the US government for refusing to rebuke the Israeli government for its wanton disregard for human life and suffering.

On the ground in Gaza, the anguish of Palestinians, including children, was on display in videos of the devastation and ongoing catastrophe posted to social media :

🚨 CATASTROPHIC SCENES IN GAZA RIGHT NOW. Heavy rainfall is flooding displaced Palestinians’ tents, leaving families exposed to the harsh winter with no alternative shelter. This is their fourth winter since Israel destroyed their homes and continues to block essential… pic.twitter.com/NI7DRgCSMs

“How long are we supposed to live like this?” declares the young boy featured in the video. “I swear I don’t know what to do. Have mercy on us for God’s sake! For the sake of God, have mercy on us!”

Rain is worsening the suffering of Gaza’s children as water pours into homes damaged by Israeli bombardment, soaking bedding and clothes. With no shelter repair materials or tarpaulins available, families are left unable to protect their children from the flooding. pic.twitter.com/OzVMGHzssI

Children are particularly impacted by the rain water and vulnerable to the increasingly dangerous conditions imposed by the floods.

The image of a little girl in Gaza standing in the rain captures a stark, painful contrast: the innocence of childhood set against the harsh reality of life in Gaza. 🍉 The winter rain has transformed the scene into a tableau that blends spontaneous, childlike joy with profound… pic.twitter.com/YkTRt4RWJW

“What remains of Gaza’s homes is collapsing under heavy rain, amid the ongoing genocide and deafening silence,” said Ramy Abdul, chairman of the human rights groups Euro-Med Monitor.

“For the fourth consecutive year,” Abdul added, “Gaza remains under a suffocating Israeli siege that prevents even the recovery of victims’ bodies from beneath the rubble.”

items.summary: For a few very strange days this week, President Trump didn’t publicly acknowledge the Republican Party’s catastrophic losses in the midterm elections. Instead, the day after the election, he took journalists on a surprise tour of his under-construction White House ballroom where he only briefly answered an election-related question, about Vice President JD Vance’s assertion […] For a few very strange days this week, President Trump didn’t publicly acknowledge the Republican Party’s catastrop...

scraped.title: Trump enters the anger stage over the GOP's catastrophic loss
scraped.description: A wounded president turns to shock appointments, flimsy fraud allegations, and an AI-made video of UFC fighters beating up journalists.
scraped.author: Anna Merlan
scraped.h1: Trump Enters the Anger Stage Over GOP’s Catastrophic Losses
scraped.body_text:
White House ballroom construction site, Nov. 4, 2026 Daniel Torok/ZUMA

For a few very strange days this week, President Trump didn’t publicly acknowledge the Republican Party’s catastrophic losses in the midterm elections. Instead, the day after the election, he took journalists on a surprise tour of his under-construction White House ballroom where he only briefly answered an election-related question, about Vice President JD Vance’s assertion that the Iran war had hurt Republicans in the midterms. (“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” the president responded, adding: “At the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long-term it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”) But until this weekend, Trump had largely stayed away from reacting to the dismal GOP results, confining himself instead to important matters like complaining on TruthSocial about daylight saving time: “It’s so dark outside, so early (Sunset was 5:06 P.M., and it was dark by 5:31 P.M. — Isn’t that ridiculous?”

Now, however, there are signs that the president has exited the denial phase of the grieving process and entered the anger stage. First came his announcement that he’d tapped Stephen Miller , an anti-immigration extremist and the most noxious and widely disliked of his advisors, as his new chief of staff. And over the weekend, Trump has made a litany of posts on TruthSocial in which he seems to be trying out various responses to the election, to see what might stick.

On Saturday, Trump reposted several posts and graphs alleging that the Democratic wins across the country had been fraudulent, including one that falsely claimed, “Democrats materialized 20 million new votes.” He also demanded a Justice Department investigation into what he claimed were threats being made by the Democratic party “against innocent Republican Donors and Party Members,” adding, “The Senate must act, and stop being pushed around to the point of the Republican Party losing Elections, and Worse!” He also reposted several posts pushing back against calls for the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and reportedly told 60 Minutes , in an interview that will air on Sunday, that while he’ll be making a “few changes,” firing Hegseth won’t be one of them.

Apparently hungry for attention, Trump also tried to make a splash with another shock appointment, claiming that he’d offered the role of White House press secretary to UFC CEO Dana White , who he called “a violent Fighter and Warrior.” He further insisted White bring various UFC fighters with him. “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote. According to CNN, White speedily declined the job offer. But on Sunday morning, Trump shared an AI-generated cartoon of White and various UFC fighters beating up journalists in the White House press briefing room, and the Wall Street Journal reported that White will meet with Trump on Monday to discuss the potential role.

On Sunday morning, Trump complained that the economy would suffer without him, writing, “America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election — Even the Stock Market, which has been a ‘ROCKETSHIP’ under ‘TRUMP,’ took a one day, 3 Trillion Dollar loss. But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!” All of this served, at least in the short term, to get Trump the shock and attention he always seems to crave. But it was also clear that what he was really wants is validation. In announcing his 60 Minutes interview, he wrote, “Hopefully, they will show all the good things we’ve done over the past 2 years, not even including the First Term, which was incredible. If we get help from the Republican Senate, we can still do things that are unbelievable!”

While there’s no doubt that Trump will likely do several more “unbelievable” things before leaving office, more insults for his ego are likely on the way. As PBS recently reported , several of his controversial pet projects, including the ballroom, his gigantic triumphal arch, a proposed “National Garden of American Heroes” and a plan to remake a golf course in East Potomac will all soon be at risk, when Democrats take control of the House, Senate, and the appropriations process needed to fund them.

items.summary: This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. It is part of a series The Dream That Oil Built, which explores the connections between climate change, fossil fuels, and the American Dream.​ To Sierra Isley, the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The […] This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. It is part of a series The Dream ...

scraped.title: The American Dream is no match for climate change
scraped.description: Homeownership is billed as a way to build wealth. For many, it’s turning into a trap.
scraped.author: Kate Yoder
scraped.h1: The American Dream Is No Match for Climate Change
scraped.body_text:
Grist/Getty

This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. It is part of a series The Dream That Oil Built , which explores the connections between climate change, fossil fuels, and the American Dream.​

To Sierra Isley , the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The house in the suburbs is just what you’re taught growing up,” the 26-year-old said. “You know, that’s what you see on TV.” What she wanted for her life was a bit different from that picket-fence ideal, but she still saw the prospect of buying her first house two years ago as a chance to live out what she called “that big dream that everybody has as a kid.”

Isley and her girlfriend, Jamie, were moving from Philadelphia to Asheville, North Carolina, and found a home they liked, a three-bedroom brick house with lots of natural light and a big tree out front. With some help from their parents, they put down a deposit and got their offer accepted. But when they went to sign the closing papers, a complication got in the way: The house had a huge lien on it. After consulting with lawyers, they decided to break the contract and hunt for an apartment to rent in Asheville.

It was a blessing in disguise. One month later, while Sierra and Jamie were still unpacking boxes and building furniture, the remnants of Hurricane Helene turned Asheville into a disaster zone. The basement of their apartment flooded, but they were luckier than some of their neighbors, whose homes had been destroyed.

Owning a home has long been seen as a cornerstone of the American Dream—a way to build wealth that you could use one day to pay for your children’s education and fund your retirement. That arrangement was always more precarious than it was made out to be. But as fires and floods damage homes and drive up insurance rates, pouring your life savings into a house has become riskier than ever. In a report called “ Property Prices in Peril ,” the firm First Street projected last year that climate risks could knock nearly $1.5 trillion off the value of American homes by 2055. For some people, the sociologist Rebecca Elliott wrote , “the American dream of homeownership may become a nightmare.”

Americans are beginning to grasp the threat that climate change poses to their aspirations. According to exclusive polling for Grist from the think tank Data for Progress, 58 percent of likely US voters believe that climate change will hinder their ability to achieve the American Dream over the next 20 years, including 42 percent of Republicans. The survey suggests that people are worried that climate change will increase the cost of living, a concern so widespread that it may have swayed the midterm elections on Tuesday.

“Those homes could become, in effect, economically worthless even before they are physically uninhabitable”

The irony is that fossil fuels have long been promoted as necessary ingredients for the American “way of life.” Starting a century ago, oil and gas companies led extensive campaigns to tie their products to comfort and prosperity, a narrative that has been repeatedly deployed by politicians and oil industry executives to thwart climate action. President Donald Trump’s administration has often said that efforts to rein in fossil fuels threaten the American Dream. Earlier this year, when the administration scrapped Biden-era rules to cut emissions from cars, along with the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority to regulate climate change, it touted the effort as “ restoring the American Dream .”

But the fossil-fueled American Dream is in the process of destroying itself. Greenhouse gas emissions from burning coal, oil, and gas have ushered in a new period of precarity, undermining the promise that each generation can expect a better life than the last. Scientific reports warn that climate change “ imperil[s] the quality of life ” for communities in the United States, disrupting livelihoods and cultural traditions.

Either Americans decide to reimagine what makes up the American Dream and abandon that oil-soaked version of prosperity, or climate change will dismantle it for them .

The memories of living through Hurricane Helene are still fresh in Isley’s mind. Hauling water from their flooded basement up to the toilet to flush it when the water ran out. Driving to Jamie’s parents’ house in Atlanta, holed up in a room with both of their cats until they couldn’t take it anymore. Coming back to Asheville and cooking meals in the Crock-Pot with disposable liners because even when the water was running again, it wasn’t safe to wash dishes with.

Two years later, Isley browses Zillow for fun, but she looks at homes through a post-disaster lens. “Now I have that fear in the back of my mind—anywhere near a river, or even a stream, if there’s a little bit of water on the map, I’m like, ‘Oh, no,’” she said. Jamie is trans, and after Trump was elected in 2024, the two of them briefly entertained the idea of moving somewhere with more protective policies, like California. But Isley’s mind immediately went to wildfires. Out of the question.

Isley had fled from hurricanes before, when she lived in Florida during college. She thought she’d be safe from them tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville was supposed to be a “ climate haven ,” somewhere that would fare better than the rest of the country as the world warmed. Those promises were shattered when almost 14 inches of rain fell on Asheville over three days in September 2024. The French Broad River overflowed its banks, flooding homes and destroying parts of the town’s River Arts District. In western North Carolina, more than 74,000 homes were damaged, and only about 4 percent had flood insurance, resulting in $9.5 billion in uninsured residential property losses.

Home values in western North Carolina have declined since the storm , especially in the hardest-hit counties. Asheville’s average home price shrunk 5 percent over the past year, while the national average increased 1.2 percent.

“We are, for a lot of people, on the edge of a dysfunctional insurance marketplace.”

To some degree, housing markets are already pricing in the risk of increased environmental hazards. Homes within FEMA’s high-risk flood zones sell for 2.8 percent less , on average, than what they would otherwise sell for, according to a 2023 study published in the journal Nature Climate Change. The researchers found that homes exposed to flood risk were still overvalued by between $121 billion and $237 billion, though—and they identified Appalachia as a hot spot of overvaluation, one year before Helene hit. The devaluation of homes in high-risk zones is unfolding unevenly and causing “tremendous social harm,” said Elliott, a sociology professor at The London School of Economics and Political Science.

Homes are billed as a way for people to build wealth, but they can turn into a trap. After Superstorm Sandy devastated New York City and the New Jersey coast in 2012, many homeowners couldn’t sell their houses for enough money to buy a new place, leaving them stranded . Even homes that haven’t seen any kind of devastation are at risk of losing value as more people become wary of living in floodplains, coastal places exposed to storms, and wildfire-prone areas. “Those homes could become, in effect, economically worthless even before they are physically uninhabitable,” Elliott wrote in a study about property values and climate change .

Insurance is meant to offer a measure of safety when taking on a huge debt for a mortgage on a house. Douglas Heller, the director of insurance at the Consumer Federation of America, called it “the safety net for the American Dream.” But insurance rates are part of what’s making homeownership unaffordable for so many. Since 2020, property insurance costs have ballooned almost 80 percent , with the average single-family mortgage holder now paying $209 per month. Homeowners in the riskiest areas are paying substantially more , and many in California have been dropped by their insurers . Home insurance rates are rising faster in the Midwest than any other region, driven by the costs of severe storms.

“We are, for a lot of people, on the edge of a dysfunctional insurance marketplace,” Heller said. The more extreme weather we’re seeing is only part of the story: He argues that the insurance industry has become a “climate opportunist,” using climate change as an excuse to justify excessive rate increases.

People relying on Social Security benefits who own condos around Lake Tahoe are particularly vulnerable to rising rates, said Andrew Engler, the founder and CEO of Rock Rose Risk, who helps people in California protect their homes against wildfire and get their insurance premiums down. They’re facing ballooning homeowners association payments, to share the cost of insurance in a risky wildfire area, on a limited paycheck. If they try to move, their properties are worth significantly less because of the huge HOA bills, Engler said. Economists estimate that rising insurance costs linked to disaster risk have reduced the growth of home prices by more than $40,000 in the most hurricane- and wildfire-prone zip codes.

Renting might make you more nimble, but it doesn’t insulate you from these costs. One reason rents are going up is because landlords’ property insurance rates are increasing . “Whether you are a homeowner or a renter, we’re all paying for living under the increased risks of climate change,” said Caroline Nagy, the associate director of housing policy at Americans for Financial Reform. That makes it harder for people to save for a home—if that’s even a good idea anymore.

When Sierra Isley walks around her neighborhood these days, she sees the evidence of Helene all around her—in the form of banners with the slogan “Asheville Strong” and shirts that say “WNC Strong.”

One of the most surprising things about disasters might be the way that people who live through them rise to the occasion and come together . In the aftermath of the Helene, with the power and cell service knocked out, Sierra and Jamie walked all around town, talking to their neighbors to try to learn what had happened. People started congregating at the fire station where there was fresh water.

“It’s hard to put into words what that experience was like, but I’ve never felt more of a community, and really having to lean on my neighbors and feeling like my neighbors were leaning on me,” Isley said.

“I owe it to people like me, in other rural communities, to use my skills to help combat climate change and natural disasters”

While the American Dream is usually all about independence and personal freedom, living through a disaster has a way of revealing how people depend on each other. The experience can prompt people to hold tightly to what they have, doubling down on protecting their communities, said Nick Tinoco, a sociology researcher in a doctoral program at the University of California, Los Angeles, who interviewed survivors of the 2018 Woolsey Fire in Los Angeles County. Some of the residents he talked to have taken things into their own hands and organized volunteer fire brigades, and plan to stay behind to defend their neighborhoods during future fires.

As supposedly safe “climate havens” like Asheville experience more disasters, the idea that people can simply move out of harm’s way is losing its grip. “I think we have to just reckon with the fact that we’re going to have to make people secure in the places that they live,” Elliott said.

She thinks it’s time to rethink the bargain of the American Dream—the expectation that so much of a person’s economic future depends on the fate of a single structure. Many young people have begun to define success differently. A poll from Ipsos last year showed that 46 percent of baby boomers associate homeownership with the American Dream, but only 13 percent of Gen Zers do, suggesting that there’s room for its defining features to change.

Sierra and Jamie couldn’t help but wonder what happened to the house they’d almost bought, and they drove over to check it out soon after Hurricane Helene hit. It was still standing, but they couldn’t see if there was any damage hidden inside. “Who knows if it flooded or anything like that, what kind of storm damage it took, and that would have immediately been our problem,” Isley said.

Living through Hurricane Helene didn’t just make Isley relieved she hadn’t bought a house in Asheville. It has shaped what she wants for her life, helping her discover a passion for public health and pushing her to want to work in emergency preparedness. Now she’s applying to schools to pursue a master’s degree in public health.

“I think I owe it to people like me, people in other rural communities who are going to face the same kind of climate change emergencies, to use my skills to help combat climate change and natural disasters,” Isley said. “I just feel such a calling.”

scraped.title: Trump just offered the press secretary gig to UFC's Dana White
scraped.description: The president praised him as a “violent Fighter and Warrior.”
scraped.author: Sophie Hurwitz
scraped.h1: Trump Just Offered the Press Secretary Gig to UFC’s Dana White
scraped.body_text:
Dana White's "violent" nature makes him a good candidate for press secretary, per Trump. Alex Brandon/AP

President Donald Trump wants Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White to be the White House press secretary, he announced Saturday.

“The Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . He also asked White to bring various muscle-bound prizefighters to the White House as assistants, presumably so that if a journalist asks a tough question, those prizefighters could then put them in a headlock.

“I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris,” Trump wrote, misspelling the name of UFC fighter Kayla Harrison. “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left.”

White, who has no fighting record or governmental record, has owned UFC since 2001. If he accepts the job, he would be Trump’s seventh press secretary, replacing Katie Zacharia, who lasted just under a week on the job before being fired by Trump on October 19th.

It is unclear how White’s potential position in the federal government would impact his other roles, such as co-leader of Zuffa Boxing, a joint venture with the head of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority. But it would not be Trump’s first collaboration with this magnate of the combat arts. In June, White’s company built a tarantula-like stage on the White House lawn to host a birthday cage fight for the President. (“ It will never happen again ,” White said afterwards.)

Beyond that, “the UFC and Dana White arguably helped Trump get elected,” as Kyle Green, a sociologist at SUNY Brockport who writes on the intersection of sports and politics, told my colleague Inae Oh in June. “They put him in contact with Joe Rogan, who puts him in contact with all the other podcast bros. That really helped Trump, especially in the last election.” Likewise, Green said, the UFC can attribute much of its newfound mainstream popularity to having a fan in the White House.

“Dana, please take the job!” Trump wrote Saturday. It is not known as of this writing whether White has accepted the position.
